questions.prompt: A logistics firm's managed instance shows storage at 96 percent used while CPU stays around 20 percent all day. The operations lead wants to add vCores to fix the storage warning. What is the best response?
choices: Add vCores, since more processing power will free up disk space
Ignore the warning, since low CPU means the instance has spare capacity for growth
Increase the storage size, because the saturated resource is storage and vCores do not add disk space
Move the instance to an instance pool so storage is shared with other instances
questions.why: Storage is set separately from compute, so the saturated resource (storage) needs a storage increase, and adding vCores does not add disk space.

questions.prompt: A retail company runs General Purpose on its managed instance. Its nightly analytics reports slow down order processing because both compete for the same primary. The team wants reports to run without touching the primary's capacity. Which service tier should they choose?
choices: General Purpose with more vCores, because extra compute gives reports their own capacity
Business Critical, because it offers a read-only secondary replica that reports can use
General Purpose with additional storage, because storage separates reports from orders
An instance pool, because pooled vCores isolate reporting from the primary
questions.why: Only Business Critical provides a read-only secondary replica, which lets reporting queries run off the primary instead of competing with orders.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between raising the vCore count and changing the service tier for a managed instance that is slow in the evenings. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by checking which resource is saturated. If CPU is pinned at the evening peak while storage has room, the bottleneck is compute, so I would raise vCores first. Raising vCores costs more each month and the change ends with a brief failover, so connections drop for a few seconds, and the application needs retry logic and a quiet window to do it safely. If reporting queries are what compete with orders, I would look at the service tier instead, because Business Critical offers a read-only secondary replica that takes reporting load off the primary. That option costs more than General Purpose and only exists in that tier, so I would only choose it if reads are the real problem. Storage size should be changed only when the data is actually filling the disk, since extra storage alone does not make queries run faster.
rubricPoints: Identifies which resource (CPU, storage, or read load) is the actual bottleneck before changing anything
Explains that vCores add compute while storage size adds only disk space
Names the brief failover or connection drop that scaling operations cause, and the need for retries
Notes that a read-only secondary replica is available in Business Critical, not General Purpose

suggested.rationale: Choosing a tier and size from a scenario is best learned by reasoning through an exam-style situation, and no listed mission covers Managed Instance sizing.

lessons.plain: SQL Server on an Azure virtual machine means you rent a computer in Microsoft's cloud and install the SQL Server database software on it yourself, so you control the operating system and the database. Making it fast and able to grow depends mostly on three choices: how big the computer is (its processors and memory), how fast its disks are, and how the database files are laid out across those disks. A slow database is often a slow disk or a poorly set memory limit rather than a slow query. This lesson covers those choices so you can pick a setup that fits a workload before anything is built.
lessons.guessPrompt: A SQL Server on a cloud VM is slow during busy hours. Before looking at any settings, which would you suspect first: the number of processor cores, the speed of the disks, or the query text? Why?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A virtual machine (VM) is a computer simulated inside a cloud data centre. Its size sets how many processor cores (vCPUs) and how much memory it has, and it also sets a ceiling on how much disk traffic it can push. A managed disk is a network-attached virtual disk that the cloud provider maintains for you; premium SSD is a faster tier of that. Throughput is data moved per second, measured in megabytes per second. IOPS is the number of separate read or write operations per second. Latency is the wait time for one operation.

Why it works: a database reads and writes files constantly, so its speed is capped by the slowest link on the path. The VM has its own ceiling and each disk has its own ceiling, and the effective limit is the lower of the two. SQL Server also has three hot spots: data files (mostly random reads and writes), the transaction log (small sequential writes where every commit waits for confirmation), and tempdb (scratch space for sorting and temporary results). Separate disks keep these from competing, and the log disk is where latency matters most.

Worked example: a VM size allows 400 MB/s of disk throughput, and the attached data disks together could deliver 600 MB/s. The ceiling is 400 MB/s, so adding disk does nothing; the fix is a larger VM size. If instead the VM allows 800 MB/s and the disks total 300 MB/s, the disks are the bottleneck, and adding a disk to a striped storage pool raises the total.

Common mistake: choosing disks by capacity alone, and leaving the SQL Server maximum memory setting unlimited so the operating system starves. Consequence: commits slow down across every application that writes, because each commit waits on the log disk.

The layout is part of the configuration: a VM sized for the memory and throughput the workload needs, separate disks for data, log and tempdb, and a memory cap that leaves room for the operating system.

questions.prompt: A payments firm, Corvane Ledger, runs SQL Server on a VM whose size allows 520 MB/s of disk throughput. Its four premium data disks together can deliver 310 MB/s. Step 1: the VM sets a ceiling of 520 MB/s. Step 2: the disks set a ceiling of 310 MB/s. Step 3: the effective limit is the lower of the two, which is 310 MB/s. Step 4 is missing: decide which resource is the bottleneck and what the sensible next change is.
choices: Neither resource limits throughput; the effective limit is the sum of the two ceilings, 830 MB/s, so there is headroom.
Throughput depends only on total disk capacity in terabytes, so count the capacity and ignore the figures above.
The VM is the bottleneck because 520 is the larger number, so resize the VM first.
The disks are the bottleneck, so add disks or move to a faster disk tier; resizing the VM will not help because its 520 MB/s ceiling is not reached.
questions.why: The effective limit is 310 MB/s, which comes from the disks, and the VM's 520 MB/s ceiling is not being reached, so only more disk throughput raises the limit.

questions.prompt: A 32 GB VM runs SQL Server for a small clinic. The SQL Server maximum memory setting is left at its unlimited default. What is the most likely result?
choices: The disks become faster because memory is freed up for caching.
Commits become faster because the transaction log is cached in memory.
Nothing changes, because the memory setting only affects tempdb.
The operating system is starved of memory and the whole server slows down.
questions.why: Leaving SQL Server's memory unlimited can let it take nearly all RAM, which starves the operating system, so a cap should leave room for it.

questions.prompt: Halden Freight's SQL Server VM keeps its transaction log and its data files on one shared disk, and commits are slow. Which change best addresses the cause?
choices: Put tempdb on the same disk so scratch work is grouped with the other files.
Give the transaction log its own disk, since small sequential log writes wait on that disk and should not compete with data-file reads.
Turn off the transaction log and rely on the data files for recovery.
Add more capacity to the shared disk so there is more room for writes.
questions.why: The log is the most latency-sensitive file because every commit waits on it, so separating it from data-file traffic protects commit speed.

questions.prompt: A nightly job on a VM reads a few very large files one after another. Which measure should you watch most closely to judge whether the storage is keeping up?
choices: Throughput in megabytes per second
The latency of the log disk alone
The count of separate IOPS operations
Total disk capacity in terabytes
questions.why: Reading large files in sequence is limited by how much data moves per second, which is throughput, rather than by the count of small operations.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why adding more disks to a SQL Server VM may not make it faster, and name one limit of the change you would try first.
lessons.modelAnswer: Adding disks only helps if the disks are the bottleneck. Every VM size has its own cap on disk throughput, and every disk has its own cap too, so the real ceiling is the lower of the two. If the VM is already at its cap, more disks change nothing, and the fix is a larger VM size. I would first check the VM's throughput limit against the total the disks can deliver, and look at log write latency, since commits wait on it. The limit of a bigger VM is cost: it is billed continuously, so I would confirm the bottleneck with measurements before resizing, and I would also check that the memory cap still leaves room for the operating system.
rubricPoints: A VM size and each disk have their own throughput ceilings, and the lower one limits the total.
Adding disks helps only when the disks are the bottleneck, not when the VM cap is.
The transaction log is latency-sensitive and usually kept on its own disk.
The first change should be confirmed by measurement, and it carries a cost or tradeoff.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a VM size and disk layout under stated limits is a judgement call best practised as an exam-style scenario, and no listed mission covers it.

lessons.plain: Table partitioning means splitting one large table into smaller pieces, called partitions, based on the value of one column, such as a date. Each row lands in exactly one piece, but queries still see the whole table. This helps when old data must be removed quickly, or when a query only needs one slice of the data. Think of a filing cabinet with one drawer per year: it is still one cabinet, but you can pull out a whole year's drawer at once instead of searching every folder. Setting it up means choosing the split column and the cut points, and that is what this lesson covers.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sales table holds five years of rows, but most reports only look at the current month. Before reading anything, what would you guess the benefit of splitting the table by sale date would be, and what would you expect it to cost?
lessons.teach:
Three named pieces make up a partitioned table. A partition function is the rule that cuts the values of one column into ranges. You give it boundary values, such as 1 January 2023 and 1 January 2024, and each boundary creates a cut point. A partition scheme maps the resulting partitions to storage locations; in SQL Server these are filegroups, while in Azure SQL Database the usual choice is the PRIMARY filegroup. The partitioning column is the column whose value decides which partition each row goes into.

The table is created on the partition scheme, and the partitioning column must be part of its clustered index. This works because the engine stores each partition's rows separately. It can skip partitions a query does not need, and it can move a whole partition in or out using a metadata operation called switching, rather than deleting millions of rows one at a time.

Boundary direction matters. With RANGE RIGHT, a boundary value belongs to the partition on its right. Take boundaries 2023-01-01 and 2024-01-01 with RANGE RIGHT. That gives three partitions: before 2023-01-01; from 2023-01-01 up to but not including 2024-01-01; and from 2024-01-01 onward. Trace a row dated 2023-06-15. It is not earlier than 2023-01-01 and it is earlier than 2024-01-01, so it lands in the middle partition.

The common mistake is expecting speed without filtering. If a query has no condition on the partitioning column, every partition is still read. Filter on that column so the engine can eliminate partitions. In a running system, a poorly chosen column or many tiny partitions makes maintenance slower and adds index work, so check the query plan after you change the layout.

Partitioning is a layout decision for performance and data management, not a substitute for backups.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Logistics stores a shipments table partitioned on ship_date, using a partition function with RANGE RIGHT and boundary values 2022-04-01 and 2022-07-01, which produces three partitions. Trace a shipment dated 2022-04-01. Step 1: the date is not earlier than 2022-04-01, so it cannot be in the first partition. Step 2: the date is earlier than 2022-07-01, so it cannot be in the last partition. Step 3, which you complete: state which partition the row lands in and the range of dates that partition covers.
choices: The middle partition, which holds dates from 2022-04-01 up to but not including 2022-07-01
The partition to the left of 2022-04-01, because a boundary value stays with the earlier range
The first partition, which holds every date before 2022-04-01
The last partition, which holds every date from 2022-07-01 onward
questions.why: With RANGE RIGHT a boundary value belongs to the partition on its right, so a row dated exactly 2022-04-01 sits in the middle partition, which starts at that boundary and ends before the next one.

questions.prompt: In a partitioned table, which named piece is the rule that cuts the values of one column into ranges by using boundary values?
choices: The partition function, which defines the cut points
The partition scheme, which maps partitions to storage
The partitioning column, which is the column being tested
The clustered index, which orders the stored rows
questions.why: The partition function is the rule that turns boundary values into cut points for the column's value ranges; the scheme maps partitions to storage and the column is only the input.

questions.prompt: A customer-orders table is partitioned by order_date. A report query filters only on customer_id and has no condition on order_date. What does the engine do?
choices: It reads only the partition holding the most recent orders
It reads only the partitions where customer_id values are stored
It fails with an error until a condition on order_date is added
It reads every partition, because no filter on the partitioning column lets it skip any
questions.why: Partition elimination depends on a filter on the partitioning column; without one, the engine has no basis to skip partitions and must read them all.

questions.prompt: A team needs to remove a full year of old log rows from a partitioned table, and the rows sit in one partition. Which approach fits best?
choices: Add a nonclustered index on the date column and rerun the delete
Switch the old partition out as a metadata operation
Take a full backup, then drop and recreate the table
Delete rows in small batches over several nights
questions.why: Switching moves a whole partition out using a metadata operation, avoiding the slow row-by-row deletes and the log growth that come with them.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says partitioning our orders table by order date will make all reports faster. Explain to them, in your own words, what partitioning actually changes, and name one limit or tradeoff they should weigh before agreeing.
lessons.modelAnswer: Partitioning splits one logical table into several physical pieces based on a column, usually a date. A partition function holds the cut points and a partition scheme says where the pieces are stored. Queries still see one table, so the application does not change, but the engine can skip pieces a query does not need when the query filters on that column. The real wins are that old months can be switched out quickly and that maintenance can target a single partition. The limit is that it only helps when queries filter on the partitioning column. A report that ignores the date still reads every partition. There is also a cost: the partitioning column must be part of the clustered index, and boundaries need ongoing care as new periods arrive. So I would check our report filters and the query plan before promising faster reports.
rubricPoints: Partitioning divides one table into pieces by a column's value while queries still address the whole table
The speed gain comes from partition elimination, which needs filters on the partitioning column
Fast removal of old data through switching or partition-level maintenance is a real benefit
Tradeoffs include clustered index requirements and ongoing boundary management

suggested.rationale: A planned SQL lab would let the learner build a partitioned table and see partition elimination in a query plan, which reading alone cannot show.

lessons.plain: Data compression means storing the same information in fewer bytes. A database whose tables are smaller reads less from disk, keeps more of its data in memory, and often answers queries faster, at the cost of extra processor work to pack and unpack the data. Configuring compression means choosing which tables or indexes to shrink and how hard to squeeze them. Think of packing a suitcase: folding clothes tightly fits more in, but you spend time folding and unfolding every time you need something. The skill is picking the places where the saving is large and the extra effort is small.
lessons.guessPrompt: A table takes 10 GB on disk, and most of its rows repeat the same few city names and status codes. Before any teaching, guess: would compressing this table save space, cost processor time, or both, and why?
lessons.teach:
Data compression means storing the same rows in fewer bytes. In SQL Server and the Azure SQL services, you choose compression per table, index, or partition. Row compression changes how each row is stored: fixed-width columns such as integers and fixed-length character types take only the space their actual values need. Page compression does that too, and also looks across a whole 8 KB page for repeated values, storing a shared prefix and a small dictionary of common values once per page. Columnstore indexes are a different, column-oriented layout that already compresses heavily and is the usual choice for analytics. Why it works: fewer pages means fewer reads, and the buffer pool (the memory area that caches data pages) can hold more of your data. The price is CPU, because every read and write must compress or decompress the data.

Worked example: a table named orders holds 10 million rows and occupies 4 GB. You run the estimate procedure for PAGE compression. It samples the table and projects 1.6 GB. You rebuild the table with DATA_COMPRESSION set to PAGE. The rebuild writes new pages, the old pages are freed, and the table now occupies about 1.6 GB with the same rows and the same queries.

Common mistake: turning on PAGE compression everywhere without measuring. Tables with heavy random updates or little repetition gain little, yet CPU use rises. Consequence in a running system: on a server that is already CPU-bound, compression can slow queries, and a large offline rebuild can block users or consume a lot of transaction log space unless an online rebuild is available and used.

Compression trades CPU for space and I/O, so measure first and compress selectively.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm keeps a table named shipment_events with 50 million rows that occupies 9 GB. An engineer runs the PAGE compression estimate, which projects 3.6 GB. The server's CPU already sits near 90 percent at peak hours. The engineer's plan has three steps: step 1 is running the estimate, step 2 is checking CPU headroom, and step 3 is missing. Which missing step completes a sound plan?
choices: Compress every table on the server with PAGE so the savings are as large as possible before anyone checks the CPU again.
Rebuild the table with PAGE compression in a low-traffic window, using an online rebuild if available, then compare CPU use and table size afterward.
Abandon compression altogether, because a CPU-bound server means any compression will slow queries and no measurement is needed.
Rebuild the table with PAGE compression immediately during the peak afternoon shift using a standard offline rebuild, since the savings are already proven.
questions.why: Compression adds CPU work, so a sound plan applies it in a window that protects users, then checks the real CPU and size effects instead of assuming them.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts row compression with page compression?
choices: Row compression is a column-oriented layout used for analytics, while page compression stores each row separately with no sharing between rows at all.
Row compression removes all CPU cost from reads and writes, while page compression always doubles the CPU use of every query on the table.
Page compression keeps row-level storage and also finds repeated values across an 8 KB page, storing a shared prefix and a small per-page dictionary.
Both settings store every row at a fixed width regardless of the actual value length, so the only difference is which pages are touched.
questions.why: Page compression builds on row compression by additionally sharing common prefixes and dictionary values across a whole page, which the other choices misdescribe.

questions.prompt: A data warehouse holds a 3 TB fact table of sales lines. Large aggregate queries scan it every night, and rows are rarely updated one at a time. Which layout is the usual fit?
choices: No compression at all, because aggregate scans only read data and so gain nothing from smaller storage anywhere in the system.
Row compression on the table with no index at all, to keep the layout simple.
A columnstore index, a column-oriented layout for analytics.
Page compression rebuilt every hour during business hours so the table stays small.
questions.why: Columnstore stores data by column, already compresses heavily, and suits large analytic scans, which is the usage pattern the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: A 2 TB table receives heavy random updates across its rows. The PAGE estimate projects only 4 percent savings. Which decision follows from the teaching text?
choices: Switch the table to a columnstore index, since columnstore always gives the best write performance for random updates.
Compress only the nonclustered indexes and leave the table alone, because the estimate applies only to index pages.
Keep the current layout, or accept the small gain only after weighing the added CPU cost, since little repetition means little benefit.
Apply PAGE anyway, because any reduction in size is worth the cost.
questions.why: The teaching text says tables with heavy random updates and little repetition gain little while CPU use rises, so the small projected saving does not justify the cost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what data compression does to a SQL table, when you would choose page compression over row compression, and one real cost you must weigh before turning it on.
lessons.modelAnswer: Compression stores the same rows in fewer bytes by changing the physical layout of a table, index, or partition. Row compression shrinks fixed-width columns so they use only the space their values need. Page compression goes further: within each 8 KB page it stores repeated prefixes and common values once, so it suits tables with many repeated values, such as status codes or city names. I would choose page over row when the estimate shows a meaningful saving and the workload is read-heavy. The main cost is CPU, since every read and write must compress or decompress data. On a server already short of processor capacity, that can slow queries. Rebuilding a large table to apply compression also takes time and log space, so I would estimate savings first and compress selectively.
rubricPoints: Compression stores the same rows in fewer bytes per table, index, or partition.
Row compression shrinks fixed-width column storage; page compression adds prefix and dictionary compression within each page.
The benefit is less I/O and more data cached in memory, and the cost is extra CPU.
Estimate savings first, apply compression selectively, and account for the rebuild cost.

suggested.rationale: Estimating savings and rebuilding a table with a chosen compression setting is hands-on SQL work that a planned SQL lab would cover best.

lessons.plain: Before you move a database to the cloud, you have to write down what the move must achieve and what the existing system depends on. Evaluating requirements means answering questions first: how much downtime the business can tolerate, how large the data is, which database features the application relies on, how fast the network between the old and new locations is, and what skills the team already has. The answers narrow the field to a few realistic destinations and a few ways of copying the data. Someone who skips this step often picks the service they know best, then discovers in production that a feature is missing or that the switch-over takes a whole weekend.
lessons.guessPrompt: A business database must be unavailable for no more than two hours during a weekend window, and it runs a nightly job that calls a second server. Before you read on, which two facts about this system would you check before choosing where it should go, and why?
lessons.teach:
A migration requirements review turns a vague goal, such as 'move our database to Azure', into a short list of facts that decide the design. Start with the source: the version and edition of the database engine, the size of the data, and the features in use. Features matter most when they live outside the ordinary tables. A scheduled job that runs inside the server, a link to another server, or a query that reads from several databases at once are common surprises, because targets support these features to different degrees.

Next, the target options differ mainly in how much of the old server environment they keep. A managed single-database service gives you the least to run but supports the fewest server-level features. A managed instance, which is a managed server rather than a single database, keeps most instance-level behaviour, so it suits applications that depend on those features. A virtual machine running SQL Server gives the widest compatibility, but you still patch the operating system and manage backups yourself.

Then choose the copy method by downtime tolerance. An offline migration stops writes to the source, copies the data, and switches the application over; it is simple, but the outage is real. An online migration keeps replicating changes while the source stays live, then performs a short cutover, meaning the moment traffic is redirected to the new system. Data volume and network bandwidth determine how long the first copy and the catch-up take.

Worked example: a 400 GB database must be down for no more than 30 minutes and runs an agent job, a scheduled job inside the server, that calls an external server. Step one: the agent job rules out a single-database target unless the job is moved elsewhere. Step two: copying 400 GB offline over a slow link will exceed 30 minutes, so an online approach is required. Step three: a managed instance with an online copy fits, provided the bandwidth check passes.

Common mistake: choosing the target before listing the dependencies, then finding the gap during cutover. The consequence is serious, because a failed cutover can leave the application pointing at a half-loaded database, so the rollback plan belongs in the requirements, not after them.

questions.prompt: A regional bank has a 250 GB customer database that must be unavailable for no more than 4 hours during its weekend maintenance window. The database runs a server-level scheduled job that emails a nightly summary, and one report query reads from two databases at once. The link between the on-premises network and Azure carries 1 Gbps, so copying 250 GB takes roughly 35 minutes. Step one: the scheduled job and the cross-database query both rule out a single-database target unless they are redesigned, so a managed instance is the candidate. Step two: [missing]. Step three: the rollback plan is written down before the weekend, so a failed cutover can be reversed.
choices: Online copy is required, because cross-database queries need continuous replication to keep the two databases consistent during the copy.
Offline copy is acceptable, because the first copy finishes well inside the 4-hour window and the scheduled job can run on a single-database target.
Online copy is required, because any outage at all breaks the rule and continuous replication is the only safe option.
Offline copy is acceptable, because the first copy finishes well inside the 4-hour window, so the copy method is settled without a downtime comparison.
questions.why: The copy method is chosen by comparing the estimated copy time against the downtime tolerance, and 35 minutes fits inside 4 hours, so an offline copy is acceptable.

questions.prompt: In the migration requirements sense, what is a cutover?
choices: The step where a scheduled job on the source server is copied to the target.
The measurement of how much bandwidth the network link provides during the first copy.
The nightly process that backs up the source database before any data is moved.
The final step of an online migration, where traffic is redirected from the source to the new system.
questions.why: The teaching text defines cutover as the moment traffic is redirected to the new system, which is the short final step of an online migration.

questions.prompt: A team wants to move an application that depends on a server-level scheduled job to a single-database target because it is the cheapest managed option, and they plan to discover the job's dependency during cutover. What is the main risk of this approach?
choices: The single-database target will automatically convert the job into a cross-database query, which slows the application.
The dependency gap appears only at cutover, when a failed switch can leave the application pointing at a half-loaded database.
The migration will take longer because the single-database target needs more bandwidth than the source server.
The copy method will switch from offline to online without the team noticing, causing a data mismatch.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that choosing a target before listing dependencies leads to finding gaps at cutover, which can leave the application pointing at a half-loaded database.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm must move a 60 GB shipment-tracking database to Azure with no more than 10 minutes of downtime. The link to Azure carries 50 Mbps. Which copy method fits the requirement, and why?
choices: An offline copy, because the outage can be shortened by simply copying faster between servers on the same network.
An online copy, because an offline copy of 60 GB over 50 Mbps would take far longer than 10 minutes.
An offline copy, because 60 GB is small enough that the first copy finishes within 10 minutes.
An online copy, because the 10-minute limit is only met when changes are replicated before the source is stopped.
questions.why: At 50 Mbps, 60 GB needs roughly 2.7 hours, which far exceeds 10 minutes, so an online copy that replicates changes while the source stays live is required.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should just move the database onto a virtual machine, since that is the safest choice. Explain to them how you would evaluate the migration requirements first, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would recommend.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not decide on a target yet. First I would list the facts: database size, engine version, downtime the business allows, and any server-level features the application uses, such as scheduled jobs, linked servers or cross-database queries. Those facts narrow the options. A virtual machine gives the widest compatibility, so it is a reasonable choice if we rely on many server features, but we would then own the operating system patching, backups and high availability ourselves, which costs ongoing effort. If the downtime window is short, I would also check whether an online copy is needed and whether our network bandwidth can finish the initial copy and catch-up in time. My recommendation is the option that meets the listed requirements with the least operational burden, and I would confirm the rollback plan before we commit.
rubricPoints: Lists requirements such as downtime tolerance, data size, and server-level dependencies before choosing a target.
Distinguishes what each target keeps from the old environment and what the team must still operate.
Connects downtime tolerance to offline versus online copy methods.
Names a concrete tradeoff, such as compatibility versus operational effort, and includes a rollback check.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission covers migration requirements, and reasoning through an exam-style scenario with competing constraints adds the most practice here.

lessons.plain: Moving a database to a new home is like moving a shop to a new building. You can close for a day, carry everything across, and reopen, or you can keep trading while staff copy each new order to the new building until the moment you switch over. The first approach is an offline migration: the source stops accepting changes during the copy, so users see downtime. The second is an online migration: the copy keeps running and new changes are streamed across, so downtime is only the brief switch. Choosing between them is a tradeoff between how much downtime the business tolerates and how much extra effort and risk you accept to avoid it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A reporting database can be unavailable for two hours on a Sunday night, but a payments database cannot be down for more than a minute. Before any teaching, which one would you expect to move offline and which online, and what single reason would you give?
lessons.teach:
An offline migration stops writes to the source database, copies all of its data to the target, verifies it, and then points applications at the target. Downtime is the whole time from the stop to the switch. An online migration does an initial full copy while the source stays live, captures every change made after the copy started, replays those changes to the target, and only stops writes briefly at the end, once the backlog of changes is nearly empty. That last gap between the source and target is called replication lag, and the final switch is called cutover.

Worked example. A database of 500 GB takes about six hours to copy. Offline: stop writes at 22:00, copy until 04:00, verify, and switch at about 04:30. Downtime is roughly six and a half hours. Online: start the copy at 22:00 while the source keeps serving users. Changes made during those hours are captured and applied to the target. At 04:00 the lag is only a few hundred changes. Stop writes for about two minutes, let the last changes drain, verify, and switch. Downtime is about two minutes.

Common mistake: treating online as having no downtime, or cutting over while lag is still large. If you switch with a big backlog, the newest orders exist only on the old database and are lost from the new one. Managed migration services such as Azure Database Migration Service offer both modes, but the same reasoning applies whichever tool you use.

The choice is decided by the downtime the business accepts, not by which mode is more impressive. Offline is simpler and cheaper when a maintenance window exists; online is needed when downtime must be minutes.

questions.prompt: A clinic booking database of 120 GB takes about two hours to copy to a new server. The clinic accepts at most 30 minutes of downtime on a Sunday night. Step 1: an offline migration needs about two hours to copy plus roughly fifteen minutes to verify, so downtime would be about two hours fifteen minutes. Step 2: that is far over the 30-minute limit. Step 3 is missing. What should the team choose next?
choices: Use offline but skip verification to fit the window
Use offline anyway, since it is simpler
Cut over right after the first copy, because the copy is already done
Use online: copy while the source stays live, then pause writes briefly
questions.why: Because the accepted downtime is far below what an offline copy needs, an online migration that keeps the source live during the copy and pauses writes only briefly at the end is the approach that fits.

questions.prompt: In an online migration, what does replication lag measure?
choices: The gap between changes made on the source and changes already applied to the target
The number of users connected to the source during the copy
The size of the initial full copy in gigabytes
The total downtime from stopping writes to switching applications
questions.why: Replication lag is the amount of source change the target has not yet received, which is the gap between the two databases.

questions.prompt: A 2 TB orders database must be migrated, and the business allows no more than 5 minutes of downtime. Which approach fits?
choices: Offline migration during the nightly maintenance window
Offline migration, with the copy run during the business day
Online migration, but cut over as soon as the initial copy starts
Online migration: copy while the source is live, replay captured changes, then pause writes briefly for cutover
questions.why: Only an online approach keeps downtime to minutes, because the bulk copy happens while the source stays live and writes stop only briefly at the end.

questions.prompt: A team cuts over to the new database while replication lag is still around 40,000 changes. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The source database is deleted during cutover
Nothing, because a lag count does not affect the data
The migration becomes offline and the cutover is rolled back automatically
Recent changes exist only on the old database and are missing from the new one
questions.why: Switching with a large backlog leaves the newest changes stranded on the source, so the new database lacks them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, when you would choose an offline migration over an online one, and name one limit or tradeoff of the online approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would pick an offline migration when the business can accept a planned maintenance window, because it is simpler: stop writes, copy, verify, switch. Its cost is downtime equal to the whole copy time, so for a large database that can be hours. An online migration takes a full copy while the source stays live, then captures and replays the changes made during that copy until the target is nearly caught up. Only a short final cutover needs writes stopped. The tradeoff is that online needs more setup, a steady way to capture changes, enough bandwidth to keep up with the write rate, and a check that replication lag is near zero before switching. If the source generates changes faster than the copy can apply them, the lag never shrinks and the cutover never becomes safe. So I would confirm the write rate and lag before promising a short outage.
rubricPoints: Offline migration stops writes and has downtime equal to the full copy and verification time
Online migration keeps the source live and replays captured changes so downtime is only the cutover
Cutover should wait until replication lag is near zero to avoid losing recent changes
Online migration needs a change-capture mechanism and enough throughput to outpace the write rate

suggested.rationale: Choosing between offline and online for a given downtime limit is an exam-style reasoning task that benefits most from working through scenarios, and no listed mission covers migration strategy.

lessons.plain: Moving a database from one place to another usually means stopping the application, copying the data, and starting again. An online migration avoids most of that stop. You copy the bulk of the data while the original database keeps serving users, then capture the changes made during the copy and apply them to the new database. When the two are nearly identical, you make a short switch, called cutover, that points the application at the new home. The result is a move with only seconds or minutes of downtime instead of hours.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop has a 40 GB orders database that takes about six hours to copy, and it accepts orders all day. If you copy it once and then switch the application over, what happens to orders placed during those six hours, and how could you avoid losing them?
lessons.teach:
Definition. An online migration moves a database while the source database stays open for reads and writes. The work splits into two phases. The first is the initial load, a full copy of the data as it existed at one moment. The second is continuous synchronization, a process that reads the source's record of changes made after that moment and applies them to the target, so the two keep converging. Cutover is the final short step: you pause writes to the source, let the last changes reach the target, confirm the target matches, and point the application at the target.

Why it works. Downtime no longer depends on the total size of the data. It depends on how long it takes to drain the remaining changes and switch connections. A large database can take hours to copy while the outage stays in minutes, as long as synchronization keeps close behind.

Worked example. The 40 GB orders database takes six hours to load. At 00:00 a snapshot is taken and the load starts. Orders keep arriving on the source. At 06:00 the load finishes, but the target is missing everything after 00:00. Change capture has recorded roughly six hours of inserts and updates, and the synchronization process applies them, so the lag shrinks to seconds. At 06:20 the team pauses writes to the source for about two minutes, waits until the target has applied the last change, checks row counts and checksums, then repoints the connection. Downtime is about two minutes.

Common mistake. Treating the end of the initial load as the finish line and cutting over while synchronization still lags. Writes the target has not received are then lost, or the two databases disagree about which orders exist.

Consequence. A system that cuts over early serves stale data from the new database and may take orders twice or miss them, which is worse than a planned, longer outage.

The tradeoff is effort. An online migration requires the source to keep a change log and requires the team to run and watch two databases in parallel.

An online migration is judged by how little the switch costs, and that cost depends on how far behind synchronization is when writes stop.

questions.prompt: A regional courier company moves its 25 GB shipments database to a new server while the old one keeps taking scans. A snapshot, which is a frozen picture of the data at one moment, is taken at 21:00 and the initial load (the full copy from that snapshot) starts. The load finishes at 03:30. Change capture, which means reading the source's log of later inserts and updates, has kept the target within about 10 seconds of the source. At 03:40 the team pauses writes to the source and waits until the target has applied the last change. Then the team checks that the target matches the source, using row counts and a checksum (a fingerprint computed over the data so two copies can be compared). Last, they point the application at the target. The step that the team must complete before repointing the application is missing here: ____. Which choice fills that gap?
choices: Delete the source database to avoid two copies receiving writes
Resume writes on the source so the outage stays under five minutes
Restart the initial load from a new snapshot so the copy is fresh
Compare row counts and checksums between the source and the target
questions.why: Before repointing, the team must confirm the target matches the source, and comparing row counts and checksums is the check that does this.

questions.prompt: In an online migration, what is the 'cutover' step?
choices: The continuous process that reads the source's change record and applies it to the target
The first full copy of the data taken at a single moment
The short final step where writes to the source are paused, the last changes reach the target, the target is confirmed, and the application is pointed at it
The period in which the source is still taken offline for a backup
questions.why: Cutover is defined as the final short step in which writes pause, the target catches up and is verified, and the application's connection is switched to the target.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team finishes the initial load of a 90 GB inventory database. Synchronization is still about four hours behind, and they cut over immediately to avoid running two databases. What is the most likely result?
choices: Downtime stays the same because the initial load already captured all changes
The source automatically rejects all writes until synchronization catches up
The target serves stale data and may take orders twice or miss them, which is worse than a planned longer outage
The migration becomes a cold copy with no further risk
questions.why: Cutting over while synchronization lags leaves changes unapplied on the target, so the target serves stale data and the two databases can disagree about which records exist.

questions.prompt: Which factor mainly determines how long the outage lasts in an online migration?
choices: How long it takes to drain the remaining changes and switch connections
The number of tables in the source schema
How many hours the initial load takes to run
The total size of the database in gigabytes
questions.why: Downtime depends on how long it takes to drain the remaining changes and switch connections, not on total data size or initial load time, as long as synchronization stays close behind.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an online migration differs from an offline one, and name one limit or tradeoff that would still lead you to choose offline.
lessons.modelAnswer: An offline migration stops the application, copies the database, and restarts it on the new server. It is simple and the copy is consistent, but downtime grows with database size, so a 500 GB database could be unavailable for a whole night. An online migration keeps the source running. You do an initial full load, then a change-capture process streams the writes that happen during the load into the target until the two are nearly in step. Only at cutover do you pause writes briefly, let the last changes land, verify the data, and repoint the application. The main limit is that the source must keep a change log and the target must catch up faster than new writes arrive. If the workload writes too heavily for synchronization to keep up, or the source cannot be configured for change capture, I would choose offline and accept a planned outage window.
rubricPoints: Online migration keeps the source serving traffic during the initial bulk copy.
Writes made during the copy are captured and applied to the target until the two are nearly in sync.
Downtime is limited to a short cutover rather than the full copy time.
A real limit: synchronization must keep up with write volume, and the source must support change capture.
Offline migration is simpler and consistent, but its downtime grows with data size.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style scenario that weighs online against offline cutover adds more than a read-only lookup.

lessons.plain: An offline migration is a move of data from an old system to a new one where the old system is stopped, or locked so nothing changes, while the copy happens. Think of moving house with the doors locked and nobody allowed to change anything inside until the last box is in the new place. It is simple and reliable, because the copy is a snapshot that cannot drift. The price is downtime: the application that depends on the database is unavailable for the whole copy and check period. Offline is the right choice when a short outage is acceptable, or when simplicity is worth more than a few hours of stopped service.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your application writes orders all day. You copy its database to a new server over six hours while the application keeps running. What is the main risk of this copy, and how would you avoid it?
lessons.teach:
An offline migration moves a database from a source (the existing database) to a target (the new cloud service) during a window in which writes to the source are stopped. A write is any change such as an insert, update or delete. Cutover is the moment you point the application at the target. Downtime is the time the application cannot accept writes, which is the cost of this strategy.

Why it works: if nothing writes to the source during the copy, the target receives one consistent snapshot, so you do not need to track and replay changes. You then verify the data, change the connection setting to the target, and reopen the application. Because there is no change tracking, the tools are simpler and failures are easier to reason about. Common methods are a native full backup restored on the target, or a BACPAC export, which is a portable package holding the schema and data that can be imported into another Azure SQL service.

Worked example. A 40 GB line-of-business database. Step 1: announce a 2 a.m. window and stop the application's writes. Step 2: take a full backup of the source, or export a BACPAC. Step 3: restore or import into the target. Step 4: compare row counts and a few key business totals between source and target. Step 5: change the connection setting to the target and bring the application back. If the copy takes three hours and checks take one, downtime is about four hours plus the switch.

Common mistake: teams start the copy while the application is still writing, then find the target missing the last hour of orders. The snapshot is consistent only if writes stop, or the source becomes read-only, before the copy starts.

Consequence: if the window overruns, customers stay blocked. Rolling back means restarting the source, and any writes already made on the target during a partial cutover are lost unless you reconcile them.

Offline is the correct strategy when the business accepts the window. When it does not, the answer changes to an online migration that keeps the source running and syncs changes.

questions.prompt: A regional parcel-tracking company runs a 75 GB order database on a Sunday night. They plan an offline move to a new Azure SQL target with a 22:00 to 02:00 window. Step 1: at 22:00 the parcel app is put into maintenance mode so customers cannot submit changes. Step 2: [missing from this plan]. Step 3: export a BACPAC from the source, which takes about 90 minutes. Step 4: import the BACPAC into the target, which takes about 2 hours. Step 5: compare row counts and total parcel counts between source and target. Step 6: change the connection setting to the target and reopen the app. Which step belongs in the gap at Step 2?
choices: Compare row counts after the import so the team knows whether the target is complete before the export begins.
Confirm that no sessions are still writing to the source, so the export captures one consistent snapshot.
Restart the target server to clear its cache before the import begins, so the import runs faster.
Enable change tracking on the source so that any writes during the export are captured and replayed later.
questions.why: The export must start only after writes to the source have stopped, because otherwise the copy is not one consistent snapshot, which is why the step belongs before the export.

questions.prompt: In the offline migration approach, what is the main thing you give up in exchange for simpler tooling and easier-to-reason-about failures?
choices: The ability to export the schema separately from the data in a BACPAC package.
The ability to verify row counts and key totals before the cutover takes place.
The ability to restore the source database from a full backup if something goes wrong.
Application availability during the copy, since writes to the source must be stopped.
questions.why: An offline migration stops writes to the source for the window, so the application cannot accept changes during that time, and that downtime is the cost of the strategy.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company runs a 200 GB database that receives writes around the clock, and customers cannot tolerate any period where orders are blocked. Which migration strategy best fits this requirement?
choices: A plan to copy the database while the application continues writing, then compare totals later.
An offline migration with a BACPAC export, scheduled for a short overnight window.
An offline migration using a native full backup restored on the target during a weekend.
An online migration that keeps the source running and synchronises changes to the target.
questions.why: When the business will not accept a write-blocking window, the teaching text says the answer changes to an online migration that keeps the source running and syncs changes.

questions.prompt: A team starts copying a source database while the application is still writing orders. After the switch, the target is missing the last hour of orders. What is the root cause?
choices: The BACPAC format cannot store orders placed in the final hour before a cutover.
The target was too small to hold the last hour of orders, so the import was truncated.
The copy began before writes to the source were stopped, so the copy was not one consistent snapshot.
The connection setting was changed before the row counts were compared.
questions.why: A consistent snapshot requires that writes stop, or the source becomes read-only, before the copy starts; otherwise changes made during the copy are missing from the target.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when an offline migration is the right choice for moving a database into Azure SQL, and name the main limit you would accept by choosing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would pick an offline migration when the business can accept a planned outage, typically a night window, and the database is not too large to copy within it. We stop writes to the source, take a full backup or export, restore or import into the Azure SQL target, then check row counts and key totals before we repoint the application. The main reason to choose it is simplicity: the copy is one consistent snapshot, so we do not need change tracking or a sync process, and failures are easier to diagnose. The limit we accept is downtime. If the copy and checks run longer than the window, the service stays down, and rolling back after a partial cutover can lose writes made on the target unless we reconcile them. If the outage is not acceptable, I would look at an online migration instead.
rubricPoints: Defines offline migration as stopping or locking writes to the source during the copy
States the main tradeoff: downtime for the whole copy and verification window
Explains why a single snapshot avoids change tracking and makes the copy simpler
Names a limit such as overrun risk or lost writes when rolling back after a partial cutover

suggested.rationale: Choosing offline versus online under a stated outage limit is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario with constraints.

lessons.plain: Moving a database to the cloud means copying its data and then switching your applications over to the new copy. The hard part is not the copy itself but the timing. If the database keeps taking new writes while you copy, you need a way to capture those changes and apply them to the new copy before you switch. You can choose to stop the system for the whole move, which is simple but causes downtime, or to keep it running and catch up on changes, which costs more effort but shortens the outage. Picking the right approach depends on how long users can afford to be locked out and what the new service supports.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has a 2 TB database that must move to Azure with only about 15 minutes of downtime. Would you stop the system and copy everything, or keep it running during most of the copy? Why?
lessons.teach:
A database migration is the process of moving a database, including its schema and data, from a source system to a target system. Here the target is an Azure SQL service such as Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, or SQL Server running on an Azure virtual machine. Three decisions shape every migration: which target fits the workload, whether the move is offline or online, and which tool moves the data. An offline migration stops writes to the source during the copy, so the database is unavailable for that window, which is called downtime. An online migration keeps the source running, copies the bulk of the data first, then captures and replays the changes made since that copy began, until the target is nearly current. Cutover is the final moment when applications are pointed at the target.

Why it works: the copy is a snapshot plus a stream of later changes, so the gap between source and target shrinks until the remaining work is small enough to finish in a short pause.

Worked example: a 400 GB SQL Server database must move with at most 15 minutes of downtime. Step 1: run an assessment tool to find features the target does not support. Step 2: copy the full data while the source keeps serving users. Step 3: replay ongoing changes until the lag is a few seconds. Step 4: stop writes to the source, let the last changes arrive, check row counts and sample checksums, then repoint connection strings. Only step 4 counts as downtime.

Common mistake: choosing a method because it is the tool you already know, instead of checking the downtime budget and feature compatibility first. Teams also skip validation after cutover.

Consequence: if cutover happens before the final changes are applied, the target is missing recent writes, so customers may see orders or positions that are minutes out of date.

An online migration reduces downtime only when change capture and validation are planned from the start.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic group moves a 40 GB SQL Server database to a SQL Server on Azure virtual machine. The offices are closed Sunday from 01:00 to 03:00, so the team accepts a 2-hour offline migration. Step 1: run a compatibility assessment and fix any blocking features on the source. Step 2: at 01:00, stop all writes to the source database. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: on the target, check row counts and sample checksums against the source. Step 5: repoint the clinic's connection strings and reopen the offices at 03:00.
choices: Start change capture on the source so that writes made after 01:00 are replayed to the target later
Repoint the connection strings to the target before the copy finishes so staff can begin testing early
Copy the full database to the virtual machine while writes stay stopped, then bring the restored copy online on the target
Skip the compatibility assessment and rely on the checksums in step 4 to catch any unsupported features
questions.why: In an offline migration writes are stopped before the copy, so the full copy taken during the frozen window is the data transfer and must be restored on the target before checks can run.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines an online database migration?
choices: The source keeps serving users while the bulk of the data is copied, then changes made since that copy are captured and applied until the target is nearly current
The migration copies only the schema first and leaves all data on the source permanently, using a linked connection
The database is copied once on a weekend, and any later changes are typed in by hand by the operations team
The source database is shut down for the whole migration, and the target is built from a fresh backup taken after the shutdown
questions.why: An online migration keeps the source running, copies the bulk of the data first, and then captures and replays later changes so that the final cutover pause is short.

questions.prompt: A ticketing platform has a 2 TB reporting database and can tolerate only 10 minutes of downtime for its move to Azure. The team's first instinct is to stop writes and copy the database over the weekend. Which approach best fits the downtime budget?
choices: Move the database with no assessment and no validation, since the data volume is the only thing that matters
Convert the reporting database into a flat file export and load it by hand after business hours
Keep the weekend offline copy because the team already knows the copy tool well
Use an online migration with change capture and a planned, validated cutover, because a full offline copy of 2 TB would likely exceed 10 minutes of downtime
questions.why: Choosing the method against the downtime budget and feature compatibility, rather than familiarity, points to an online approach for a large database with a tight downtime allowance.

questions.prompt: A team finishes the bulk copy of a ticketing database and cuts over the application right away, before replaying the changes that were made during the copy. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The source still holds every record, so the target is complete as long as the source is kept running
The target catches up automatically within a few minutes of cutover, so nothing is lost
Cutover fails with an error, so the team notices immediately and no customer sees stale data
The target is missing the recent writes, so customers may see tickets that are minutes out of date, and writes split between the two systems
questions.why: Cutover before the final changes are applied leaves the target without recent writes, and once applications write to the target the two copies diverge.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between an offline and an online database migration, and name one limit or tradeoff of the online approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: An offline migration stops writes to the source database, copies everything, and then starts the application on the target. It is simple and the data is consistent by construction, but users are locked out for the whole copy, so it only suits systems that can tolerate that outage. An online migration keeps the source running. It copies the bulk of the data first, then captures the changes made since that copy began and applies them to the target until the lag is small. The outage is then limited to a short cutover pause. The main tradeoff is complexity: the team must make sure changes are captured reliably, handle features the target does not support, and validate the target carefully before switching. If the cutover is rushed, the target can be missing recent writes, so checking row counts and sample data is part of the migration, not an optional extra.
rubricPoints: Defines offline migration as stopping writes during the copy, causing downtime
Defines online migration as copying first and replaying changes until a short cutover
Names the tradeoff: online reduces downtime but adds complexity and capture risk
Notes that validation before cutover prevents missing recent writes

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario with a downtime budget and feature constraints forces the learner to choose an offline or online strategy and justify it, which adds more than reading alone.

lessons.plain: Moving a database from one hosted home to another is a migration. Azure offers several places a SQL database can live: a fully managed single database, a managed instance that behaves much like a full SQL Server, and a SQL Server you run yourself on a virtual machine. Implementing a migration means actually carrying the data, and the work that depends on it, across to the new place. The main choice is whether you can stop writes for a while (offline, simpler, with downtime) or need to keep the old system running and catch up its changes before a short switchover (online, with more moving parts). Before you start, you confirm the target supports every feature the source uses and that the data will behave the same once it arrives.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your application writes orders to a database for 8 hours a day and can tolerate a 30-minute outage at midnight. Would you copy the data while writes are stopped, or keep copying while the app keeps running? Why?
lessons.teach:
An offline migration stops writes to the source, copies the data to the target, and then points the application at the target. It is simple and easy to verify, but the application is down for the whole copy. An online migration takes an initial copy while the source keeps running, then continuously captures the changes made since that copy and applies them to the target. The cutover is the short moment when you stop writes, let the last changes arrive, and repoint the application connection to the target. The source is the old database, and the target is the new Azure service.

Why it works: the copy and the change replay together bring the target up to date, so the downtime is only the time needed to drain the final changes. Example: a 40 GB database takes about 2 hours to copy. Offline, the app is down for roughly 2 hours. Online, you start the copy at 1 a.m. while the app keeps writing, the tool records changes made during those 2 hours and applies them to the target, and at 3 a.m. the lag is near zero. You stop writes for about 5 minutes, confirm the target has the last change, and switch the connection string.

Common mistake: cutting over while lag is still non-zero, which silently loses the most recent writes. Another is assuming the target supports everything the source uses, such as agent jobs, linked servers or cross-database queries, which may need redesign before cutover.

Consequence: if the cutover misses changes, the old and new databases diverge, and returning to the source means a reverse sync that is slow and risky. A migration is finished only when the target is verified against the source, not when the copy job reports success.

questions.prompt: A regional clinic group has a 25 GB appointments database that takes about 90 minutes to copy to its new Azure SQL target. Staff book appointments all day, so the application cannot be offline for the whole copy. The team starts an online migration at 22:00 with the initial copy running while the application keeps writing. A change-capture process (the tool that records every write made to the source after the copy began) runs alongside it and applies those changes to the target. By 23:45 the replication lag (the delay between a change on the source and its arrival on the target) has dropped to a few seconds. At 23:50 the team stops writes to the source for a short period. The final step, which the team must complete before pointing the application at the target, is missing from this description. Which step is it?
choices: Delete the source database so that storage costs stop accruing
Confirm that the replication lag is zero and that the target holds the last change written to the source
Repoint the application connection string to the target and then start the copy again
Keep the source writable for a week so that staff can compare the two databases later
questions.why: Cutover is only safe once the lag is zero and the target has every final change, because switching while changes are still in transit silently loses the most recent writes.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is the main trade-off of an offline migration compared with an online one?
choices: An offline migration makes the application unavailable for the whole copy, but it is simpler to verify
An offline migration avoids any need to repoint the application connection
An offline migration captures changes continuously, so the target is never behind
An offline migration keeps the source writable, so it costs less to run
questions.why: An offline migration stops writes during the entire copy, which means downtime for the full duration, but its simplicity makes it easier to verify than an online migration.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a nightly job on its source database that depends on scheduled agent jobs and a linked server to another database. The team plans an online migration and cuts over after lag reaches zero, then notices the nightly reports never ran. Which explanation best fits this failure?
choices: The initial copy was too slow, so the nightly job timed out during the copy phase
The lag was not measured correctly, so the cutover happened before the copy finished
The target does not support every feature the source relies on, and those dependencies needed redesign before cutover
The change-capture process failed to replay write statements, so the job's inserts were lost
questions.why: Lag measures only whether data changes arrived; it says nothing about features such as agent jobs or linked servers, which the target may not support and which therefore need planning before cutover.

questions.prompt: A media archive holds a 300 GB database that can be unavailable for a single six-hour weekend window. The team wants the simplest migration that is easy to check afterward. Which approach fits best?
choices: An offline migration, because the copy fits inside the window and verification is straightforward
A hybrid approach that keeps both databases writable so staff can choose which one to use
An online migration with change capture, because it always gives the shortest downtime
An online migration with a manual cutover at the end of the month to avoid weekend work
questions.why: When the full copy fits inside an acceptable downtime window, an offline migration is simpler and easier to verify, so the online approach's extra complexity is not needed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between an offline and an online migration of a SQL Server database to Azure SQL Managed Instance, and name one limit or tradeoff of the online route.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the downtime the business allows. If the database can be unavailable for the full copy window, offline is simpler, because I stop writes, copy, verify and switch. If the window is too short, I choose online: I take an initial copy while the source keeps running, let the migration tool capture and apply ongoing changes, and watch the lag until it is near zero. Then I stop writes briefly, confirm the last changes arrived, and repoint the application. The tradeoff with online is that it has more moving parts. The source must keep changes recorded for the sync, the network must stay healthy for the whole run, and the cutover still needs a brief write stop. I also check that the target supports every feature the application depends on before I begin, because a feature gap found at cutover is much harder to fix.
rubricPoints: Chooses offline or online based on the allowed downtime window
Explains that online migration copies first, then syncs ongoing changes until lag is near zero
Names a real tradeoff of online, such as added complexity, sync dependencies or a brief cutover write stop
Mentions checking feature compatibility between source and target before starting

suggested.rationale: Choosing between offline and online routes for a given downtime budget is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario.

lessons.plain: A database copy or move means taking a database that lives in one place and putting a working version somewhere else, or under a new name on the same server, without losing the data inside it. Azure SQL Managed Instance is a managed SQL Server that Azure runs for you, so you do not patch the operating system, but you still decide how the data travels. The job is to pick a method that keeps the data correct, keeps downtime acceptable, and leaves a clean way back if something goes wrong. Think of it like moving house: you can copy the contents while you still live there, or pack everything up and switch over on a single day.
lessons.guessPrompt: A production database keeps taking writes all day. If you need a second, identical database for testing, what could go wrong if you simply copy the underlying files while writes continue?
lessons.teach:
A managed instance is a SQL Server engine that Azure operates for you, placed inside a virtual network you control. A copy creates a new database from an existing one while the source stays online and keeps serving users. A move is a copy followed by switching applications to the new database and then retiring the old one. A backup is a saved file of a database at a point in time, and a restore rebuilds a database from that file. A transactionally consistent copy means every change is either fully included or fully excluded, so the copy never holds half of a business operation.

Why it works: the engine reads the source as of one moment and writes that state into the new database, so the copy reflects a coherent point in time instead of a mix of older and newer rows. Because the source keeps running, users are not stopped while the copy is made. A restore from a backup file works similarly but starts from the saved file rather than the live database, which suits moving data between environments.

Worked example: a team needs a test copy of a 200 GB orders database on the same managed instance, named orders_test. Step one: they start a copy of orders into orders_test. Step two: the engine records a consistent point in time for the source and writes that state into the new database. Step three: production keeps taking orders, and those later orders do not appear in orders_test. Step four: the team points the test app at orders_test and runs its checks. Production saw no downtime.

Common mistake: teams assume a copy is a live sync. It is not. After the copy finishes, the two databases diverge, and changes to one never appear in the other. A move that cuts over while writes still hit the source loses every change made after the copy's point in time.

Consequence: in a running order system, a cutover without a write freeze leaves some orders only on the old database, and the new one quietly misses them. Plan a short write freeze, or a sync-based migration, whenever lost writes are unacceptable.

In short, copy when you need a second database and the source must stay live, restore from a backup when that file is your source of truth, and use a move with a write freeze when the old database must retire without losing any changes.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a shipments database on a managed instance (a SQL Server engine that Azure operates for you inside a virtual network the firm controls). It needs a staging copy named shipments_stage to test a schema change. A write freeze here means a short pause in which the source accepts no new changes. Step 1: the team freezes writes to shipments. Step 2: they start a copy of shipments into shipments_stage. Step 3: the copy records one consistent point in time, which falls after the freeze, so it holds every shipment update. Step 4: ______ . Step 5: once checks pass, shipments is retired. Which action fills Step 4?
choices: shipments is deleted before the app is switched, so that only one database exists.
Writes are unfrozen on shipments while the app is also pointed at shipments_stage.
The app is switched to shipments_stage and writes resume there, so no update is lost.
The app stays on shipments, and the copy is left to sync changes automatically from then on.
questions.why: After the freeze-consistent copy, the cutover switches the application to the new database, and only later is the old database retired; the other options either skip the switch, retire too early, or leave two live writers.

questions.prompt: A payroll company runs its live payroll database on a managed instance (a SQL Server engine that Azure operates for it inside a virtual network). It needs a second database for a month-end report while payroll keeps processing. Which approach fits best?
choices: Restore a backup file over the live payroll database so the report reads a clean version.
Create a copy, which leaves the source online and gives a fixed point-in-time version for the report.
Move payroll to a new database and retire the old one the same afternoon, without any write freeze.
Set up a live sync so both databases always match each other for the report.
questions.why: A copy keeps the source online and produces a database fixed at one consistent moment, which suits a report; restoring over the live database, moving without a freeze, and live sync each misfit the stated need.

questions.prompt: A retailer copied its inventory database yesterday. Today its store app still writes to the old database, and staff notice that the copy lacks today's stock counts. What is the most accurate explanation?
choices: The copy was taken from a backup file, which always lags the live data by a day.
A copy is not a live sync, so changes made after its point in time stay only in the source and the two databases diverge.
The copy is still catching up and will include today's counts within the hour.
The managed instance hid today's rows to protect the copy from partial writes.
questions.why: A copy captures one consistent moment and then stops tracking the source, so changes after that moment exist only in the source.

questions.prompt: A school district must retire its old gradebook database on a managed instance without losing any grade entered during the switch. Which plan meets that requirement?
choices: Copy the database, then point the apps at the copy with no write freeze, because the copy already holds every grade.
Freeze writes on the gradebook, make the copy, switch the apps to the copy, and retire the old database only after checks pass.
Copy the database and keep both live, letting teachers enter grades into either one.
Restore last night's backup file, switch the apps to it, and retire the old database immediately.
questions.why: A short write freeze before the consistent copy, followed by the app switch and only then retirement, is the move pattern that prevents lost writes, while the other plans either lose changes or create two diverging writers.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between copying and moving a database on Azure SQL Managed Instance, and name one limit or tradeoff you would check before using a copy for a production cutover.
lessons.modelAnswer: A copy makes a second database from a consistent point-in-time snapshot of the source while the source stays online and keeps taking writes. After that, the two databases diverge, and nothing keeps them in sync. A move is that copy plus switching the application to the new database and retiring the old one. The main tradeoff is the gap: any writes made to the source after the snapshot are missing from the copy. Before using a copy for a production cutover, I would check whether writes can be frozen during the cutover window, how long the copy takes at this database size, and how we would roll back if the new database turns out to be missing data.
