You then call a function such as ENCRYPTBYKEY, which takes the key's GUID (its unique identifier) and the plaintext, and returns varbinary bytes. The reverse function is DECRYPTBYKEY. ENCRYPTBYKEY adds a random initialization vector, so the same input encrypts to different bytes each time.

Worked example: a column named CardNumber holds encrypted bytes. Step one, an authorized session opens the symmetric key. Step two, the insert passes the typed value through ENCRYPTBYKEY and stores the resulting bytes. Step three, when an authorized user reads the row, the session runs DECRYPTBYKEY on the column, converts the result back to text, and closes the key.

Common mistake: assuming encryption hides data from anyone with enough permissions. Any principal allowed to open and use the key can read the values, so access control still matters.

Consequence in a running system: because stored values are random bytes, an equality search on the column cannot use a normal index or match plaintext, so queries must decrypt each row or the design must change. Losing the certificate or its private key makes the encrypted values permanently unreadable.

questions.prompt: A school district stores staff bank account numbers in a column named BankAcct. The setup runs in this order: (1) the database master key is created, and it protects the certificate; (2) a certificate is created, and it protects the symmetric key SalaryKey; (3) the step that is missing from this list; (4) an authorized payroll session opens SalaryKey before it reads any value. Which step fills the gap at position 3?
choices: On each write, the symmetric key SalaryKey scrambles the account number through ENCRYPTBYKEY, so the column stores encrypted bytes.
The master key is exported to a file and then deleted from the database, so no one can protect the certificate.
A second plain text copy of each account number is kept in another column so that equality searches stay fast.
A normal index is built on BankAcct so that lookups by account number can match the stored values directly.
questions.why: The symmetric key is the layer that actually scrambles the values, so the write step must pass each value through it, and the other three options either break the layering or defeat the protection.

questions.prompt: In the layered design where a master key protects a certificate and the certificate protects a key, which element is the one that actually scrambles the stored values?
choices: The symmetric key, because one secret key is used both to encrypt and to decrypt the values.
The backup of the database file, because a backup holds a copy of every stored value.
The certificate, because it is a signed credential that gives the database its identity.
The master key, because it sits at the top of the database and protects every other key in it.
questions.why: A symmetric key is defined as the single secret key that both encrypts and decrypts, and the text names it as the key that scrambles the data, while the master key and certificate only protect it.

questions.prompt: A regional airline encrypts passport numbers in one column. A developer argues that the column is safe because only the booking application's service account can run the queries, so no further controls on the symmetric key are needed. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
choices: The master key, not the service account, is what decrypts the values, so the service account can never read them at all.
Random initialization vectors make every stored value unreadable to any query, so the column cannot be read even by the application.
Encryption with ENCRYPTBYKEY already prevents any principal from reading values, even one with full permissions, so the developer is right.
Any principal allowed to open and use the symmetric key can decrypt the values, so access to the key itself still has to be controlled.
questions.why: Object-level encryption does not hide data from principals who are permitted to use the key, so access to the key must still be governed, which is why the other options that claim encryption alone blocks access are wrong.

questions.prompt: An online shop stores customer email addresses encrypted in a column. A support engineer runs a WHERE clause that checks for one exact address, and it is slow and does not find a row that is present. Which explanation fits the design described in the teaching text?
choices: The certificate protecting the symmetric key has expired, so the query is refused before it runs.
The symmetric key was opened twice in the same session, which corrupts the comparison.
The index on the column has been dropped by the encryption process, so the engine must scan every row.
Because stored values are random bytes, an equality search cannot use a normal index or match plaintext, so queries must decrypt rows or the design must change.
questions.why: The text states that random stored bytes prevent a normal index from matching plaintext on equality searches, which is why the query has to decrypt each row or the design has to change, and the other options invent causes not described in the text.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should just turn on encryption for the whole database and skip encrypting individual columns. In your own words, explain what object-level encryption adds on top of whole-database encryption, and name one limit or tradeoff of using it on a column.
lessons.modelAnswer: Whole-database encryption protects the stored files, so the data is safe if someone steals a disk or backup, but anyone who can connect and query normally still sees readable values. Object-level encryption adds a second protection: a specific column is stored as scrambled bytes, and a session must open a symmetric key, which itself is protected by a certificate and the database master key, before it can read the plaintext. That lets us limit a few sensitive fields without hiding everything. The tradeoff is that the encrypted column cannot be searched or compared the way plaintext can, because the random bytes defeat normal indexes and equality checks. We also have to protect the certificate and its private key, since losing them makes the values unrecoverable.
rubricPoints: Whole-database encryption protects stored files but not query access by permitted users
Object-level encryption scrambles specific columns using a key that must be opened per session
The key chain runs from master key to certificate to symmetric key, and access to the key is still a permission question
Encrypted columns cannot be searched or indexed like plaintext, and losing the certificate makes data unreadable

suggested.rationale: The planned envelope encryption lab mirrors the wrapped-key hierarchy (data key protected by a key-encryption key) that this objective depends on.

lessons.plain: A firewall rule is an entry on a list that says which network addresses are allowed to connect to a database server. Anything not on the list is turned away before anyone tries a password. Picture a building with a front gate that applies to everyone and a separate lock on one office inside. The gate is a server-level rule, covering every room. The office lock is a database-level rule, covering only that room. This lesson covers how those two kinds of entry differ, how the system decides between them, and why an overly generous entry is a risk even when passwords are strong.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a database server has one rule that allows the office address range, and one database on that server has its own rule that allows a single partner address. Can the partner reach a different database on the same server, and can the office reach the database that has the partner rule?
lessons.teach: An IP address is the numeric address of a device on a network. A firewall rule is one entry in a filter that checks the source address of each incoming connection before passing it on. A rule can name one address or a range, and a range is often written in CIDR notation, which pairs a base address with a prefix length that sets how many addresses are included. An Azure SQL Database logical server is the management endpoint that hosts one or more databases; it is not a single machine.  There are two levels. A server-level rule is stored at the logical server and applies to every database on it. A database-level rule is stored inside one database, is created with T-SQL (Transact-SQL, Microsoft's dialect of SQL), and applies only to that database. Server-level rules are checked first. If a client address matches any server-level rule, it can reach any database on the server. If none match, the database-level rules of the database being requested are checked. A match there lets the client reach only that database. If nothing matches, the connection is refused.  Worked example. Server rule: 203.0.113.0/24 (the office). Database rule on Orders: 198.51.100.7 (a partner's fixed address). Step 1: the partner connects to Orders. The server rule does not match, but the Orders rule does, so it is allowed. Step 2: the partner connects to Inventory. The server rule does not match, and Inventory has no database rule, so it is refused. Step 3: an office host at 203.0.113.20 connects to Inventory. The server rule matches, so it is allowed.  Common mistake: adding a broad server-level rule to fix one application's connection. That opens every database on the server to the whole range. The narrower fix is a database-level rule on the one database that needs it.  Consequence in a running system: a stale or overly wide rule stays open after its reason has gone. Conversely, if the office IP changes and the server rule is not updated, every application from the office loses access at once, which looks like a database outage. The firewall checks the address the server actually sees, so a NAT gateway or a changed provider address changes the match.

questions.prompt: A clinic has one logical server, which is the management endpoint that hosts its databases. The server has one server-level rule, 192.0.2.0/25, which covers the front desk addresses from 192.0.2.0 to 192.0.2.127. The database Billing has one database-level rule for the fixed address 198.51.100.44. A lab system at 192.0.2.150 connects to the database Scheduling, which has no database-level rule. Step 1: the server-level rules are checked first, and 192.0.2.150 is outside 192.0.2.0/25 because that range stops at .127, so the server rule does not match. Step 2: [one step is missing here]. Step 3: the connection result is stated.
choices: Check the database-level rules on Billing, since it is the only database with a rule.
Check the database-level rules on Scheduling; none match, so the connection is refused.
Widen the server-level rule to 192.0.2.0/24 so that the lab system matches and is allowed.
Allow the lab system because it sits on the same network as the front desk.
questions.why: After the server-level rules fail to match, the firewall checks only the database-level rules of the database being requested, which here is Scheduling, and finds none, so the connection is refused.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a server-level firewall rule apply to?
choices: Only connections that are written in T-SQL
Every database hosted on the logical server
Only the single database that the rule was created inside
Only the operating system of the machine running the server
questions.why: A server-level rule is stored at the logical server and applies to every database on it, unlike a database-level rule that applies to one database only.

questions.prompt: A reporting app runs from the single address 172.16.4.9 and needs to reach only the database Reports on a logical server. Which change fits the requirement most closely?
choices: Delete all database-level rules so that only the server-level rules decide access
Add a server-level rule for 172.16.4.9 so the app can reach the whole server
Add a database-level rule for 172.16.4.9 inside the database Reports
Add a server-level rule for the range 172.16.0.0/16 so future apps are covered
questions.why: A database-level rule created inside Reports lets the app reach that database alone, which matches the need without opening any other database on the server.

questions.prompt: An office has a server-level rule 203.0.113.0/24. The office changes internet provider and its clients now appear to the server as 198.18.7.33, which is outside that range. No database-level rules match 198.18.7.33. What is the result?
choices: Only the database with the newest rule loses access, because rules are checked in the order they were created
The office keeps access, because the firewall remembers the old address for existing clients
Nothing changes, because the server-level rule is matched by its name rather than by address
Every database on the server refuses office clients, because no rule matches their new address
questions.why: The firewall matches the address the server actually sees, so once the office address falls outside the server rule and no database-level rule matches, every database on the server refuses those clients.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a server-level firewall rule and a database-level firewall rule on Azure SQL Database, including the order in which they are checked. Name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: A server-level rule lives on the logical server and lets a matching address reach every database on that server. A database-level rule lives inside one database and lets a matching address reach only that database. When a connection arrives, the server-level rules are checked first, then the database-level rules of the requested database, and if neither matches the connection is refused. The tradeoff with server-level rules is reach: one entry opens all databases on the server, so it is hard to audit and easy to over-grant. The tradeoff with database-level rules is management: each rule must be created in each database, so they are more work to keep consistent across many databases. For one partner who needs one database, I would add a database-level rule and keep the server list short.
rubricPoints: Server-level rules apply to all databases on the logical server; database-level rules apply only to the database where they are stored.
Server-level rules are checked first, then database-level rules for the requested database; no match means refusal.
Each level has a tradeoff: server-level rules over-grant reach, database-level rules add per-database management work.
A narrow database-level rule is usually the safer fix for a single client needing a single database.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission covers database firewall rules, and the core material is levels, check order, and console or T-SQL steps that are best read first.

lessons.plain: Always Encrypted is a way to keep certain database columns, such as national ID numbers or card details, scrambled even from the people who run the database server. The scrambling and unscrambling happen inside the application's own database driver, so the database engine only ever stores and handles scrambled values. The keys that unlock the data live in a separate key store that you control, so a database administrator with full server access still sees only unreadable values in those columns. The trade-off is that the database can do less with data it cannot read, and that shapes how you design queries.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database administrator has full admin rights on the server. You need them to keep running backups and tuning, but never to see plaintext card numbers in one column. Why might ordinary encryption of the disk files not be enough for that goal, and what would you need instead?
lessons.teach:
Always Encrypted protects individual columns by encrypting them on the client side, which means inside the application's database driver before data is sent to the server. Two kinds of key are involved. The column master key (CMK) is held outside the database, usually in Azure Key Vault or another external key store that you control. The column encryption key (CEK) is the key that actually encrypts column values. It is stored in the database, but only in a form that is itself encrypted by the CMK. Encryption at rest, which protects database files on disk, does not stop someone with query access from reading the rows. Always Encrypted does, because the server never holds the unwrapped key.

The column can use deterministic or randomized encryption. Deterministic encryption always turns the same plaintext into the same ciphertext, so equality filters, joins and grouping still work, but patterns can leak. Randomized encryption produces different ciphertext each time, which is stronger, but the server cannot compare values, so it cannot filter on that column.

Worked example: a column CustomerCard is deterministic. The application runs a lookup for one card number. Step 1: the driver reads the column metadata and sees it is encrypted. Step 2: it fetches the CEK through the CMK in the key store. Step 3: it encrypts the search value locally. Step 4: the server compares ciphertext to ciphertext and finds the row. Step 5: the driver decrypts the returned value for the application.

A common mistake is leaving the column encryption setting off in the connection string, so the application receives ciphertext or fails. Another is encrypting a column randomized and then filtering on it in SQL. In a running system, a search or report that worked yesterday can break the day the column is encrypted, and if the key store becomes unreachable, reads and writes on those columns stop until access is restored. Always Encrypted moves trust to the application and its key store, so every query on an encrypted column has to be designed around that.

questions.prompt: A regional pharmacy chain stores each member's phone number in a column MemberPhone, encrypted with deterministic Always Encrypted. Deterministic means the same plaintext always produces the same ciphertext, so equality lookups still work. A call-center app looks up one member and the flow runs as follows. Step 1: the driver reads the column metadata and sees MemberPhone is encrypted. Step 2: the driver unwraps the column encryption key (CEK) using the column master key (CMK) held in Azure Key Vault. Step 3: the driver encrypts the searched phone number locally. Step 4: the server compares that ciphertext with the stored ciphertext and returns the matching row. The final step is left out. Which choice correctly completes the flow?
choices: The server decrypts the matching row with the CMK before returning it, so the driver receives plaintext.
The driver fetches the CEK again from the MemberPhone column, because the stored key is what decrypts values.
The app copies the CMK from Key Vault into the database so the server can decrypt the row.
The driver decrypts the returned ciphertext locally with the CEK it already unwrapped, so the app sees the phone number.
questions.why: After the server returns ciphertext, the driver uses the CEK it already unwrapped to decrypt the value for the application, because the server never holds the unwrapped key.

questions.prompt: A team encrypts a column Notes with randomized Always Encrypted and then runs a query filtering on Notes equal to a fixed text value. Which statement is true?
choices: The filter works, because the server holds the CEK and decrypts Notes during the comparison.
The query returns every matching row, because the driver decrypts each row before comparing it.
The filter works only if the column is also set to deterministic encryption.
The filter may not match as expected, because randomized encryption gives the same text different ciphertext each time, and the server cannot compare values.
questions.why: Randomized encryption produces different ciphertext for the same plaintext, so the server has no way to compare values for equality, which is why filtering on such a column fails.

questions.prompt: An app team turns on Always Encrypted for a column TaxNumber in a supplier table but does not enable column encryption in the application's connection string. What is the most likely result?
choices: The CMK is copied into the database and used automatically on the next request.
The column is decrypted on the server and returned as plaintext, so nothing breaks.
The database rejects writes to every column in the table.
The application receives encrypted bytes or an error when reading TaxNumber, because the driver is not set up to decrypt it.
questions.why: Decryption happens in the client driver, so without the connection setting the driver does not decrypt the column and the application sees ciphertext or a failure.

questions.prompt: A company's Azure Key Vault becomes unreachable for one hour. Which effect is most accurate for the Always Encrypted columns in its database?
choices: Only inserts fail, while reads continue from plaintext cached on the server.
Nothing changes, because encryption at rest keeps the rows readable.
Every unencrypted column in the same table also stops working.
Reads and writes on the encrypted columns stop until the key store is reachable again, because the driver cannot obtain the CEK.
questions.why: The driver needs the CMK in the external key store to unwrap the CEK, so without that access it cannot encrypt or decrypt those columns, and operations on them stop.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Always Encrypted keeps a column hidden from a database administrator, and name one limit or tradeoff the team must plan for when choosing between deterministic and randomized encryption.
lessons.modelAnswer: Always Encrypted encrypts the column values in the application's database driver before they reach the server, using a column encryption key. That key is wrapped by a column master key that lives in an external key store such as Azure Key Vault, so the server only ever holds ciphertext and an administrator with full server rights cannot read the values. The main tradeoff is in the encryption type. Deterministic encryption keeps equality filters, joins and grouping working, but identical values produce identical ciphertext, which can reveal patterns. Randomized encryption is stronger, but the server cannot compare those values, so any search on that column has to be redesigned. The team also needs to remember that losing access to the key store blocks reads and writes on those columns.
rubricPoints: Column values are encrypted and decrypted by the client driver, so the server never sees plaintext.
Column master key sits in an external key store and wraps the column encryption key.
Deterministic encryption allows equality queries but can leak patterns; randomized is stronger but blocks server-side filtering.
Key store availability and driver configuration are operational dependencies that can stop reads and writes.

suggested.rationale: The planned envelope encryption lab practises wrapping a data key with a master key, the same layering Always Encrypted uses, so it is the closest hands-on match.

lessons.plain: Always Encrypted keeps certain database columns, such as national ID numbers or salaries, scrambled even from the people who run the database server. The application's own driver does the scrambling and unscrambling, so the server only stores and handles coded values. The difficulty is that scrambled values are hard to search or compare. An enclave is a sealed, protected area inside the server where the database can make those comparisons on readable values without exposing them to anyone else. A VBS enclave uses Windows virtualization security to make that sealed area stronger.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database administrator with full server rights runs SELECT on a salary column that is encrypted so only the application can read it. What do they get back, and what would stop a WHERE salary > 50000 filter from working as the server normally runs it?
lessons.teach:
Always Encrypted is a column-level feature in which the client driver, not the database engine, encrypts values before they are sent and decrypts them after they are received. A column master key (CMK) is a key kept outside the database, typically in a key vault or certificate store. It protects a column encryption key (CEK), the key that actually encrypts column values. Only the wrapped form of the CEK is stored in the database, so the engine never holds a usable plaintext key and an administrator with full server rights sees only ciphertext.

Two encryption types matter. Deterministic encryption always turns the same input into the same output, so equality lookups, joins and grouping still work, but repeated values can reveal patterns. Randomized encryption gives different output each time, which is stronger, but the server cannot compare or search it directly.

An enclave closes that gap. A secure enclave is a protected memory region inside the server. Before the driver sends a key into it, the driver checks an attestation, a signed proof that the enclave is genuine and running in a healthy, isolated state. A VBS enclave uses Windows hypervisor isolation to keep that region separate even from the operating system. Inside it, the engine can run comparisons such as LIKE or range filters on decrypted values without exposing them outside.

Worked example: a salary column uses randomized encryption with an enclave-enabled CEK. The app runs WHERE salary > 50000 with the parameter encrypted by the driver. Step 1: the driver attests the enclave and sets up a session key. Step 2: it sends the encrypted parameter. Step 3: the enclave decrypts the values in protected memory and compares them. Step 4: the server returns encrypted matching rows, and the driver decrypts them for the app.

Common mistake: assuming that encryption at rest or a restricted DBA role is enough. If the CMK is deleted or access to its key vault is revoked, the application can no longer decrypt, and the data cannot be recovered without that key. Plaintext copied into client logs also defeats the scheme.

Choose the encryption type and key-custody plan at design time, because changing them later means re-encrypting the column.

questions.prompt: A regional clinic stores patient surnames in a column that uses randomized encryption with an enclave-enabled column encryption key. A staff app searches for surnames beginning with 'Oh'. The flow is: (1) the driver attests the enclave and sets up a session key; (2) the driver encrypts the search pattern 'Oh%' and sends it to the server; (3) [missing step]; (4) the server returns the encrypted matching rows and the driver decrypts them for the app. Which step fills the gap at position 3?
choices: The database loads the column master key from the key vault and stores it in the surname table.
The server engine decrypts the surnames on disk and runs the LIKE comparison in ordinary query memory.
The driver writes the decrypted search pattern and surnames into the application log for auditing.
The enclave decrypts the surnames in its protected memory region and evaluates the LIKE pattern against each one.
questions.why: The enclave is the only place inside the server where the engine can compare decrypted values, so the pattern match happens there, and the plaintext never leaves protected memory.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team stores payment card numbers with deterministic encryption so they can count how many orders share each card. Which property of deterministic encryption makes that grouping possible?
choices: Each row gets a fresh random output, so the server can count duplicates only after decrypting on the client.
The output is longer than the input, so the server can detect repeated patterns by length alone.
The encryption key is stored in the table beside the column, so the server can reverse each value during grouping.
The same input always produces the same encrypted output, so equal values can be matched and grouped without decrypting them.
questions.why: Deterministic encryption maps identical plaintext to identical ciphertext, which is what allows equality lookups, joins and grouping on encrypted values; the other options describe randomized encryption or misstate how keys are stored.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm loses access to the key vault that holds its column master key after a permissions change. What is the direct consequence for the encrypted columns in its database?
choices: The application can no longer unwrap the column encryption key, so it cannot decrypt those values, and the data is unrecoverable without that key.
The server re-encrypts the columns with a new key from the engine's own built-in store, so no data is lost.
Only administrators lose access, while the application keeps working because the driver caches the plaintext keys permanently.
The database automatically switches those columns to plaintext storage until access is restored.
questions.why: The column master key protects the column encryption key, so losing it blocks decryption; the scheme never stores a plaintext copy inside the database that could be used instead.

questions.prompt: A bank wants to run range filters such as salary greater than 50000 on a column encrypted with randomized encryption. Which combination of design choices makes that server-side filtering possible?
choices: Plaintext storage of the column with transparent data encryption applied to the whole database file.
An enclave-enabled column encryption key, with the driver attesting the enclave before sending keys into it.
Deterministic encryption on the column, with no enclave, because equal ciphertexts can be ordered by the server.
A column master key stored inside the database engine so the server can decrypt values during the query.
questions.why: Randomized ciphertext cannot be compared directly by the server, so the comparison must run inside a VBS enclave after attestation confirms that enclave is genuine and isolated.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Always Encrypted with a VBS enclave protects, what it does not protect, and the main tradeoff between deterministic and randomized encryption.
lessons.modelAnswer: Always Encrypted means the driver encrypts and decrypts the column, so the database engine and anyone with server admin rights only see ciphertext. The column master key lives outside the database, and the column encryption key is stored wrapped by it. What it does not protect is the application itself: whatever the app does with decrypted values, including logging them, is outside the scheme. Deterministic encryption lets the server do equality matches, joins and grouping, but identical values produce identical ciphertext, so frequency patterns can leak. Randomized encryption hides those patterns but blocks server-side comparisons unless the query runs in an enclave. An enclave adds attestation, so the driver verifies the enclave is genuine before sending keys. The tradeoff is stronger privacy versus query capability and operational complexity, including key rotation and key vault availability.
rubricPoints: Client driver encrypts and decrypts, so the server never sees plaintext for protected columns
Column master key stays outside the database and protects the column encryption key
Deterministic encryption allows equality operations but can leak patterns; randomized hides patterns but blocks server-side comparisons
Enclave with attestation lets the engine compare decrypted values in protected memory, and losing the key means losing the data

suggested.rationale: The envelope-crypto lab would have the learner work through the same key-wrapping pattern (a master key wrapping data keys) that Always Encrypted depends on.

lessons.plain: Imagine a bank vault that anyone on the public street can knock on. Private links and service endpoints are ways of building a private corridor from your own office to the vault, so visitors from the street cannot even see the door. A managed database normally has a public address. These features let your private network reach it through an internal route, and in the stricter form the public door can be closed completely. Choosing the right corridor, and making sure people actually find it, is the core of the job.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your application runs in one subnet of a virtual network, and the company's on-premises office must also reach the database without using the public internet. Before reading, what kind of network setting do you think would let both reach it, and what would you still have to check?
lessons.teach:
A virtual network (VNet) is your private network in the cloud. A subnet is a slice of it with its own address range. A service endpoint is a setting on a subnet that sends that subnet's database traffic over the cloud provider's internal backbone instead of the open internet, and tags the traffic with the subnet's identity. The database keeps its public address, so you then open its firewall to that subnet. A service endpoint does not give anything a private IP inside your network.

A private endpoint, also called the private link option, is different. It creates a network interface with a private IP address from one of your subnets and maps it to one specific database. Clients use that private address, so peered networks and on-premises networks reached over a VPN or dedicated circuit can connect, and public access can be turned off entirely.

Why it works: a client must resolve the server's name to the address it should use. For a private endpoint, a private DNS zone linked to the VNet maps the server name to the private IP. Without that link, the name resolves to the public address.

Worked example: the application subnet is 10.0.1.0/24 in VNet Prod. You create a private endpoint in subnet 10.0.2.0/24, and it receives 10.0.2.4. The private DNS zone maps the server name to 10.0.2.4. An app server in 10.0.1.0/24 resolves the name, gets 10.0.2.4, and connects privately. Public access is then disabled, so a laptop on the internet cannot reach the server.

Common mistake: creating the private endpoint but skipping the DNS link. Clients keep resolving the public name, and once public access is disabled they fail.

Consequence: a DNS gap can take every application offline during an incident even though the database itself is healthy. A private endpoint is the control that keeps data off the public address entirely, while a service endpoint only restricts which subnets may use the public one.

questions.prompt: Lakeside Clinic runs a managed SQL database. Its app servers sit in subnet 172.16.5.0/24 of VNet Clinic-Net. The team creates a private endpoint in subnet 172.16.9.0/24, and it receives the private IP 172.16.9.7. A private DNS zone linked to Clinic-Net maps the server name to 172.16.9.7, so the app servers connect privately. Public access is then turned off. A reporting server in the clinic's on-premises network, at 10.50.0.0/16 and reached over a VPN, also needs the private path, and its DNS queries go to the on-premises DNS server. The steps are: 1. Create the private endpoint in 172.16.9.0/24, which receives 172.16.9.7. 2. Link the private DNS zone to Clinic-Net. 3. [SKIPPED STEP] 4. Turn off public access. Which step belongs in position 3 so that the on-premises reporting server resolves the server name to 172.16.9.7?
choices: Configure the on-premises DNS server to forward the server's zone to a resolver that can see the private DNS zone.
Open the server firewall to the VPN public IP address so that on-premises clients can reach the public name.
Add a service endpoint on the on-premises gateway subnet and add that subnet to the server firewall.
Create a second private endpoint inside the 10.50.0.0/16 range so the on-premises clients get their own private IP.
questions.why: On-premises clients use their own DNS server, so that server must forward the database's name to a resolver that sees the private DNS zone, otherwise they keep getting the public address and fail once public access is off.

questions.prompt: A team wants a database to accept traffic only from one subnet, while the database keeps its public address. Which control fits, and what does it do in plain terms?
choices: A service endpoint on that subnet plus a firewall rule on the database, which sends the subnet's traffic over the provider backbone and restricts which subnet may use the public address.
A network security group on the database's public address, which encrypts all incoming traffic automatically.
A VPN gateway, which gives the subnet its own copy of the database inside the on-premises network.
A private endpoint, which gives the database a private IP inside the subnet and removes the public address.
questions.why: A service endpoint keeps the public address and limits access to chosen subnets, while a private endpoint is the one that assigns a private IP and can remove public access.

questions.prompt: A VNet called Orion-Net, with subnet 192.168.40.0/24, is peered to a VNet called Vega-Net that holds a managed database. Orion-Net's analysts must reach the database without any traffic touching the public internet. Which setup fits?
choices: Turn on a service endpoint for 192.168.40.0/24 and leave the database's public access enabled.
Create a private endpoint in 192.168.40.0/24 and skip the DNS link, since peering handles name resolution by itself.
Publish the database's public address in Orion-Net's routing table so traffic stays inside the peering.
Create a private endpoint for the database in a subnet of Vega-Net, link a private DNS zone to Orion-Net, and turn off public access.
questions.why: Because the analysts need a private address reachable over peering and the DNS name must resolve to it, a private endpoint with a DNS link is required, so the first option is wrong and that one is the answer only if it is listed correctly; the correct choice is the private endpoint with the linked DNS zone.

questions.prompt: After a team disables public access on a database, applications in a peered VNet begin failing with connection errors. The database is healthy and its private endpoint shows an assigned private IP. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The database's encryption key expired when public access was disabled.
The private endpoint was created in a subnet with too small an address range to hold the database.
The database name still resolves to its public address because no private DNS zone is linked to the application VNet.
The applications are using a service endpoint, which cannot carry traffic once public access is off.
questions.why: Clients resolve the server name to whatever address the DNS zone gives them, and without a linked private DNS zone they keep trying the public address, which is now closed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a service endpoint and a private endpoint for a managed SQL database, and name one limit or tradeoff of choosing the service endpoint over the private endpoint.
lessons.modelAnswer: A service endpoint is set on a subnet. It sends that subnet's database traffic over the cloud provider's internal backbone and tags it with the subnet's identity, so the database firewall can allow that subnet. The server keeps its public address, and the endpoint gives no private IP inside our network. The limit is that on-premises users cannot use it simply by being in a subnet. A private endpoint creates a network interface with a private IP in our subnet, tied to one database. Peered and on-premises networks can then reach it privately, and we can turn public access off. The tradeoff is more setup, since a private DNS zone must map the server name to the private IP, and the endpoint has a cost. I would use a service endpoint for a simple subnet-to-database case and a private endpoint when the data must not touch the public address.
rubricPoints: Service endpoint is a subnet-level setting that keeps traffic on the backbone but keeps the public address.
Private endpoint gives the database a private IP in a chosen subnet, scoped to one resource.
Private endpoints need DNS resolution to the private IP, or clients fail.
Tradeoff: service endpoints are simpler, while private endpoints reach on-premises and peered networks and allow public access to be disabled.

suggested.rationale: Tracing which network path a client's name resolves to and where traffic actually goes is the core skill here, and the planned virtual network path tracer would practise it.

lessons.plain: Data classification is the habit of sorting the information a company stores into groups by how sensitive it is and what kind of information it is, then writing those labels on the data itself. A customer's card number and a public product name should not be protected the same way. Once each column has a label, the team can decide which protections it needs, such as hiding it from some users, scrambling it when stored, or keeping a record of who reads it. Think of stamping folders in a filing cabinet with 'public', 'internal' or 'secret' so everyone knows how to handle what is inside before they open it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database has a table with customer names, email addresses, city names and card numbers. Before any training, which column would you protect most strictly, and what would you want to know about each column before deciding how to protect it?
lessons.teach:
A sensitivity label is a level that says how careful you must be with data, such as public, internal, confidential or highly confidential. An information type is a category that says what the data is about, such as personal contact details or financial details. Classification is the act of attaching both to a specific column. Discovery is an automated scan of a database that suggests which columns look sensitive; a person still confirms each suggestion. Classification works because controls are chosen per label, so one clear rule applies to every column with the same label instead of a guess made column by column.

Worked example. A Customers table has Name, Email, City and CardNumber. Step 1: a discovery scan flags Email and CardNumber as personal data and financial data. Step 2: an engineer confirms the suggestion and sets CardNumber to highly confidential with information type financial, sets Email and Name to confidential with personal contact data, and sets City to internal. Step 3: the team maps each label to controls, so highly confidential columns need the strongest protections and reviewed access, while internal columns need only basic access rules.

Common mistake: classifying the database once and never again. A migration adds a LoyaltyCardNumber column with no label, so it is silently treated as ordinary data. Consequence in a running system: a support report built by a junior engineer returns raw card numbers, and the audit later finds no record of who saw them because the column was never marked as sensitive.

A classification strategy is only as good as its labels, so every new column needs a label before it reaches production.

questions.prompt: A regional courier firm has a Drivers table with DriverId, LicenseNumber, Phone and ShiftStart. Step 1: a discovery scan flags LicenseNumber as a government identifier and Phone as personal contact data. Step 2: an engineer confirms both suggestions, sets LicenseNumber to highly confidential with information type government ID, sets Phone to confidential with information type personal contact data, and sets ShiftStart to internal. Step 3: a later release adds a column called TruckGpsHistory that holds location trails for each driver. Before this column reaches production, the team must ___
choices: attach a sensitivity label and an information type to the column, after a person confirms the choice
make it public so that support staff can query it without needing any review
copy the label from DriverId because it is the closest existing column in the table
leave it unlabelled until the next scheduled discovery scan runs, since the scan will label it automatically
questions.why: Every new column needs a label before production, and the label is set by a person confirming the choice, so an unlabelled or auto-assigned column would be treated as ordinary data.

questions.prompt: In a classification strategy, what is the difference between a sensitivity label and an information type?
choices: A sensitivity label says how carefully the data must be handled, while an information type says what kind of data the column holds.
A sensitivity label says what kind of data the column holds, while an information type says how carefully it must be handled.
Both are the same setting and the two names are interchangeable in the classification tool.
A sensitivity label is a password for reading the column, while an information type is the encryption method applied to it.
questions.why: The teaching text defines the sensitivity label as the level of care required and the information type as the category describing what the data is about.

questions.prompt: A university stores a Students table with StudentNumber, EmailAddress and ExamScore. The team labels EmailAddress and StudentNumber as confidential and ExamScore as internal. Why does classifying each column by label, rather than deciding column by column, help the team?
choices: It removes the need for any review, because the label itself enforces the rule without a person checking it.
It lets the team skip labelling new columns, because the rule for each label covers all future columns.
Each column with the same label gets the same clear rule, so the team does not have to guess a protection for every column.
It makes ExamScore automatically public, since internal columns are shared with every student.
questions.why: The teaching text says controls are chosen per label so one rule applies to every column with the same label instead of a separate guess for each column.

questions.prompt: A logistics company ran its discovery scan in March and labelled its columns. In June, a developer adds a RecoveryPin column to a customer table and no one labels it. What is the most likely consequence in the running system?
choices: Nothing changes, because labels apply to the whole database and not to individual columns.
The column is encrypted by default, so the missing label has no effect on who can see it.
The column is treated as ordinary data, so it may be read or reported without the stricter access rules that a sensitive label would require, and no audit trail shows who saw it.
The database automatically blocks all reads of RecoveryPin until someone labels it, which stops the reporting process completely.
questions.why: An unlabelled column gets no sensitive-data controls, so it can be exposed in reports and left out of the audit record, which is why every new column needs a label before production.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what data classification is, why a label on each column is more useful than one rule for the whole database, and name one limit of relying on automated discovery.
lessons.modelAnswer: Data classification means giving each column a sensitivity level and an information type, like confidential financial data or internal city names, so the team knows how to handle it. The advantage over a single rule for the whole database is that different data needs different protection. A blanket rule either over-protects harmless columns, which slows people down, or under-protects card numbers. Once labels exist, each label maps to controls such as masking, access limits and audit logging. The main limit of automated discovery is that it only finds patterns it recognises, so an unusual column name or a free-text field can be missed. A person must review the results and label anything the scan skipped, and must label new columns as they are added.
rubricPoints: Defines sensitivity label and information type as separate things attached to a column
Explains that controls are chosen per label, so one rule applies consistently
Notes that automated discovery only suggests labels and a human must confirm them
Names a limit: missed columns or new columns added later stay unlabeled

suggested.rationale: Choosing which label and which control fits a given sensitive column is a reasoning skill best practiced through an exam-style situation.

lessons.plain: An audit is a running record of what happens to a database: who logged in, which kinds of commands were run, and who changed permissions. Auditing does not stop anything by itself. It writes each event to a separate log that you can search later when someone asks what happened. Think of a security camera in a room. The camera does not lock the door, but if something goes missing, the footage shows who was there and when. Setting up an audit means choosing what to record, where the records are stored, and how long they are kept.
lessons.guessPrompt: A regulator requires proof of every time a staff member reads a customer's payment details, with records kept for seven years. Would it be enough to record only failed login attempts? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
An audit log is a stored, time-stamped list of events that happened on a database server or inside one database. An audit policy is the set of rules that decides which events get written down. Events are grouped into audit action groups, which are named bundles of event types, such as successful logins, failed logins, or statements that read data from a given schema. The audit destination is where the log is written: typically a storage account, a Log Analytics workspace (a central place to query logs), or an event stream.

Scope matters. A server-level policy applies to every database on that server, which is useful when a rule must cover all data uniformly. A database-level policy applies to one database and can add detail for sensitive data without recording everything elsewhere. Both can be used together.

Worked example. A payroll rule requires a record of every read of the salary table, kept for one year. Step 1: place the sensitive table in a database that gets its own database-level audit. Step 2: include the action group that covers reads of data in that schema. Step 3: send the output to a destination with one-year retention, so the records outlive the rule. Step 4: restrict who can read the log, because an audit trail that anyone can edit proves little.

Common mistake: assuming a failed-login log proves what people did with data. Failed logins only show attempts that were refused, so they say nothing about successful reads. Another mistake is setting short retention, so the evidence is gone before the audit happens.

Auditing records events; it does not block them. Its consequence in a running system is that a gap in retention or scope leaves a hole in your evidence that cannot be filled afterwards.

questions.prompt: A small clinic keeps its patient billing table in one database and must keep a record of every read of that table for 18 months. Its audit setup follows four steps. Step 1: place the billing table in a database that has its own database-level audit. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: send the audit output to a storage account with 18-month retention, so the records outlive the rule. Step 4: restrict who can read the log, so the trail cannot be edited by the people it watches. Which entry correctly completes the missing Step 2?
choices: Include the action group that covers reads of data in the billing schema, so those reads are written to the log.
Set the audit to block any update to the billing table, which both records and stops changes.
Turn on a server-wide policy that also records every successful login on the server, so the billing table is covered too.
Enable only the failed-login action group, since failed logins show who tried to reach the billing table.
questions.why: An action group bundles the event types to record, and reads of the billing schema are what the rule requires, while auditing records events rather than blocking them.

questions.prompt: In an audit setup, what is an audit action group?
choices: The rule that decides, for each database, whether the audit is turned on or off.
The storage account where the audit log is written and kept for its retention period.
A named bundle of event types, such as successful logins or reads of a given schema.
The query tool that a team uses to search the log for a specific user.
questions.why: The teaching text defines an action group as a named bundle of event types, which is what the policy uses to decide what gets written down.

questions.prompt: A team reviews only the failed-login entries for the last month of a payroll audit and concludes that nobody read the salary table. What is the main flaw in that conclusion?
choices: Failed-login entries are stored in the wrong destination, so the team must move them to a Log Analytics workspace first.
A one-month window is too short, because audit logs must cover at least a full year before anyone can review them.
Failed-login entries only show refused attempts, so successful reads of the salary table would not appear in that view at all.
Failed-login entries are blocked from being written whenever a table is read, so the log is always empty for reads.
questions.why: Failed logins record only refused attempts, so they cannot show what authorised users did with data, which requires logging of the successful events.

questions.prompt: A company runs 40 databases on one server. It wants one rule that records a uniform set of events across all 40, and it also wants extra detail recorded only for one database that holds card data. Which combination fits the scope guidance?
choices: Only a server-level policy, because a server-level policy cannot be combined with a database-level one.
Only a database-level policy on the card-data database, which leaves the other 39 databases with no audit.
A server-level policy for uniform coverage across all 40, plus a database-level policy adding detail for the card-data database.
A database-level policy on each of the 40 databases, with no server-level policy at all.
questions.why: A server-level policy covers every database uniformly, and a database-level policy can add detail for one sensitive database, and the two can be used together.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a database audit records, how you would decide between server-level and database-level scope, and one limit or tradeoff of relying on audit logs as your only control.
lessons.modelAnswer: An audit records events such as logins, failed logins, and data-access statements, and writes them to a destination like a storage account or a log workspace. I would choose scope based on the rule. If every database on the server holds regulated data, a server-level policy covers all of them uniformly. If only one database holds sensitive records, a database-level policy keeps the scope tight and avoids recording noise elsewhere. The main limit is that auditing only records. It does not block a bad action, so it must be paired with access controls. Another tradeoff is cost and volume: detailed action groups produce large logs, and retention has to match the rule, or the evidence disappears before anyone needs it. We also need to restrict who can read or change the log, because an audit trail that can be edited is weak proof.
rubricPoints: Audit records events and writes them to a destination; it does not prevent actions
Server-level scope covers all databases; database-level scope targets one database
Action groups select which event types are captured, so coverage must match the requirement
Retention must match the compliance period, and log access must be restricted
Auditing is evidence, not protection; pair it with access controls

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right audit scope, action groups, and retention for a compliance requirement is a reasoning task that a scenario builds better than a list of console steps.

lessons.plain: Change tracking is a database feature that notes which rows in a table were added, edited or removed since a point you choose, using a running version number. It does not keep copies of old values. Instead, a program that copies data elsewhere can ask what changed since its last visit, receive just the affected keys, and then fetch the current rows itself. It helps keep another system in step with a database without rereading every row each time. Think of a sign-in sheet that records which shelves were touched, not the books themselves.
lessons.guessPrompt: A search index copies a table of 500,000 products. To keep it current cheaply, what is the smallest thing the sync job needs to remember between runs, and why not just copy the whole table each time?
lessons.teach:
Change tracking is a feature of SQL Server and Azure SQL that records which rows in a table were inserted, updated or deleted, and gives each committed change a version number. Think of it as a log of which keys changed, not a copy of the data. It is built for consumers that check a database periodically and want only what is new since their last check, such as a sync job feeding a search index.

Two switches are involved. First you turn tracking on for the database and set how long change records are kept, called the retention period. Then you turn it on for each table, which should have a primary key so every change can be identified by its key. The database keeps a current version counter that rises as transactions commit. A consumer stores the version it last processed.

Worked example: a sync job last processed version 40. It asks for all changes after 40. The answer lists the keys of rows changed since then, each with an operation code (I for insert, U for update, D for delete). The job reads the live rows for inserted and updated keys from the base table, removes deleted keys from its index, and saves the newest version as its next starting point. The steps are: read the stored version, query the changes, apply them, store the new version.

Common mistake: assuming change tracking stores old values or a full history. It records only that a row changed and its key, so the consumer must fetch current data from the table. Another mistake is letting a consumer fall behind by more than the retention period. Its stored version then drops below the minimum valid version, and it must rebuild its copy in full.

In a running system, retention is both a storage cost and a recovery window. Longer retention keeps more change records but gives a stalled consumer more room to catch up, while shorter retention saves space and risks forced full resyncs.

questions.prompt: A travel firm's bookings sync stored change-tracking version 58 the last time it ran. The database's retention period has since cleaned up old change records, so the minimum valid version is now 60. Step 1: the job compares its stored version (58) with the minimum valid version (60) and sees that 58 is below the floor. Step 2: ___
choices: Wait for the next retention cleanup before running the sync again
Query changes after version 58 anyway, because older change rows may still exist
Move the stored version up to 60 and keep applying changes from there
Rebuild the whole copy from the live tables, since changes before version 60 are gone
questions.why: When a consumer's stored version falls below the minimum valid version, the change records it needs are gone, so it must rebuild its copy in full from the live tables.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team asks what a change-tracking query returns for a table. Which answer is correct?
choices: The old and new values of every changed column, for every row
The key and operation code of each changed row, with its version number
A binary copy of the table pages that changed since the last backup
A complete history of every row since the table was created
questions.why: Change tracking records only which keys changed, the operation (insert, update or delete), and a version number, so the consumer must read current data from the table itself.

questions.prompt: A search index sync stored version 300. The database's minimum valid version is now 340. Which outcome is correct?
choices: The consumer skips versions 300 to 339 and applies only the newest changes
The consumer must rebuild its copy in full, since its stored version is below the minimum valid version
Nothing happens, because the minimum valid version only affects how much storage is used
The database quietly moves the consumer's stored version forward to 340 and continues
questions.why: A stored version below the minimum valid version means the change records between them no longer exist, so the only safe recovery is a full rebuild of the copy.

questions.prompt: A payroll team needs the salary value an employee had before each update, for an audit trail. Which statement is correct?
choices: Change tracking alone cannot supply old values, so the team needs a separate mechanism that captures them
Use the change version number to work backward and recover the previous salary
Enable change tracking on the employee table and then read the stored old values from it
Lower the retention period so that old values are kept for longer
questions.why: Change tracking stores only keys, operation codes and version numbers, not old values, so it cannot meet an audit need for previous data on its own.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how change tracking lets a sync job find only the rows that changed, and name one limit or tradeoff they must plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Change tracking gives each committed change in a tracked table a version number, and the database records which keys changed at each version. A sync job remembers the last version it processed. On its next run it asks for changes after that version, gets back the keys with an operation code, reads current rows for inserts and updates from the table itself, and removes deleted keys from its copy. Then it saves the newest version. The main limit is that tracking only says a row changed, not what its old values were, so it cannot serve as an audit trail or an undo mechanism. The other tradeoff is retention: change records are kept only for a set period, so a consumer that falls behind past that window has to rebuild from scratch. We should set retention to cover our longest expected outage and alert when a job's lag approaches it.
rubricPoints: The consumer stores the last processed version and asks only for changes after it.
Change tracking records keys and operation types, not old values or full history.
The consumer must read current row data from the base table.
Retention limits how far back a consumer can catch up; falling behind forces a full resync.

suggested.rationale: Querying changes by version number is hands-on SQL practice that the planned SQL lab engine would cover.

lessons.plain: Dynamic data masking is a setting on a database column that changes what people see when they read it, without changing what is actually stored. Think of a receipt that prints only the last four digits of a card number: the full number exists in the card system, but the printout hides most of it. In Azure SQL Database, you mark a column such as a phone number or email address as masked, and anyone without special permission gets a disguised version in their query results. Users with the right permission still see the real value. It helps prevent accidental exposure, such as an analyst browsing production rows, but it is not a lock on the data itself.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support agent needs to confirm a customer's phone number but should not see the full number. A colleague says the fix is to encrypt the phone column. Without knowing any database internals, what would you expect a control that only changes what the agent sees to do differently from encryption, and which one matches the agent's need?
lessons.teach:
A masking rule is a function attached to one column that decides how that column's value is displayed to a user who lacks permission to see the real value. A masked column is a column with such a rule. The UNMASK permission is a database permission that lets a user or role see real values in masked columns. Masking happens at query time: when the database builds results, it applies the rule before returning each value to a user who lacks UNMASK. The stored bytes never change. Built-in rules include default, which replaces the value with a fixed placeholder based on the data type; email, which keeps the first letter and a fixed domain suffix; partial, which keeps a chosen number of characters at the start and end and fills the middle with a padding string you specify; and random, which returns a random number within a range you set for numeric columns.

Why it works: each time a query returns a masked column, the engine checks whether the caller holds UNMASK. If not, it substitutes the masked form. Permissions are granted to users or roles, and anyone with control rights over the database can grant UNMASK, so the control is only as strong as who holds that right.

Worked example: a Customers table has a Phone column holding 555-867-5309, with the rule partial(0, 'XXX-XXX-', 4). Step 1: a support agent runs SELECT Phone FROM Customers. Step 2: the engine sees the agent lacks UNMASK. Step 3: it keeps the last four characters, 5309, and fills the rest with the padding, returning XXX-XXX-5309. Step 4: the stored value is still 555-867-5309, and a user holding UNMASK receives the full number.

Common mistake: treating masking as security against a determined user. A user without UNMASK can still run filters such as WHERE Phone = '555-867-5309' and see whether a row matches, so they can infer the value. Masking also does not protect against anyone who can read the underlying data through backups or other copies.

Consequence in a running system: a report exported by a user without UNMASK contains disguised values, while the same export run by a privileged account contains real values, so the exporting role determines what leaves the system. Masking limits casual exposure by design; when a requirement says who may read the real value, pair it with least-privilege permissions and stronger controls.

questions.prompt: A gym chain stores member cards in a Members table. The Card column holds 4471-0826-3159-2048 and has the rule partial(0, 'XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-', 4). Step 1: a call-centre user without UNMASK runs SELECT Card FROM Members WHERE MemberId = 17. Step 2: the engine checks for UNMASK, finds it missing, and applies the rule. Step 3: this step is missing from the trace. Step 4: the stored card number is still 4471-0826-3159-2048, unchanged. What is missing at Step 3?
choices: The engine returns the full card number because the MemberId filter already limits which rows the user can see.
The engine returns the value with its last four digits replaced by XXXX, so the result ends in XXXX.
The engine returns XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-2048 to the call-centre user as the query result.
The engine stops the query and returns an access error because the user lacks UNMASK.
questions.why: The partial rule keeps the last four characters and fills the front with the padding string, so the masked form returned to a user without UNMASK is XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-2048.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is the UNMASK permission in a database that uses dynamic data masking?
choices: A permission that lets a user or role see real values in masked columns when results are built.
A role that is given automatically to every database owner and cannot be granted to others.
A permission that lets a user change the masking rule attached to a column.
A setting that encrypts a masked column on disk so that backups cannot read it.
questions.why: UNMASK is the database permission that lets a holder receive real values from masked columns, and it is checked at query time.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm masks the Email column in its Suppliers table with the email rule. A reporting account that lacks UNMASK exports the whole table to a spreadsheet, and a separate account holding UNMASK runs the same export. What does each export contain?
choices: Both exports contain masked addresses, because the email rule applies to every account that reads the Suppliers table.
The reporting account's export is blocked with an error, and the UNMASK account's export contains masked addresses.
Both exports contain the real addresses, because masking only changes the stored bytes once the export is saved.
The reporting account's export contains masked addresses, and the UNMASK account's export contains real addresses, because the exporting role decides what the query returns.
questions.why: Masking is applied when each query returns results, so the role running the export determines whether the output shows disguised or real values.

questions.prompt: A freight company has a Drivers table with a LicenceCode column that is masked with the default rule. A contractor without UNMASK runs SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Drivers WHERE LicenceCode = 'K7Q-220'. The count comes back as 1. What does this result show, and what should the team conclude?
choices: The count is a mistake caused by the default rule, and the stored code is not 'K7Q-220'.
The contractor cannot learn anything about the stored value, so masking fully protects the column from this kind of query.
The contractor can infer that a row with that code exists, so masking alone does not stop a determined user from testing values.
The contractor now holds UNMASK because the query returned a row, so the team should revoke the permission.
questions.why: Masking changes only what is displayed, so filters still run against the real stored values and a user can test a guess by checking whether rows match.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what dynamic data masking does in Azure SQL Database, when it is the right control for a requirement, and one limit a reviewer must not overlook.
lessons.modelAnswer: Dynamic data masking changes what a user sees in query results for specific columns, based on a rule like partial or email, while the stored data stays the same. Users who hold the UNMASK permission still see real values. It fits a requirement such as hiding phone numbers from support staff during routine work, or from analysts querying production. The main limit is that it is not access control. A user without UNMASK can still run filters, such as a WHERE clause on the exact value, and infer what the hidden data says. Anyone with control rights can also grant UNMASK, and backups or other copies of the data are not masked at all. So when a requirement says who must never read the real value, masking alone is not enough. It needs least-privilege permissions and other controls alongside it.
rubricPoints: Masking changes only what is returned to users without UNMASK; stored data is unchanged.
Name the masking functions and what each one shows, such as partial or email.
Identify UNMASK as the permission that reveals real values.
State the limit: filter-based inference and copies or backups are not protected, so it is not a security boundary alone.

suggested.rationale: The planned SQL lab would let the learner apply masking rules and test what different users see, which is the hands-on core of this objective.

lessons.plain: Imagine a notebook where each entry is glued to a fingerprint of everything written before it. If someone secretly rips out or rewrites a page later, the fingerprints stop matching, and you can see that something was changed. Azure SQL's ledger feature works this way for certain database tables. It does not stop a determined administrator from changing data, but it makes tampering detectable. Auditors and compliance teams use it when they need proof that financial or regulated records were not quietly edited. You will learn the two kinds of ledger table, what a digest is, and where the proof must be kept so it can be trusted.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a database administrator with full rights edits a row in a payments table yesterday, what would you need in order to prove later that the row was changed, and where would you keep that proof so the administrator could not also alter it?
lessons.teach:
A ledger table is a table in Azure SQL whose changes are recorded in a tamper-evident way. Azure SQL offers two kinds. An append-only ledger table accepts inserts only; existing rows cannot be updated or deleted. An updatable ledger table allows normal updates and deletes, and keeps every earlier version of each row in a companion history table. Each committed transaction is turned into a hash, which is a fixed-length fingerprint of its content; changing any input changes the fingerprint. Hashes of transactions are grouped into blocks, and each block's hash also depends on the previous block, forming a chain. A digest is a saved snapshot of the latest block hash at a point in time.

Why it works: the chain means that editing any old row changes the hash of its block and every block after it. When you verify the database, the system recomputes the chain and compares it with the digests you saved earlier. A mismatch shows that the data no longer matches what was originally committed.

Worked example: a payments ledger table receives transactions 1 to 5. Their hashes form blocks, and you save the digest of the latest block, D. Later, someone edits an amount directly in the history table. You run verification against D. The recomputed chain differs from the chain that D describes, so verification reports a mismatch at the affected block and you investigate.

Common mistake: storing digests in the same database as the data. An administrator who can rewrite the data can often rewrite the digests too, so the proof is worthless. Digests belong in separate, write-once storage that the database administrator cannot change.

Consequence: ledger does not block changes and does not run verification by itself. Someone must run verification on a schedule, and a failed check is an incident. Ledger tables also add some write overhead, which matters for high-volume workloads.

Ledger gives you evidence of tampering, not prevention. Access control and auditing still do the prevention work.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy keeps stock counts in an updatable ledger table. Step 1: each committed stock change is turned into a hash. Step 2: the hashes are grouped into blocks, and each block's hash depends on the block before it. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: someone edits a stock count directly in the history table. Step 5: verification is run against the saved digest and reports a mismatch at the affected block. What is the missing step 3?
choices: The database automatically blocks the edit in step 4 to protect the stock count.
The administrator recalculates each block hash after the edit so the chain matches again.
The administrator deletes the history table so the edit leaves no trace.
The administrator saves the latest block hash as a digest in write-once storage outside the database.
questions.why: A digest must be a saved snapshot of the latest block hash, kept in separate write-once storage, and it has to exist before the edit so verification has something earlier to compare against.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an append-only ledger table and an updatable ledger table?
choices: Append-only accepts inserts only; updatable allows updates and deletes and keeps earlier row versions in a history table.
Append-only allows deletes but not inserts; updatable allows inserts only.
Both kinds block all changes and differ only in how quickly their hashes are computed.
An updatable table deletes the old version of each row, so its history survives only inside digests.
questions.why: An append-only table accepts only inserts, while an updatable table allows updates and deletes and preserves each earlier row version in a companion history table.

questions.prompt: A team keeps its digests in the same database as its ledger data. An administrator with write access rewrites a payment amount and also rewrites the stored digest. What is the consequence?
choices: Nothing is proven, because a person who can rewrite the data may be able to rewrite the digests too, which removes the evidence.
The digests grow longer and the chain changes shape, which makes the rewrite easy to spot by eye.
Verification will flag the rewrite automatically, because digests stored in the same database are always checked against each other.
The rewrite is blocked at the point of change, so no digest is needed at all.
questions.why: Digests only work as evidence when they sit in separate write-once storage that the administrator cannot change; otherwise the tamper trail can be rewritten along with the data.

questions.prompt: A manager asks whether a ledger table prevents an employee from editing an existing row. Which statement is accurate?
choices: It does not stop the edit; it lets a later verification run detect that the data no longer matches the saved digests.
It stores a copy of every edit inside the digest, so no separate verification is needed.
It requires the digest to be stored in the same database so the edit can be undone.
It stops any edit at the moment it is attempted, so verification is only a backup check.
questions.why: Ledger provides tamper evidence rather than prevention, so a change is detectable only when verification is actually run and a failed check is treated as an incident.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never used ledger tables why a saved digest must be kept outside the database, and name one limit or tradeoff of choosing an append-only ledger table instead of an updatable one.
lessons.modelAnswer: Ledger makes changes tamper-evident by chaining hashes of committed transactions into blocks, and a digest is a saved snapshot of the latest block hash. The digest has to live outside the database, in write-once storage, because if the same person who can change the data can also change the digest, they can rewrite both and the proof disappears. Verification recomputes the chain and compares it against the digests you kept, so an edit shows up as a mismatch. The tradeoff with an append-only table is that it is strict: rows cannot be updated or deleted, so it suits records like audit trails or event logs, but it cannot hold data that legitimately needs correction. An updatable ledger table allows changes and keeps history, which is more flexible, but the history table has to be protected and monitored just as carefully. Ledger also adds write overhead, and it proves tampering rather than preventing it.
rubricPoints: Digests must be stored outside the database in write-once storage, otherwise tampering can rewrite the proof.
Verification recomputes the hash chain and compares it with saved digests to reveal mismatches.
Append-only tables accept inserts only, which suits immutable records but cannot hold corrections.
Updatable ledger tables allow changes and keep history, so the history table needs protection too.
Ledger detects tampering but does not prevent it, and adds some write overhead.

suggested.rationale: Hashing a chain of changes and detecting an edited row is best learned by building and breaking a small ledger-style table in a SQL lab.

lessons.plain: Row-level security is a rule attached to a table that decides which rows each person can see or change. Imagine a shared filing cabinet where each folder is tagged with an owner, and each drawer checks the tag against whoever opens it. The check works no matter which clerk asks or how they ask, so nobody has to remember to run it.
