Take two samples of the wait totals a known interval apart and compare the difference between them.
questions.why: Cumulative totals only describe the change between two points in time when you subtract an earlier sample from a later one over a known interval.

questions.prompt: After a failover, a team sees that the totals in sys.dm_exec_query_stats have dropped to almost zero compared with the previous day. What is the most likely explanation, and what should they do next?
choices: The plan cache doubled the counts during the failover, so the totals are duplicated and should be halved.
The view has been damaged by the failover and must be rebuilt before any numbers can be trusted at all.
The query tuning worked so well that the whole workload is now much cheaper, so they should close the investigation.
The failover cleared the cumulative counters, so they should start a fresh baseline and compare later samples against it.
questions.why: A failover or plan-cache eviction resets cumulative counters, so a sudden drop is usually a reset and needs a new baseline rather than a conclusion that the problem is fixed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use DMVs to tell whether a slow database is short on CPU capacity or running one expensive query, and name one limit of the data you would be relying on.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the resource-usage view for the recent window, which on Azure SQL Database is sys.dm_db_resource_stats, to see whether CPU or data I/O is close to the limit of the service tier. If CPU is pinned at the ceiling across the whole window, the cause is likely capacity or many queries together. If it spikes while the rest stays moderate, I would look at sys.dm_exec_query_stats sorted by total CPU time to find the query that dominates, then read its text with sys.dm_exec_sql_text. The limit I would name is that query stats are cumulative since the plan was cached, so a plan evicted or a restart resets them, and I would take two samples a few minutes apart to see what is happening now, not what happened since the last reset. The resource-usage view also keeps only about an hour of detail, so a problem from yesterday needs a different source.
rubricPoints: Names a current-state window and a cumulative window and says which fits a live symptom
Explains that the resource-usage view shows percentages against the service tier limit
Shows how to link an expensive query to its text using a DMV
States a limit such as resets on restart or plan eviction, or short retention

suggested.rationale: Running DMV queries against a live or simulated database and comparing samples is the hands-on skill, and the planned SQL lab would provide it.

lessons.plain: An index is a separate, sorted copy of some of a table's columns, with pointers back to the full rows, so the database can find matching rows without reading the whole table. It works like the index at the back of a textbook: you jump to the topic instead of flipping every page. Choosing index changes means finding which lookups are slow, adding an index that speeds them up, and removing indexes that cost more in writes than they save. The work is a trade-off: reads get faster, but every insert, update and delete must also update the indexes.
lessons.guessPrompt: A table has ten million rows and a query asks for the orders of one customer, filtering on customer_id, but it takes many seconds. With no other information, what single change would you most likely try first, and what might that change cost?
lessons.teach:
An index is a data structure the database keeps alongside a table. A nonclustered index stores a sorted list of chosen key columns, plus a pointer to each matching row. The clustered index is the table's main ordering, usually on the primary key. A key column is a column the index is sorted by. An included column is a non-key column stored in the index so a query can read it without going back to the table. A covering index holds every column a query needs, so no extra lookup is required. A seek is a targeted search through the sorted index; a scan reads every row or index entry.

Why it works: searching a sorted structure takes a few steps down a tree rather than reading every page, so the database touches far fewer pages when a query filters on the key columns.

Worked example: a query runs SELECT order_id, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42. First, without an index on customer_id, the engine scans all ten million rows. Second, you create a nonclustered index on customer_id with total included. Third, the engine seeks to customer 42 in that index, reads the matching entries, and returns the totals without touching the base table. Fourth, the execution plan now shows an index seek where it showed a scan.

Common mistake: adding indexes based on one slow query, or piling up indexes that duplicate each other. Each index uses storage and must be maintained on every write, so an over-indexed table gets slower to insert into. Before dropping an index, check whether it is actually used. Missing-index suggestions from the dynamic management views (DMVs, system views that expose the server's internal state) are hints to investigate, not orders to follow.

Consequence: on a busy transactional system, an over-indexed table can slow order entry at peak time even while the reports that use it run faster.

Index changes are worth making only when measurement shows that a specific query benefits and the write cost is acceptable.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm keeps a delivery_log table with forty million rows. The query SELECT parcel_id, eta FROM delivery_log WHERE depot_id = 17 scans every row. The team creates a nonclustered index on depot_id with eta included, and the execution plan now shows an index seek instead of a scan. The sequence has one missing step: step 4 is left blank. Which choice completes the sequence?
choices: Measure the insert and update rate on delivery_log to confirm the extra write cost of the new index is acceptable.
Accept the missing-index suggestions from the system views for more columns without checking whether they are used.
Add a second index on eta so that future queries filtering on eta also seek.
Rebuild the clustered index on parcel_id so the table's sort order matches the query's output column.
questions.why: After confirming a specific query benefits, the teaching text says an index change is justified only when the write cost is also acceptable, so measuring the insert and update load is the missing check.

questions.prompt: In a nonclustered index created as (store_id) with sales_amount included on a sales table, what role does each column play?
choices: store_id is an included column and sales_amount is the key column the index is sorted by.
store_id is the key column the index is sorted by, and sales_amount is a non-key column stored so reads can avoid the table.
Both store_id and sales_amount are key columns that set the sort order of the index.
Neither column is stored in the index; it holds only pointers to the table rows.
questions.why: A key column is the one the index is sorted by, while an included column is a non-key column stored in the index so a query can read it without going back to the table.

questions.prompt: A system view reports a missing-index suggestion for a three-minute reporting query on a busy order-entry table. Insert latency rose at peak hours after a similar index was added. What is the most sound response?
choices: Create the suggested index immediately, since the system view recommends it.
Investigate by measuring whether the query truly benefits and whether the added write cost at peak is acceptable before deciding.
Drop the clustered index, since it is the cause of the insert slowdown.
Ignore the system view entirely, because system views cannot report on indexes.
questions.why: The teaching text treats missing-index suggestions as hints to investigate, and an index change is justified only when measurement shows both a benefit and an acceptable write cost.

questions.prompt: On a clinic appointments table, a query filters on status and then selects patient_name and visit_time. The only index is on status, so each matching row needs an extra lookup back to the table. Which change removes those lookups?
choices: Add a second index on patient_name so the engine can scan it instead.
Remove status from the index so the engine scans the whole table rather than seeking.
Make the index clustered so the table is sorted by status.
Include patient_name and visit_time in the index so it covers every column the query needs.
questions.why: A covering index holds every column a query needs, so no extra lookup to the base table is required, and including the two columns achieves that.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should add an index on every column that appears in a WHERE clause so queries never scan. Explain to them in your own words what an index is, when it helps, and the limit or cost they are missing.
lessons.modelAnswer: An index is a sorted copy of selected columns with pointers to the full rows, so the database can seek to matching rows instead of scanning the whole table. It helps when a query filters on columns that select only a small fraction of rows, and it helps more when the index also includes the columns the query returns, so there is no extra lookup back to the table. The limit is that every insert, update and delete has to maintain each index, and each index uses storage. Indexing every filtered column would make writes slower and bloat storage, and it would not help columns where most rows match anyway. The sensible approach is to check the execution plan and the real workload first, add targeted indexes for the slow queries, and remove indexes that are never used.
rubricPoints: Defines an index as a sorted structure with pointers that enables seeks instead of scans.
States that an index helps most when the filter is selective and the query's needed columns are covered.
Names the write cost: every insert, update and delete must maintain each index.
Notes that indexes use storage and that unused or duplicate indexes should be found and removed.
Says index decisions should be based on measured query plans and workload, not on blanket rules.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission exercises index design, but the planned SQL lab would let the learner compare plans before and after an index change.

lessons.plain: When a database query is slow or uses too much computing power, one fix is to change how the query is written instead of adding hardware. This is about the query's construct: the particular patterns it uses, such as which columns it asks for, whether it wraps a column in a function, or whether it handles rows one at a time in a loop. Recommending a change means looking at measured resource use, such as how much data was read or how much processor time was spent, and then choosing the rewrite that lowers that use for the same result. The skill is pairing a specific construct with a specific symptom, not just saying make it faster.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two queries return the same rows from a large orders table. One filters with WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2024 and the other with OrderDate >= '2024-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2025-01-01'. Which one would you expect to read less data, and why?
lessons.teach:
A query construct is a specific pattern inside a SQL statement, such as the select list, a predicate (a condition in the WHERE clause), a join, a function call, or a loop. Resource usage is what the engine spends to run it. The main measures are logical reads (the number of data pages the engine touched, the usual main cost), CPU time (processor time), and elapsed time. In a test session you can see logical reads and time with SET STATISTICS IO ON and SET STATISTICS TIME ON. Query Store is a built-in history of query runtime statistics that shows which statements cost the most over time.

Why a rewrite helps: the engine can jump straight to matching rows through an index only when a filtered column is compared as stored. A predicate that wraps the column in a function forces the engine to compute the function for every row, so it cannot seek. A predicate that keeps the column bare is called sargable (able to use a search argument), and it lets the engine seek. Rewriting YEAR(OrderDate) = 2024 as a date range keeps the column bare.

Worked example (illustrative numbers): Step 1, Query Store shows the statement with high total CPU. Step 2, with STATISTICS IO on, the original reports 48,000 logical reads on Orders. Step 3, rewrite the predicate as a date range and run it against the same data. Step 4, the rewrite reports about 1,200 logical reads, because the engine now seeks instead of scanning.

Common mistake: assuming a rewrite is faster without measuring. Compare logical reads and CPU before and after on the same data. A change that saves reads on a query that runs once a day may not matter.

Consequence: on a shared database, a function-wrapped predicate on a busy table can raise CPU for every session, so one query can slow the whole service.

questions.prompt: A reporting team runs a query on a Shipments table that uses the predicate CONVERT(varchar(10), ShippedAt, 23) = '2025-03-14' to find one day of shipments. Query Store shows this statement has high total CPU. With statistics IO turned on, the query reports 310,000 logical reads on Shipments. Step 3, which is the missing step, is to replace that predicate with a version that keeps the ShippedAt column bare, then re-run the query on the same data. Which replacement is the correct one?
choices: ShippedAt >= '2025-03-14' AND ShippedAt < '2025-03-15'
LEFT(CONVERT(varchar(30), ShippedAt, 126), 10) = '2025-03-14'
CAST(ShippedAt AS date) = '2025-03-14'
questions.why: The date range leaves ShippedAt unwrapped, so the engine can seek on an index, whereas the other three choices still apply a function to the column for every row.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does it mean for a predicate to be sargable?
choices: The query returns its rows in a sorted order without an ORDER BY clause.
The predicate compares the column as stored, so the engine can seek into an index.
The statement is split across several processors so it finishes sooner.
The query stores its results in a temporary table for reuse by other sessions.
questions.why: A sargable predicate keeps the filtered column bare, which lets the engine jump to matching rows instead of checking each one.

questions.prompt: A product team has an index on Products.Price and runs SELECT Name FROM Products WHERE ISNULL(Price, 0) > 100. CPU is high on the shared database. Which change most directly addresses the cause?
choices: Raise the server's maximum memory setting so more pages stay cached.
Replace SELECT Name with SELECT * so the optimizer has more column choices.
Add a query hint that forces a parallel plan so the scan finishes sooner.
Move the ISNULL call out of the column side, for example by comparing Price > 100 directly.
questions.why: Wrapping Price in ISNULL stops the engine from seeking the index on Price, so removing the function from the column side is the construct change that fixes the cause.

questions.prompt: A team rewrote a nightly batch query to remove a function from its filter. Logical reads dropped from 9,000 to 8,500 on the same test data, and the query runs once a night. What is the most sensible conclusion?
choices: The saving is small for a once-nightly run, so check whether CPU and reads actually change the running service before calling it a win.
Logical reads are not a useful measure, so the change should be judged only by elapsed time.
Query Store will automatically confirm the improvement, so no further measurement is needed.
The rewrite is clearly faster, so it should be deployed to every query that uses functions.
questions.why: Measuring before and after on the same data is required, and a small read saving on a query that runs once a day may not affect the service at all.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why rewriting a WHERE clause that wraps a date column in YEAR() as a date range can reduce resource use, and name one limit or tradeoff of making that change.
lessons.modelAnswer: When a column is wrapped in a function, the engine has to calculate the function for every row, so it usually scans the whole table instead of seeking to matching rows. Writing the filter as a date range leaves the column bare, so the engine can seek through an index on it and read far fewer pages. That shows up as lower logical reads and CPU in the same test. The limit is that the gain depends on the table being indexed on that column and on the test data being realistic. Also, the rewrite must return exactly the same rows, including the boundary at the end of the year. I would confirm the result set matches and compare logical reads before and after before recommending it.
rubricPoints: Explains that a function on the column forces per-row computation and prevents an index seek
Describes the date range rewrite as keeping the column bare so the engine can seek
Names a measurable signal such as logical reads or CPU to confirm the gain
States a limit such as needing a suitable index, realistic data, or matching results exactly

suggested.rationale: The skill is comparing query rewrites against measured reads and CPU, which a planned SQL lab would let the learner do directly.

lessons.plain: When you ask a database for data, it does not simply fetch it. It first works out a route: whether to read a whole table or jump straight to matching rows, which index to use, and which order to combine tables in. The map of that chosen route is called an execution plan. Reviewing a plan means reading that map to see where the time and effort go, much like checking a satnav route that took a strange detour. Engineers do this when a query is slow, to find the step doing far more work than it should.
lessons.guessPrompt: A query that looks up one customer's orders runs slowly on a table with ten million rows, yet the query only returns twenty rows. Before any teaching, what do you think the database might be doing with all those rows, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
An execution plan is the sequence of steps the database engine chose to answer a query. Each step is an operator. A scan reads every row of a table or index. A seek jumps directly to matching rows through an index. A join combines two inputs, and a sort orders rows. Tools such as SQL Server Management Studio draw the plan as a graphic, and each operator shows a cost percentage. That percentage is an estimate made before anything runs, so treat it as a hint rather than a measurement.

The engine chooses a route using statistics, which are summaries of how many rows a column holds and how its values are spread. Good statistics let the engine estimate row counts and pick a sensible route. There are two main kinds of plan. An estimated plan is produced without running the query. An actual plan runs the query and records the real row counts beside the estimates.

Worked example: a query asks for orders from one customer. The actual plan shows a clustered index scan on a ten-million-row table. Step one: read the plan in data-flow order, which in the graphical view runs from right to left. Step two: the scan operator shows an estimate of 20 rows but an actual count of 9,800,000. Step three: that large gap means the statistics are stale or misleading, so the engine chose a scan it believed was cheap. Step four: updating statistics, or adding a suitable index on the customer column, lets the engine seek instead.

Common mistake: fixing the operator with the highest cost percentage without first checking whether the row estimate was far off. The cost figure is built on the same estimate, so it can mislead.

On a live system, a plan can change after a statistics update or a different parameter value, so the same query may suddenly become slow. A plan review is how you explain why.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a query for shipments bound for one port. The actual plan shows a clustered index scan on a 4-million-row shipments table. Step one: read the plan in data-flow order, which in the graphical view runs from right to left. Step two: the scan operator shows an estimate of 75 rows but an actual count of 2,600,000. Step three is missing and you must supply it. Step four: refresh the statistics on the port column, then check that the plan now uses a seek. Which choice correctly completes step three?
choices: Sort the cost percentages and fix whichever operator is highest, since that figure is the most reliable number in the plan
Conclude the statistics are stale or misleading, since the row gap shows a scan chosen on a cheap-looking estimate
Conclude the table is too small to need an index, so the scan is the right route and the query can be left alone
Run an estimated plan to replace the actual counts with predictions before deciding anything
questions.why: A large gap between estimated and actual row counts signals that the statistics behind the engine's choice are stale or misleading, which is why the scan was picked.

questions.prompt: A clinic's appointments system runs a lookup by patient ID, and its plan shows a seek on the patient index. What does that seek tell you about how the engine reached the rows?
choices: It read every row in the appointments table and filtered them afterward
It sorted the appointments by date before returning any rows
It stored a new estimate of how many patients the clinic has
It navigated an index directly to the matching appointment rows instead of reading the whole table
questions.why: A seek jumps straight to matching rows through an index, whereas a scan reads every row.

questions.prompt: A bank analyst wants real row counts for a slow ledger report, not predictions. Which kind of plan should they capture?
choices: An estimated plan, because it is produced without running the query
A statistics summary of the ledger's column value spread
An actual plan, because it runs the query and records real row counts beside the estimates
A plan showing only the cost percentage of each operator
questions.why: Only an actual plan runs the query and records the real row counts next to the estimates, so it answers the analyst's question.

questions.prompt: A retail team sees the highest cost percentage on a hash join and rewrites that join, but the query stays slow. An earlier step in the same plan shows an estimate of 1,200 rows against 18 million actual rows. What was the mistake?
choices: They should have deleted the statistics so the engine would reset its estimates to zero
They should have ignored the join and only tuned the final sort step
They acted on the cost percentage without first checking the row estimate, which the cost figure is built on
They should have run an estimated plan instead of an actual plan
questions.why: The cost percentage rests on the same row estimate, so a large estimate error upstream must be checked before fixing the most expensive-looking operator.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a slow query's execution plan is the real problem. Name one limit of the plan you are relying on.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first get an actual execution plan, not just an estimated one, because the actual plan records real row counts next to the engine's estimates. I would read the operators in data-flow order and look for a scan on a large table where I expected a seek, or a big gap between estimated and actual rows. A large gap usually means the statistics are stale or the query is hitting a case the engine misjudged. I would then check whether an index supports the filter, and update statistics before changing the query. The limit is that a plan shows one run under one set of conditions. A plan captured with one parameter value may not match what happens for other values or at peak load, so I would confirm the fix against real workload data before calling it solved.
rubricPoints: Distinguish an estimated plan from an actual plan and say which shows real row counts
Explain that a large gap between estimated and actual rows points to stale or misleading statistics
Identify a scan on a large table versus a seek as a signal to check indexing
Name a limit, such as a plan reflecting one run, one parameter value, or estimates before execution
Note that cost percentages are estimates and should not be the only evidence

suggested.rationale: No listed mission has the learner read execution plans, but the planned SQL lab would let them compare estimated and actual plans on a real query.

lessons.plain: Intelligent Insights is a built-in watchdog for a managed cloud database. It keeps an eye on how the database is working and notices when something goes wrong, such as queries suddenly slowing down or requests piling up behind each other. It then writes a plain explanation of the likely cause, along with suggested fixes. Instead of staring at graphs all day, you get a first round of detective work already done, and a trail of findings you can review, export, or send to other tools.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database that was fast last week is now timing out for users, and nobody changed the application code. Before any teaching, what would you want an automatic service to tell you first, and how would you expect it to decide that something is wrong?
lessons.teach:
Intelligent Insights is an automated diagnosis feature for Azure SQL Database. A diagnosis here means a finding that states what is wrong, why it is probably happening, and what to try next. The service watches telemetry, meaning recorded measurements of the database's work such as CPU use, waits (time queries spend waiting for a resource), and query run times. It compares the current workload with the database's normal behaviour, called its baseline, and raises an insight when the workload is clearly over a limit or performing worse than usual. Blocking is one pattern it looks for: one session holds a lock that another session needs, so the second session stalls.

Why it works: most slowdowns follow a few known patterns, such as CPU saturation, blocking, or a query whose execution plan (the strategy the engine picks to run it) has become worse. The service checks for these patterns continuously, so you do not need to know in advance which one to search for. Each insight is written to a log category called SQLInsights. You can route that log through diagnostic settings, which are the configuration that sends logs to a destination such as a Log Analytics workspace (a log store you can query), a storage account, or an event hub (a message stream). The portal also shows the findings on a dashboard.

Worked example: at 14:00 response times double. Step 1, the service samples telemetry and sees CPU close to its limit. Step 2, it sees that one query's duration rose sharply compared with its baseline. Step 3, it writes an insight naming that query and the pattern, with a suggested action. Step 4, you open the insight, read the query text, check the underlying metrics, and decide the fix.

Common mistake: treating an insight as proven fact and applying its suggestion blindly. An insight is an interpretation of telemetry, so confirm it against the actual metrics before changing anything. Intelligent Insights is also different from automatic tuning, which acts on the database itself; Intelligent Insights reports and explains, and it does not change the database on its own.

Consequence in a running system: a finding that is never routed to a log you read is no help during an incident, so the diagnostic routing is part of the setup, not an optional extra. Intelligent Insights gives you the explanation and the evidence trail, and a person still decides and carries out the fix.

questions.prompt: Harbor Freight Logistics runs an Azure SQL Database called orders-db for its warehouse team. At 09:30, the order-picking screen starts timing out. Intelligent Insights reports that one session holds a lock that another session needs, so the second session stalls. Step 1: the service samples telemetry and sees that the second session is waiting on that lock for much longer than its baseline. Step 2: the service identifies the blocking pattern and records a finding for it. Step 3: [missing step, to be chosen below]. Step 4: the on-call engineer opens the finding in the portal, reads the query text, checks the underlying metrics, and decides on the fix.
choices: The finding is written to the SQLInsights log, which diagnostic settings send to a destination the team can query.
The service saves the blocked query as the new baseline, so later findings stop flagging it.
The admin restarts orders-db so the service can write a fresh finding to the log.
The service ends the blocking session on its own, which clears the lock before anyone reads the finding.
questions.why: Each insight is written to the SQLInsights log, and diagnostic settings are what route that log to a queryable destination, so this is the step that makes the finding available to the team.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines what Intelligent Insights does in Azure SQL Database?
choices: It automatically creates and drops indexes on the database to keep query plans stable.
It measures disk latency for each physical drive that backs the database server.
It watches telemetry, compares the current workload with the baseline, and writes a finding that says what is wrong, why, and what to try, without changing the database itself.
It replaces the Log Analytics workspace as the store where the database's query history is kept.
questions.why: Intelligent Insights is an automated diagnosis feature that reports and explains findings from telemetry, and it does not change the database on its own.

questions.prompt: A retail company called Pemberton Outfitters sees its nightly sales report run much slower than usual. Intelligent Insights flags one query whose duration is far above its baseline. What is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Turn off Intelligent Insights so that the slow query stops being reported while the team investigates.
Assume the finding is wrong because the report is slow only at night, and leave the database as it is.
Open the finding, read the query text, and check the underlying metrics to confirm the explanation before changing anything.
Apply the index change the finding suggests straight away, since the finding is an accurate diagnosis.
questions.why: An insight is an interpretation of telemetry, so the correct practice is to confirm it against the actual metrics and query before acting on its suggestion.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has Intelligent Insights running on its Azure SQL Database, but it never set up diagnostic settings for the database. During a slowdown, the on-call engineer checks the Log Analytics workspace the team normally reads. What is the consequence?
choices: The team cannot query the finding from a log they read, so the finding gives them no help during the incident.
The service stops generating findings until diagnostic settings are added, so there is nothing to read later.
The database tunes itself using the finding, so the slowdown clears without any human action.
The finding is stored in the portal only, so the engineer can read it there with no further setup.
questions.why: A finding that is never routed to a log the team reads is no help during an incident, which is why diagnostic routing is part of the setup.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says Intelligent Insights will fix slow queries on our Azure SQL database automatically, so we can drop our own monitoring. Explain to them what the feature does, what it does not do, and one limit or tradeoff we must plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Intelligent Insights watches the database's telemetry, compares current behaviour with its normal baseline, and writes an insight when it finds a known pattern such as CPU saturation, blocking, or a query that has become slower than usual. Each insight names the likely cause and suggests an action. It does not fix anything by itself; a person still checks the evidence and makes the change. It also should not replace our own monitoring. The tradeoff is that insights only exist if the SQLInsights log is routed to a destination we actually read, such as a Log Analytics workspace with alerts on it. If that routing is missing, the findings sit unseen during an incident. We should keep our own metrics and alerts and treat the insights as one extra source of explanation.
rubricPoints: States that the feature detects and explains performance problems, using telemetry compared with a baseline
Says it reports and suggests but does not automatically fix the database
Names a limit: findings only help if the SQLInsights log is routed somewhere someone reads
Advises confirming an insight against the actual metrics rather than trusting it blindly

suggested.rationale: This is a product feature whose facts (what it reports, where logs go) are best learned from reading, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Index maintenance is the regular upkeep of the lookup structures a database uses to find rows quickly. An index works like the index at the back of a book: it lets the engine jump to the right page instead of reading everything. Over time, inserts, updates and deletes scatter an index's pages out of order and leave gaps, so lookups read more pages than they need. Maintenance means measuring that disorder and then either tidying the index in place or rebuilding it from scratch, at the right moment and without hurting the people using the system.
lessons.guessPrompt: A table's index has grown messy after months of updates and deletes, and queries are reading more pages than they used to. Before you learn the terms, what would you check first, and would you tidy the index in place or rebuild it? Give your reasoning.
lessons.teach:
Fragmentation is the term for how out of order an index is on storage. Logical fragmentation means the index pages are not in the sequence the index expects, and page density means how full each page is. Fragmentation grows as rows are inserted into the middle of a full page, which forces the engine to split that page and leave both halves partly empty. You measure it with a dynamic management function, which is a built-in view of the engine's internal state. In Azure SQL Database and SQL Server this is sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats, which reports the average fragmentation percentage and page count for each index.

There are two main actions. Reorganize walks the leaf level and compacts pages in place. It is online, uses little extra log and temporary space, and can be stopped partway without losing the work already done. Rebuild drops and recreates the index. That removes fragmentation and can reset the fill factor, a setting that reserves free space on each page for future inserts. Rebuild is heavier and uses more transaction log and temporary space, but it does the most work. A common rule of thumb is to reorganize when fragmentation is moderate and rebuild when it is high, with exact thresholds set by your workload rather than copied blindly.

Worked example: an index shows 45 percent fragmentation across 200,000 pages. The page count is large enough to matter, so you schedule a rebuild in a low-traffic window, enable online operations where the edition supports them, and then measure again to confirm the number dropped.

Common mistake: rebuilding every index every night regardless of measured fragmentation. This wastes log space, locks and time, and adds load to any replica that receives the changes. Small indexes often gain nothing from maintenance at all.

In a running system, a heavy rebuild during peak hours can block writers or slow replication, so timing matters as much as the command itself.

Index maintenance is a measured decision: check the fragmentation, choose the lighter action when it is enough, and schedule the heavier one with care.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs an Azure SQL Database with a shipments table. Its clustered index reports 28 percent average fragmentation across 12,000 pages. The index is large enough to matter, so you keep the measurement, and because the reading is moderate and the lighter action should be enough, you choose the action that compacts leaf pages in place, which is online, uses little log, and can be stopped partway. You then run it in a low-traffic window and measure again to confirm the number dropped. Which action did you choose?
choices: Rebuild, because a rebuild does the most work and removes all fragmentation
Skip maintenance, because 12,000 pages is too small for any index work to help
Drop and recreate the index by hand, because that is the only way to clear fragmentation
Reorganize, because it compacts leaf pages in place with little extra log and can be stopped partway
questions.why: Reorganize is the lighter action for moderate fragmentation, and the scenario explicitly says the lighter action is enough, so it is the right choice.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does logical fragmentation of an index describe?
choices: Each page holds too many rows for the engine to read
The table has more columns than the index covers
The index has been disabled by an administrator
The index pages are not in the sequence the index expects
questions.why: Logical fragmentation means index pages are out of the sequence the index expects, which is the definition given in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company's Azure SQL Database runs a nightly job that rebuilds every index without first checking fragmentation. Which consequence best describes the risk?
choices: The fill factor of every index is permanently set to zero
Queries fail with a syntax error on the next run
It wastes transaction log and temporary space and adds replication load, even on indexes that were barely fragmented
The engine stops collecting performance statistics for the database
questions.why: Rebuilding unmeasured indexes wastes log space, locks and time, and adds load to replicas, which is the common mistake described in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: A database administrator wants the average fragmentation percentage and page count for each index in an Azure SQL Database. Which built-in source fits this need?
choices: The Azure portal CPU percentage chart for the database
The SQL Server error log file
A manual row count of each table, run once a month
sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats, a dynamic management function that reports fragmentation and page count per index
questions.why: sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats is the dynamic management function the teaching text names for reporting average fragmentation percentage and page count per index.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would reorganize an index instead of rebuilding it, and name one limit or tradeoff of the method you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would reorganize when fragmentation is moderate and the index is large enough that a full rebuild would be expensive. Reorganize moves pages around inside the existing structure, so it needs little extra log and temporary space, it can run while users are active, and if it is interrupted the work done so far is kept. The tradeoff is that it does not reset the fill factor or fully clear heavy fragmentation, so on a badly fragmented index it may be too weak and may need several passes. In that case I would rebuild, accepting more log and locking cost, and I would schedule it in a quiet window and measure again afterward to confirm the result. Either way I base the choice on the measured fragmentation and page count, not on a fixed nightly job.
rubricPoints: Reorganize is lighter, runs in place, and can be stopped without losing progress.
Rebuild fully recreates the index and can reset the fill factor, at higher log and locking cost.
The choice depends on measured fragmentation and index size, not on a fixed schedule.
Names a tradeoff: reorganize may be too weak for heavy fragmentation, while rebuild costs more.

suggested.rationale: A SQL lab would let the learner measure fragmentation on a sample table and compare reorganize with rebuild, which reading alone does not provide.

lessons.plain: A database keeps a small summary of how the values in each column are spread out, such as how many rows hold each value or range of values. These summaries are called statistics. The query optimizer, the part of the database that decides how to run a query, reads them to guess how many rows a filter will return, then picks a plan based on that guess. When the summaries fall behind the data, the guesses go wrong and queries slow down. Statistics maintenance is the routine work of keeping these summaries fresh, by letting the database refresh them automatically and scheduling refreshes where automatic updates are not enough.
lessons.guessPrompt: A table grew from 10,000 rows to 2,000,000 rows, but a query on it suddenly got much slower without any change to the query text. What is the most likely reason, and what single action would you try first?
lessons.teach:
A statistic is a database object that stores a histogram, meaning a summary of the values in one column or a set of columns. The histogram groups values into ranges and records roughly how many rows fall in each range, along with an estimate of how many distinct values exist. Indexes create statistics automatically, and the database can also create statistics on columns used in filters. The optimizer uses them to estimate row counts, and those estimates drive choices such as seek versus scan, which join method to use, and how much memory to reserve.

Statistics go stale as rows change. The database can update them automatically once enough rows have changed. Older rules required roughly 20 percent of rows plus 500 changed rows; newer compatibility levels use a threshold that shrinks as tables grow, so large tables refresh sooner in proportion to their size. Automatic updates often sample only part of the table, which is faster but less precise when values are unevenly spread.

Worked example: an orders table had statistics built when it held 10,000 rows, when status 'open' was rare. It now holds 1,000,000 rows, and 600,000 of them are open. Step 1: the histogram still says 'open' is rare, so the optimizer estimates only a few matching rows. Step 2: it therefore chooses a nested loop join, which suits small inputs. Step 3: at run time that join performs hundreds of thousands of lookups. Step 4: a scheduled UPDATE STATISTICS with a full scan rebuilds the histogram, which now shows 'open' is common, so the optimizer chooses a hash join instead.

Common mistake: assuming that an index reorganize refreshes statistics. A reorganize only compacts index pages and does not update statistics, whereas a rebuild does refresh them with a full scan. Another mistake is trusting automatic updates for skewed data without checking whether sampling is hiding the skew.

In a running system, stale statistics produce plans that look fine on small test data but collapse at production volume, and a targeted statistics update is often the cheapest fix.

questions.prompt: A logistics company keeps a parcels table. Its statistics were built when the table held 5,000 rows, and only about 100 of those rows had status 'in_transit'. The table now holds 400,000 rows, and 300,000 of them are 'in_transit'. Step 1: the histogram still records 'in_transit' as rare, so the optimizer estimates very few matching rows. Step 2: the optimizer therefore expects a small input and chooses a nested loop join that does one index lookup per matching row. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: a full-scan statistics update rebuilds the histogram, which now shows 'in_transit' as common, so the optimizer picks a hash join.
choices: The optimizer reserves less memory for the query because it thinks few rows will match, and the sort spills to disk.
At run time the nested loop performs roughly 300,000 lookups, far more than the few it planned for, so the query runs very slowly.
The optimizer switches to a hash join during execution because the actual row count is larger than the estimate.
The optimizer rebuilds the statistics on its own before the query starts, so the plan changes without any action from the team.
questions.why: The nested loop was chosen for a small estimated input, so at run time it actually performs about 300,000 lookups, which is the cost the stale histogram hid.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a statistic store in the database?
choices: The exact list of every row in the column, kept in order so that searches never need the table.
A log of every query that has run against the column, with its elapsed time.
A summary of a column's values, grouped into ranges with a rough count of rows per range and an estimate of distinct values.
The physical page layout of an index, used to decide when to compact pages.
questions.why: A statistic is a histogram: grouped value ranges with approximate row counts, plus a distinct-value estimate, which the optimizer uses to estimate row counts.

questions.prompt: A team reorganizes all indexes on a sales database every night. Query plans still go bad after large data loads, and the team asks whether the nightly job refreshes the statistics. What is the correct answer?
choices: No, because a reorganize only compacts index pages and does not update statistics; a rebuild or an explicit statistics update with a full scan would refresh them.
Yes, because reorganizing an index rebuilds its histogram with a full scan of the table.
No, because statistics can only be refreshed by restarting the database server.
Yes, because reorganizing deletes the old statistics and forces the database to recreate them from a sample.
questions.why: A reorganize compacts index pages but leaves statistics stale, so the fix is a rebuild or an explicit statistics update with a full scan."

questions.prompt: Under the newer threshold behaviour described for automatic statistics updates, why do very large tables get their statistics refreshed sooner, in proportion to their size, than under the older fixed rule?
choices: Because the newer rule refreshes statistics on a fixed schedule regardless of how many rows changed.
Because the newer rule only applies to tables that have no indexes, which are usually the largest.
Because the newer rule always scans every row, so no sampling error can occur on large tables.
Because the threshold of changed rows shrinks as the table grows, so a smaller share of rows changing is enough to trigger an update.
questions.why: The newer compatibility levels use a threshold that shrinks as tables grow, so a smaller fraction of changed rows triggers an automatic update on a big table.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a query that was fast last month became slow after a large data load, and name one limit or tradeoff of the fix you would propose.
lessons.modelAnswer: The data load changed the spread of values in the table, but the statistics the optimizer uses still describe the old data. Those stale histograms make the optimizer estimate far fewer matching rows than actually exist, so it picks a plan built for small inputs, such as nested loop joins, and that plan does far too much work at the new volume. I would check whether the statistics on the filtered columns were last updated before the load, then run an update with a full scan on those tables. The limit is that a full scan takes time and resources on a large table, so I would schedule it off-peak. Also, the update only fixes the estimates. If the query still performs poorly, the cause may be a missing index or the query shape, and those need separate checks.
rubricPoints: Stale statistics describe the old data distribution, so row estimates are wrong.
Wrong estimates lead the optimizer to choose a plan unsuited to the current volume.
A targeted statistics update, ideally with a full scan, refreshes the histogram.
A full scan costs time and resources, so scheduling and tradeoffs matter.
Statistics fix estimates only; other causes such as missing indexes must be checked separately.

suggested.rationale: A planned SQL lab would let the learner watch row estimates change before and after a statistics update, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Database integrity checks are routine tests that ask whether the data inside a database is still internally consistent. They confirm that every block of storage can be read, that indexes point to the right rows, and that the records tracking which storage belongs to which table still match what is actually there. A database can look healthy for months while a disk quietly alters a bit or a bug writes a bad link. An integrity check finds that damage early, while clean backups still exist to recover from. Think of it as a building inspector walking the floors before a ceiling falls.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a database returns correct-looking results every day, what might still be wrong with it, and how would you find out without waiting for a customer to complain?
lessons.teach:
A page is the fixed-size block (8 KB in SQL Server) that a database engine reads and writes as one unit. Corruption means a page or a structure built from pages no longer matches the rules the engine relies on. A checksum is a small number computed from a page's bytes and stored with it. When the page is written, the engine computes and stores the checksum. When the page is later read, the engine recomputes it; if the numbers differ, the page changed after it was written, and the engine raises an error instead of quietly returning bad values. The page verify setting controls this behaviour, and CHECKSUM is the mode that stores and verifies these numbers.

A single page read only sees one page, so a full check is needed for cross-links. DBCC CHECKDB is the command that checks an entire database: allocation records, table and index structure, and the links between pages. DBCC CHECKTABLE narrows the check to one table, which costs less time and I/O on large databases.

Worked example: a page is written with checksum 4711. Months later a failing disk returns slightly different bytes. Step one, the read fetches the page. Step two, the engine recomputes the checksum and gets a different value. Step three, it reports an error for that page. Step four, the team restores or repairs that page from known-good data, rather than letting a query silently return a wrong balance.

Common mistake: treating a successful backup as proof of health. A backup can copy corrupt pages, so the only way to know is to run the check. Another mistake is running repair options in production without a current backup, because some repair choices delete the damaged rows.

Consequence: if nobody checks, a corrupt index on a billing table can keep serving wrong totals for weeks, and each new backup carries the damage forward. Scheduled integrity checks, plus page checksums and tested restores, keep the last clean copy recent and usable.

questions.prompt: A payroll archive database runs on a SQL Server virtual machine. A page in its salary history table was written with checksum 30215. Weeks later, a read of that page recomputes the checksum and gets 30290, so the page no longer matches what was stored. Step one: the read fetches the page. Step two: the engine recomputes the checksum and gets 30290, which differs from the stored 30215. Step three: ____. Step four: the team restores that page from known-good data before anyone relies on the salary figures.
choices: The engine stores 30290 as the new checksum so that later reads of the page pass without an error.
The engine raises an error for that page instead of quietly returning the altered values.
The engine returns the page to the query with a warning, and the query's results are used as normal.
The engine automatically runs DBCC CHECKDB on the whole database and drops the damaged table.
questions.why: Because the recomputed checksum differs from the stored one, the page changed after it was written, and the engine's design is to raise an error rather than silently return bad values.

questions.prompt: Which check examines allocation records, table and index structure, and the links between pages across an entire database?
choices: DBCC CHECKDB, which checks the whole database
Checking the row count of each table against the previous night
Running a backup with the verify option turned on
Reading a single page to confirm its checksum matches
questions.why: DBCC CHECKDB covers the full database, including cross-links between pages, which a single page read cannot see.

questions.prompt: A team's order database has passed its nightly backup for six months without a failure. Someone concludes the database has no corruption. What is the flaw in that conclusion?
choices: Backups compress pages, so they always hide small errors that a check would catch.
Six months is too short a period for any corruption to appear in a database.
Backups never copy index pages, so index corruption cannot be carried forward.
A successful backup only shows the copy finished; it can copy corrupt pages, so an integrity check is still needed.
questions.why: A backup copies whatever pages exist, corrupt or not, so only running an integrity check proves health.

questions.prompt: A reporting table on an Azure SQL Managed Instance shows corruption errors. A colleague proposes running a repair option right away, and there is no recent backup of the database. What should happen first?
choices: Restore last month's backup over the database without first checking whether the current data is damaged.
Run the repair immediately, since the table is only used for reports and can be rebuilt later.
Take and verify a current backup before running any repair, because some repair choices delete damaged rows.
Turn off page checksums so the errors stop appearing while the repair is planned.
questions.why: Some repair options remove damaged rows, so a current, verified backup must exist first to avoid permanent data loss.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we run a full integrity check on a schedule even when the database seems to be working fine, and name one limit or cost of doing so.
lessons.modelAnswer: A database can look healthy while storage or a bug has quietly damaged a page or an index. Users only notice when a query returns a wrong result or fails, and by then every new backup may contain the damage. A scheduled full check, such as DBCC CHECKDB, reads the whole database and cross-checks its internal structures, so we find corruption while a clean backup from before it still exists. The limit is cost: a full check reads everything, takes time and I/O, and can slow other work, so on large databases we might check one table at a time or run it in a quiet window. A clean check also only proves the state at that moment, which is why we pair it with page checksums and test restores.
rubricPoints: A full integrity check reads and cross-checks the whole database, not just one page.
Corruption can be silent, and backups can carry damage forward.
Scheduling the check preserves a clean backup to restore from.
The cost is I/O and time, so large databases may check table by table in quiet windows.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission exercises integrity checks, and the core skill is explaining the scheduling and cost tradeoff in your own words.

lessons.plain: Automatic tuning is a database service that watches how your queries run and makes certain fixes on its own, without a person writing the change. Think of a navigation app that notices a road is blocked, reroutes you, then checks whether the new route is actually faster and goes back if it is not. In Azure SQL Database you choose which kinds of fix it may apply: switching a query back to a plan that used to work, adding an index that would speed up a slow query, or removing an index that nobody uses. You can set this for one database or let it follow a server-wide default. The skill is knowing which fixes are safe to allow automatically and which need a person to review them first.
lessons.guessPrompt: A query that ran in 20 ms last week now takes 900 ms, and nobody changed its code. What could have changed in the database, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A query plan is the database's step-by-step recipe for answering a query, such as which index to read and in what order. An index is a sorted lookup structure that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table. Query Store is a built-in history inside the database that records each query, the plans it used, and how long those plans took over time. Automatic tuning in Azure SQL Database depends on Query Store, so Query Store must be on.

Automatic tuning has three options. FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN watches for plan regression, meaning a query became slower after the database switched to a newer plan, and pins the query back to the last plan that performed well. CREATE_INDEX looks for queries that scan too much data and creates an index that would help them. DROP_INDEX removes an index that costs time on every write and is not helping any query. Each option can be set to apply its changes automatically, or to only recommend them for a person to apply. After an automatic change, the service checks the result and reverts it if performance got worse.

Worked example. On Monday a query runs in 20 ms. On Tuesday, a statistics update changes the optimizer's estimates and it picks a new plan, and the query takes 900 ms. Step 1: Query Store already holds the Monday plan and its timings. Step 2: FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN detects that the new plan runs much slower. Step 3: it forces the Monday plan for that query. Step 4: the query returns to about 20 ms, and the action is recorded so you can see what changed and when.

Common mistake: treating automatic tuning as a switch that fixes everything. It only acts on what Query Store has recorded and on the options you enabled. Turning on automatic index creation for a write-heavy table can slow every insert and update, because each new index must be maintained.

In a running system, an automatically created index may speed up reads while adding write cost, so the tuning actions should be reviewed regularly.

questions.prompt: A shipping company's database has a query that lists late parcels. Last week it ran in 60 ms. After a statistics update, the optimizer chose a new plan and the query now takes 1,500 ms. Query Store, the built-in history of plans and their timings, still holds the earlier 60 ms plan. Step 1: FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN notices the new plan is much slower than the recorded one. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: The query returns to about 60 ms and the action is logged so the change can be reviewed. Which choice correctly fills the missing step?
choices: The service pins the query back to the earlier plan that performed well.
The service deletes the slow plan from Query Store so it can never be chosen again.
The service switches Query Store off so the slowdown stops being recorded.
The service creates a new index on every table the parcel query touches.
questions.why: FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN responds to plan regression by pinning the query to the last plan that performed well, which is the plan Query Store recorded, while the other choices either remove history, create unrelated indexes, or disable the recording that automatic tuning depends on.

questions.prompt: Which automatic tuning option looks for an index that adds cost to every write and is not helping any query, then removes it?
choices: Query Store
DROP_INDEX
FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN
CREATE_INDEX
questions.why: DROP_INDEX targets indexes that slow writes without benefiting any query, while FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN handles plan regression and CREATE_INDEX adds indexes rather than removing them.

questions.prompt: A team enabled automatic tuning on their Azure SQL Database but has Query Store turned off. What is the most likely result?
choices: Query Store turns itself on the first time an index is created by the service.
All queries run faster because the service skips recording plan history.
Automatic tuning has no recorded plan and timing history to act on, so it cannot make informed changes.
Automatic tuning works normally because each option collects its own history.
questions.why: Automatic tuning depends on Query Store, so with Query Store off there is no recorded history for the tuning actions to rely on.

questions.prompt: A write-heavy orders table is getting slower inserts after automatic index creation was enabled. The team still wants index suggestions, but wants a person to review them before anything is built. Which setting fits this requirement?
choices: Turn on DROP_INDEX automatically to offset the new index cost.
Turn off Query Store so the service stops creating indexes.
Set CREATE_INDEX to recommend only, so a person applies changes after review.
Set FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN to apply changes automatically on this table.
questions.why: Each automatic tuning option can be set to recommend changes rather than apply them, and CREATE_INDEX in recommend-only mode fits the need to review before building an index.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Azure SQL Database automatic tuning does, and name one limit or tradeoff you would warn them about before they let it create indexes automatically.
lessons.modelAnswer: Automatic tuning in Azure SQL Database uses Query Store's history of query plans and timings to make fixes without a person doing them. The main options are forcing a query back to its last known good plan when a newer plan regresses, creating an index that helps a query scanning too much data, and dropping an index that is not used. Each option can apply changes automatically or only recommend them. The limit I would flag is that automatic index creation is not free. Every new index has to be updated on each insert, update, and delete, so a write-heavy table can get slower even while some reads get faster. Before enabling index changes automatically, I would check the write load and review the recorded tuning actions, and I would keep the plan-forcing option separate from index decisions when I evaluate results.
rubricPoints: Describes automatic tuning as service-driven fixes based on Query Store history
Names at least two options such as forcing the last good plan, creating indexes, or dropping indexes
Explains that automatic index changes add write maintenance cost
Mentions that actions should be reviewed or that the setting can be limited to recommendations

suggested.rationale: A planned SQL lab would let the learner watch a plan regression and the effect of a forced plan or index change directly, which is the reasoning this objective needs.

lessons.plain: A database server has a set of instance-wide switches and dials that control how it uses processors, memory and parallel work for every database it hosts. Configuring server settings for performance means checking those dials against the machine and the workload, then changing only the ones that help. It is like the house rules for a busy kitchen: how many cooks may work on one dish at once, how much counter space is kept for the stove, and when a task is big enough to split across the team. The defaults are generic, so they are rarely the best fit for every server. A careful engineer writes down the current value, changes one thing, and measures the effect before moving on.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server has 16 processor cores and most of its queries are small, quick lookups. Before any teaching, what do you think happens if the server lets every query split its work across all 16 cores, even the tiny ones?
lessons.teach:
A server setting is an instance-wide option that changes how the database engine behaves for every database on that server. On SQL Server and Azure SQL Managed Instance you read and change these options with the system stored procedure sp_configure, and you apply a change with RECONFIGURE. Advanced options must be shown before they can be changed. Azure SQL Database does not expose most instance-level settings; there you tune behaviour per database using database-scoped configurations instead.

Three settings matter most. Max degree of parallelism (MAXDOP) caps how many processor threads a single query may use at once; the default of 0 lets the engine use as many as it likes, with no fixed cap. Cost threshold for parallelism sets how expensive a query plan must be before the engine bothers to run it in parallel; the default of 5 is low on modern hardware, so many small queries split across threads for little gain. Max server memory caps how much memory the engine's buffer pool may take, leaving room for the operating system.

Why it works: parallelism pays off only when a query is big enough that splitting its work beats the cost of coordinating the threads. Raising the threshold keeps small queries on a single thread and leaves the other cores free for the large queries that really benefit.

Worked example. A 16-core server runs an order-entry workload full of short lookups. Step 1: read the current values with sp_configure and note that cost threshold is 5 and MAXDOP is 0. Step 2: set cost threshold for parallelism to 50 and MAXDOP to 8. Step 3: run RECONFIGURE to apply the change. Step 4: compare query durations and CPU use against the baseline captured before the change.

Common mistake: setting max server memory to the full physical RAM, which starves the operating system, causes paging, and slows everything on the machine.

Consequence: a poor parallelism setting can make the whole server slower under load, not just one query, because threads queue behind each other. Every instance-level change affects all workloads on that server, so each change must be measured.

questions.prompt: A reporting server runs SQL Server on an Azure VM with 24 cores. Its nightly ETL jobs are slow, and the team wants to test whether parallelism is the cause. Step 1: run sp_configure to read the current values; cost threshold for parallelism is 5 and MAXDOP is 0. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: run RECONFIGURE to apply the change. Step 4: compare the ETL run times and CPU use against a baseline captured before the change. What belongs in Step 2?
choices: Set MAXDOP to 0 so the engine can choose freely, and leave the cost threshold at 5
Set max server memory to the full 128 GB of installed RAM
Change the database-scoped configuration on the reporting database to 30
Use sp_configure to set cost threshold for parallelism to 30 and MAXDOP to 6
questions.why: Step 2 is where the new values are written with sp_configure, and the RECONFIGURE in Step 3 then applies them; the other options either leave the values unchanged or use the wrong setting.

questions.prompt: Which server-level setting caps how many processor threads one query may use at the same time?
choices: Max server memory
Database-scoped configuration
Cost threshold for parallelism
Max degree of parallelism (MAXDOP)
questions.why: MAXDOP is the instance-wide cap on threads per query, while cost threshold decides whether a plan runs in parallel at all.

questions.prompt: An administrator sets max server memory on a 64 GB SQL Server machine to 64 GB and runs RECONFIGURE. What is the most likely result?
choices: The operating system is starved of memory, causing paging that slows everything on the machine
Queries get faster because the buffer pool can use every byte of RAM
Nothing changes, because the cap only applies to databases created afterwards
The engine automatically lowers its own cap to leave room for the OS, so there is no effect on other work
questions.why: Setting the cap to all physical RAM leaves no room for the operating system, which leads to paging and a slower machine overall.

questions.prompt: You manage an Azure SQL Database and want to change how it handles query parallelism for one database only. Which approach fits?
choices: Edit cost threshold for parallelism in a shared server setting
Set a database-scoped configuration on that database, because most instance-level settings are not exposed in Azure SQL Database
Change max server memory through the instance settings
Run sp_configure on the logical server to change MAXDOP for every database
questions.why: Azure SQL Database does not expose most instance-level settings, so per-database database-scoped configurations are the tuning control to use.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why letting every query run in parallel across all cores can slow a busy server down, and name one limit or risk of changing these server settings without first capturing a baseline.
lessons.modelAnswer: Parallelism splits one query's work across several threads, and that only helps when the query is big enough to make the split worthwhile. For a short lookup, the engine spends more time starting, coordinating and merging threads than it saves, and under load those threads compete with other requests for the same cores, so the whole server gets slower. The fix is at server level: raise cost threshold for parallelism so small plans stay serial, and cap MAXDOP so one query cannot take every core. The limit is that these settings apply to the whole instance, so a value that helps reporting queries may hurt the transactional workload. Without a baseline of current durations and CPU use, you cannot tell whether a change helped or caused the regression.
rubricPoints: Parallelism only helps when a query is large enough to outweigh thread coordination overhead
Cost threshold for parallelism keeps small plans serial; MAXDOP caps threads per query
Instance-level settings affect every database and workload on the server
Capture a baseline before changing a setting so the effect can be measured

suggested.rationale: A planned SQL lab would let the learner change instance settings on a safe copy and measure the effect against a baseline, which is the skill this objective tests.

lessons.plain: Resource Governor is a feature in SQL Server that lets an administrator set limits on how much processor, memory and disk work different kinds of requests can take from a shared server. Think of a restaurant kitchen with one stove: if the bulk-catering team gets a set share of burners, a huge catering order cannot starve the people ordering single dishes. Sessions are sorted into groups as they connect, and each group draws from a pool with a floor and a ceiling. The goal is predictable performance for important work when several kinds of work compete, not making any single query faster.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a nightly report and the customer-facing app share one database server, and the report keeps the processor busy enough to slow the app, what kind of setting would you change to protect the app without rewriting either program?
lessons.teach:
Resource Governor is a SQL Server feature that controls how shared server resources are split between workloads. It is available in some editions and deployments only, so check which product you are working with, since Azure SQL Database manages limits through its service tier. Three named parts work together. A workload group is a bucket of sessions that share the same settings. A resource pool is the slice of CPU, memory and disk I/O that one or more groups draw from. A classifier function is a small user-defined function that runs when a new session connects and returns the name of the workload group that session should join.

Why it works: the pool sets a minimum (guaranteed only when resources are contended) and a maximum (a hard ceiling). Group settings can further limit concurrent requests, memory grant size per request, and degree of parallelism. Because limits are enforced per group, a reporting workload can be capped without touching its queries.

Worked example: an administrator creates a pool capped at 40 percent CPU and assigns a group named reporting to it. Step 1: a report tool connects using a login called reporting_user. Step 2: the classifier function reads the login name and returns the reporting group. Step 3: the reporting requests now compete only inside the 40 percent ceiling, so sessions in the default group keep the remaining capacity. Step 4: the administrator runs the reconfigure command so the changes take effect.

Common mistake: assuming a change applies to sessions that are already connected. The classifier runs only when a session connects, so existing sessions keep their group until they reconnect.

Consequence: a classifier that errors or always returns the default group quietly disables the intended limits, so checking the actual usage of each group is the only reliable way to confirm the setup works. Resource Governor controls sharing; it does not make a slow query faster.

questions.prompt: A payroll company uses Resource Governor to keep its month-end close from starving the rest of the server. The administrator sets a pool with a minimum of 10 percent CPU and a maximum of 30 percent CPU, and creates a group named month_end that draws from that pool. A classifier function is updated so that a login named close_svc returns the month_end group. Step 1: at 09:00 a close_svc session connects before the change and is already running. Step 2: the administrator runs the reconfigure command so the new pool and classifier are active. Step 3: the administrator checks the open close_svc session and finds it still reports the default group. Missing step: what must happen for that already-open session to move into month_end?
choices: The administrator must raise the pool maximum above 30 percent so the session can claim the new group.
The server must be restarted so the pool minimum of 10 percent is reserved for the session.
The administrator must rename the close_svc login to match the group name month_end.
The session must disconnect and connect again, because the classifier runs only when a session connects.
questions.why: The classifier runs only at connection time, so an existing session keeps its original group until it reconnects and the classifier runs again.

questions.prompt: In Resource Governor, what does a classifier function do?
choices: It returns the name of the workload group a newly connecting session should join.
It lists every login that has ever connected to the server.
It sets the hard CPU ceiling for a resource pool.
It rewrites slow queries so they use fewer resources.
questions.why: The classifier is a small user-defined function that runs when a session connects and returns the workload group name for that session.

questions.prompt: A nightly export job on a shared database server is slowing down daytime users. The team wants to cap how much CPU the export can use without editing the export's queries. Which Resource Governor setting fits this requirement?
choices: Set the resource pool minimum for the default group to 90 percent.
Rename the export login so it falls into the default group.
Increase the degree of parallelism on the default group only.
Put the export's group in a pool with a maximum CPU ceiling.
questions.why: Limits are enforced per group through the pool, and a pool maximum is a hard ceiling, so the export can be capped without changing its queries.

questions.prompt: A team creates a classifier function and a group, but after reconfiguring, every session still reports the default group and the intended limits never appear to apply. What is the most likely cause, and how should it be confirmed?
choices: The classifier is returning the default group or erroring, so the intended limits are silently bypassed; checking actual usage per group confirms it.
The queries must be rewritten, because Resource Governor makes slow queries faster.
Resource Governor cannot cap CPU, so the group limits are always ignored by design.
The pool minimum is too high, so the limits are switched off automatically.
questions.why: A classifier that errors or always returns the default group quietly disables the intended limits, and checking each group's real usage is the reliable way to confirm the setup works.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Resource Governor does and why you would use it, then name one limit or tradeoff of using it instead of tuning the slow query itself.
lessons.modelAnswer: Resource Governor splits a shared SQL Server between workloads. You define workload groups, each attached to a resource pool with a minimum and maximum share of CPU, memory and disk. A classifier function runs when a session connects and decides which group it joins, so a reporting login can be kept inside a 40 percent CPU ceiling while the application keeps the rest. The main limit is that it only controls sharing and never makes a query faster, so a badly written query still does the same work, just within its cap. Another tradeoff is that the classifier only runs at connection time, so changes do not affect sessions already connected until they reconnect. You also need to watch each group's real usage to confirm the classifier is routing sessions where you intended.
rubricPoints: Defines workload group, resource pool and classifier function in plain words
Explains that limits apply per group and protect other workloads on a shared server
States that Resource Governor controls resource sharing and does not tune the query itself
Names a real limitation such as the classifier running only at connection time or the feature depending on edition or deployment

suggested.rationale: A scenario where a reporting job starves an application is best reasoned through, choosing the right control and checking its effect, rather than read as a list of settings.

lessons.plain: A database has many dials that control how it runs queries, such as how many processor cores one query may use at once, or which method it uses to estimate how many rows a query will return. Database-scoped configuration means setting those dials for one specific database, rather than for the whole server that hosts many databases. It lets one busy application get its own tuning without changing its neighbours. The skill is knowing which dial to touch, what it changes, and how to check that it actually helped.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your server hosts three databases. Database A runs reports that spread one query across many cores, which slows the other two. Would you change the setting for the whole server or only for Database A, and why?
lessons.teach:
Database-scoped configuration is a set of options that apply to one database rather than to the whole database engine. The engine is the program that stores data and runs queries, and a single server often hosts many databases at once. A server-level setting affects all of them. A database-scoped setting changes behaviour only inside the database where you set it, and the other databases keep their own values.

Why this works: many of the engine's choices, such as how many processor cores one query may use in parallel, or which version of its row-count estimator it follows, suit some workloads better than others. A nightly reporting database and a small transactional database rarely want the same answer. Scoping the change limits the blast radius, so tuning one workload does not quietly alter another.

Worked example. The server default allows up to eight cores per query. Database R runs large nightly reports, and those queries starve other work.
