questions.prompt: A weekly step inserts a daily invoice total row into 5 databases. The step may be retried after a partial failure. Which way of writing the step is safe to run again?
choices: Insert the row each time the step runs, so a retry always leaves at least one copy
Insert the row only if no row for that date already exists, so a repeat run does nothing new
Insert the row twice in each database so the second run can replace the first
Delete all invoice total rows before each insert so duplicates cannot accumulate
questions.why: A retry can apply the same change twice on some databases, so the step should check for an existing row first, making a second run harmless.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Azure SQL elastic jobs are for, when you would choose them over running a script yourself, and one limit or tradeoff they bring.
lessons.modelAnswer: Elastic jobs let us define a T-SQL script once and run it on a managed schedule across a group of Azure SQL databases, such as an elastic pool or a list of databases, without connecting to each one by hand. The job agent stores its definitions and history in a job database, and it uses a stored credential to reach every target. We would pick it over a personal script when the same maintenance has to repeat across many databases and we want per-database results in one place. The tradeoff is that the credential needs rights on every target, and a step that writes data can run twice on some databases if it is retried after a partial failure, so the script should be safe to rerun. We also have to maintain the job agent and job database as their own resources.
rubricPoints: Defines an elastic job as a managed way to run a script across a group of databases on a schedule
Names the job agent, job database, target group and credential as its moving parts
Explains that results are recorded per database so one failure does not hide the rest
States a limit: credentials must cover every target, and retried writes must be safe to repeat

suggested.rationale: A planned SQL lab could let the learner run one script against a simulated group of databases and see per-database results, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: A database task is any routine piece of database work that should happen without someone typing it each time, such as a nightly cleanup, a backup check, or a weekly statistics refresh. Automating it means writing down what should run, when, and where, and letting a tool run it reliably. Different tools fit different jobs. Some live inside the database server and run on its own clock. Others sit outside and reach many databases at once. Some do not run data work at all and instead build the infrastructure the database lives on. Choosing the right one is the core skill here.
lessons.guessPrompt: You need to delete rows older than 90 days from the same table in 200 separate customer databases every night. Before reading on, which would you reach for first: a job inside one database server, a scheduler that reaches across many databases, or a template that builds servers? Why?
lessons.teach:
A database task is a unit of database work that runs without a person starting it, such as purging old rows, verifying a backup, or rebuilding an index. Automation means defining the task once and letting a scheduler run it on a timer or in response to an event. The first question is where the work runs and how far it must reach.

SQL Server Agent is a scheduler that lives inside a SQL Server instance. A job is a named set of steps, each step runs T-SQL or another command, and the job runs on a schedule. SQL Server Agent is available on SQL Server on Azure virtual machines and on Azure SQL Managed Instance. Azure SQL Database does not include it.

Elastic jobs are the Azure SQL Database mechanism for work that spans many databases. A job agent is a managed scheduler resource. You point it at a target group of databases, and the same script runs against each one. A single-database scheduler cannot reach the others, which is why this exists.

ARM templates and Bicep files are different in kind. They are declarative descriptions of Azure resources, such as a server, a database, or a job agent with its settings, and deploying them creates or changes that infrastructure. They do not run a purge or a backup on a schedule. Using them as the mechanism for a recurring data task is a category mistake.

Worked example. Requirement: every night, delete rows older than 90 days in 200 customer databases on one logical server. Step 1: the work is recurring and must repeat across many databases. Step 2: Azure SQL Database has no Agent, so an in-server job cannot cover this. Step 3: a job agent with a target group containing all 200 databases runs the same delete step each night. The answer is elastic jobs.

The common mistake is choosing a template because it sounds like automation. It provisions resources but does not run recurring work. The consequence matters: an elastic job runs one script against every target, so a wrong target group or a missing retention check removes data in all of them at once. Target scope and the script must be reviewed before the schedule is turned on. Matching the tool to where the work runs and how far it must reach is what this objective tests.

questions.prompt: A retailer runs one Azure SQL Managed Instance, which is a managed server that hosts several databases and includes SQL Server Agent, the scheduler that lives inside a SQL Server instance. It has four databases. Each night, old rows must be purged from one of them, Orders_Archive. Step 1: the work is recurring and touches only databases on this one instance. Step 2: Managed Instance includes SQL Server Agent, so an in-instance job can run the purge. Step 3: [missing]. Which action completes the setup?
choices: Deploy a Bicep file whose properties include the nightly purge so the instance runs it.
Create an elastic job agent whose target group contains the four databases.
Run the purge once by hand and rely on the instance to repeat it.
Create a SQL Server Agent job on the instance with a T-SQL purge step and a nightly schedule.
questions.why: The missing step is creating the Agent job itself, with the purge as a T-SQL step and a nightly schedule, because that is the scheduler that lives inside this instance.

questions.prompt: A company runs 15 Azure SQL Database databases on one logical server and wants a weekly script that purges old rows from all 15. Which automation tool fits best?
choices: An ARM template whose settings include the purge script
A Bicep file deployed on a weekly timer to run the purge
SQL Server Agent job created on the logical server
An elastic job agent with a target group containing the 15 databases
questions.why: Elastic jobs are the mechanism for recurring work that spans many Azure SQL Database databases, and a job agent with a target group runs the same script against each one, while the other options either are unavailable or only describe infrastructure.

questions.prompt: A team wants each quarter to provision a new SQL Server on an Azure virtual machine along with its settings, so the environment is recreated the same way every time. Which tool matches this need?
choices: SQL Server Agent, scheduled to create the virtual machine
Elastic jobs, targeting the new virtual machine
A single-database scheduler inside the existing server
Bicep or an ARM template, deployed on the quarterly schedule
questions.why: ARM templates and Bicep files are declarative descriptions of Azure resources and their settings, and deploying them creates or changes infrastructure, so they match provisioning, while the other tools run database work rather than create resources.

questions.prompt: A developer sets up an elastic job to delete rows older than a retention period. The target group accidentally includes a production database, and the script has no retention check. What should have happened before the schedule was turned on?
choices: The target group membership and the script should have been reviewed before enabling the schedule.
The job frequency should have been increased so that errors surface sooner.
An ARM template should have been used to lock the job so it cannot run against production.
The schedule should have been enabled first so the job logs could reveal the problem.
questions.why: An elastic job runs one script against every target, so reviewing target scope and the script before enabling the schedule is the control that prevents mass data removal.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate suggests putting a Bicep file in the repository to run the nightly cleanup across our customer databases. Explain to them, in your own words, which tool fits the cleanup, why the Bicep idea does not work for it, and one limit or tradeoff of the tool you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: Bicep is a declarative language for describing Azure resources, so it is good at creating a server, a database, or an elastic job agent with the right settings. It does not run a delete statement on a schedule, so it cannot do the cleanup itself. The nightly purge is recurring T-SQL work across many databases, which fits elastic jobs. We create a job agent, put the 200 databases into a target group, and schedule the purge step against that group. The tradeoff is scope. The job runs the same script everywhere it targets, so a wrong group or a missing retention check removes data in all of them at once. We should dry-run the script against one test database, confirm the target group membership, and keep the retention condition in code review before enabling the schedule. Bicep can still deploy the job agent itself, so the two tools cooperate rather than compete.
rubricPoints: Bicep or ARM describes and deploys resources; it does not execute recurring data work.
Elastic jobs run one script on a schedule across a target group of many Azure SQL databases.
Names a real limit: one script runs against every target, so scope and the script need review before scheduling.
Notes that the tools can cooperate, for example a template provisioning the job agent that runs the task.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right tool from a realistic recurring requirement is best practised by reasoning through a situation, and no listed mission covers it directly.

lessons.plain: An alert is a rule that watches something about a database, such as CPU use, storage filling up, or a job failing, and sends a message when a condition is met. A notification is that message, delivered to the people or systems that need to act, by email, text, or a call to another tool. Think of a smoke detector wired to a phone: the detector decides when something is wrong, and the wiring decides who hears about it. Setting this up well means choosing the right signal, a threshold that means something, and a destination that someone actually watches. Without it, problems are discovered when users complain instead of when the team is told.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly backup job on a database fails at 2 a.m., and nobody is told until a customer complains the next morning. What single piece of setup would have prevented that delay, and what would you need to decide before setting it up?
lessons.teach:
A metric is a number measured over time, such as CPU percentage, storage used, or failed connections. A threshold is the value a metric must cross to count as a problem. An alert rule combines a signal, a condition, and a time window. A notification target is where the message goes. In Azure Monitor, the Microsoft monitoring service, that target list is called an action group. On SQL Server instances, the equivalent idea is an operator, a named person or address that receives job and error messages.

Why it works: the monitoring service evaluates the signal on a schedule. When the condition holds across the time window, the rule fires and sends a message to each target. The time window stops a single noisy sample from paging someone.

Worked example: a managed database's CPU is sampled every minute. The rule says: fire when the average CPU over 5 minutes is above 80 percent. At 10:00 CPU is 60 percent, so nothing happens. From 10:01 to 10:05 the readings are 85, 90, 88, 84 and 86. Their average is 86.6, which is above 80. The rule fires, and the on-call group receives an email and a text. When the average falls back below 80, the alert resolves.

Common mistake: setting thresholds without thinking about them, or setting up a rule with no reachable destination. Too many messages train people to ignore the channel, and a rule that notifies nobody protects nothing.

Consequence: on a running system, a noisy alert channel means the real outage message gets lost among the false alarms. An alert is only as useful as its threshold and its audience.

questions.prompt: A SQL Server on an Azure VM has its free disk space percentage sampled every 2 minutes. The rule fires when the average free space over a 10-minute window is below 15 percent. Readings from 09:00 to 09:08 are 22, 19, 16, 14 and 13 percent. The window holds 5 samples and their average is 16.8. What is the next step, and what is its result?
choices: The average of 16.8 is below 15, so the rule fires and sends a message to each target.
The rule fires because the latest reading of 13 is below 15, so the average does not matter.
The rule fires only after another 10 minutes pass, regardless of what the readings show.
The average of 16.8 is not below 15, so the condition does not hold and the rule does not fire yet.
questions.why: The condition is judged on the window average, and 16.8 is not below 15, so the rule does not fire at this point.

questions.prompt: In Azure Monitor, what does an action group provide?
choices: The list of targets that receive a message when a rule fires.
The percentage above which a metric counts as a problem.
The metric values that the alert rule samples on each run.
The time window over which the condition is checked.
questions.why: An action group is the named list of notification targets, which the teaching text defines as where the message goes.

questions.prompt: An alert rule has a sensible threshold and time window, but no notification target is attached to it. What is the most likely result?
choices: The rule fires, and the message waits in a queue until a target is added later.
The rule fires, and the monitoring service sends the message to a default administrator automatically.
The rule can fire, yet no one receives the message, so it gives no real protection.
The monitoring service disables the rule until a notification target is attached.
questions.why: A rule with no reachable destination fires without informing anyone, which the teaching text names as a common mistake that protects nothing.

questions.prompt: A VM's CPU is sampled every minute. The rule fires when the average CPU over 5 minutes is above 80 percent. In the latest window, one sample reached 97 percent while the other four were around 55 percent, giving an average of 62 percent. What happens?
choices: The rule fires after the window ends, with each sample checked separately against 80.
The rule does not fire, because the averaged value of 62 is below 80.
The rule fires only if the 97 percent reading repeats in the next window.
The rule fires at once, because a single reading above the threshold is enough.
questions.why: The condition is evaluated on the averaged value across the time window, and 62 is below the 80 percent threshold, so the rule stays quiet.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make sure a failing database job reaches a person, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by defining the failure as a signal. For a job, that is its outcome or a related error. For a resource, it is a metric such as CPU or storage. Then I attach a rule with a threshold and a time window, so it fires on a real problem rather than one noisy sample. The rule points at a notification group that holds the email addresses, phone numbers, or webhook endpoints of the people who act on it. The main tradeoff is sensitivity against noise. A tight threshold catches problems early but produces messages people learn to ignore. A loose one stays quiet until users are already affected. Another limit is that an alert only tells people something happened. It does not fix the cause. I would also test the path by triggering the alert once and confirming the right person actually received it.
rubricPoints: Names a clear signal, such as a job outcome or a metric, that defines the failure
Explains that a threshold and time window stop single noisy readings from firing the alert
Identifies a notification target, such as an action group or operator, and that it must be reachable
States a real tradeoff between early detection and alert noise or fatigue

suggested.rationale: The planned metric alarm builder would let the learner practise choosing a signal, threshold, window, and destination, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: A scheduled database task is a job that runs by itself at set times, such as a nightly backup or a clean-up of old data. Troubleshooting one means finding out why it did not finish, or finished wrongly, when nobody was watching. Usually the clues are already written down: a run history that records each start, end and outcome, plus an error message from the step that broke. The skill is reading that record in order, asking what the job was allowed to do, what it depended on, and when it ran, then changing one thing at a time and checking again. The job fails without anyone at the keyboard, so the written record is the main evidence you have.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job copies yesterday's rows into a reporting table. For a month it succeeded every night. Then it started reporting success, but the reporting table was empty each morning. Before any teaching, which three things would you check first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A scheduled job is a unit of work, such as a script or a set of database steps, that a scheduler starts at fixed times without a person. A job step is one action inside the job. A run history is the log of each execution, with its start time, end time, outcome and any messages. The identity is the account the job runs as, and its permissions decide what it may read and write. A dependency is anything the job needs before it can work, such as another job finishing, a file arriving or a network path being open.

This works because a scheduled job gives you no live feedback. Its only evidence is the run history and the output of each step, so a troubleshooter reads those in order: outcome first, then each step, then the inputs and the account used.

Worked example. A job runs at 02:00 and copies rows from a staging table to a reporting table. Step 1: the run history says Succeeded at 02:00 with zero rows copied. Step 2: the step output shows the copy query ran and matched nothing. Step 3: the staging load is scheduled for 02:30, so at 02:00 the staging table is still empty. The job was not broken; it started before its input existed. The fix is to order the jobs so the load finishes first, or to make the copy wait for it.

Common mistake: trusting a Succeeded status without reading what the step did, then rerunning the job by hand. The rerun may look fine, but the timing problem returns the next night. Another mistake is changing permissions or credentials before checking the error text.

Consequence: the reporting table is stale or empty when dispatchers read it in the morning, so they make decisions on wrong data. Before rerunning any job that writes data, confirm it is safe to run twice, because a repeated copy can duplicate rows.

A successful status only means the scheduler finished the run; it does not prove the work was correct.

questions.prompt: A nightly job at 01:15 exports open invoices from a billing database to a file share for the finance team. Its run history shows Failed at 01:15 with the message: access denied when writing to the share. Until last Monday the job ran under a personal administrator account; that Monday the team switched it to a dedicated service account. Step 1: the outcome is Failed, so the job did not silently succeed. Step 2: the step output shows the export query finished and the failure happens at the file write. Step 3: [missing step]. Only after that step should anyone change the job or rerun it.
choices: Rewrite the export query, since a query that finishes cannot be the cause of a write failure
Rerun the job by hand to see whether the write works this time
Check whether the dedicated service account has write permission on the file share, because the job's identity decides what it may write
Schedule the job to run every ten minutes so it retries sooner
questions.why: The identity the job runs as decides its permissions, and the failure is at the write step right after the identity changed, so checking that account's write permission is the next correct step.

questions.prompt: In a scheduled database job, what is the run history?
choices: The list of steps the job contains, in the order they were written
The set of files or other jobs that must finish before the job can start
The log of each execution, with its start time, end time, outcome and any messages
The account that the job uses to log in to the database
questions.why: The run history is the per-execution log of start time, end time, outcome and messages, while the other options describe steps, the identity, or dependencies.

questions.prompt: A weekly job that rebuilds a summary table shows Succeeded in the scheduler. A colleague proposes rerunning it immediately. What should you check first?
choices: Whether the job's identity has been changed in the last hour
Whether the job's step output shows the rebuild actually wrote the expected rows
Whether the job can be rerun without changing the summary table's contents
Whether the scheduler's clock matches the server's clock
questions.why: A Succeeded status only means the scheduler finished the run, so you should read what the step did, and before any rerun confirm it is safe to run twice; the strongest answer is the one that covers both checks, so choose the option about safe reruns and the actual outcome.

questions.prompt: A job that loads a daily file into a table is scheduled for 03:00, but the file is usually delivered at 03:20. What is the most likely consequence on a running system?
choices: The job fails with a permissions error every night
The job runs, finds the input missing, and downstream readers see an empty or stale table in the morning
The job runs on time, loads the old file, and the table is ready for the morning readers with yesterday's data
The scheduler cancels the job permanently after the first missed dependency
questions.why: The job starts before its dependency, the file, exists, so it does its work on nothing and the downstream table is left empty or stale when people read it.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says a nightly maintenance job 'failed silently' last week. Explain to them, in your own words, how you would troubleshoot it, and name one limit of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the run history, not the job script. I would check the outcome, then each step's output and the exact time of the error, because a job can report success while doing nothing useful. Next I would check what the job depended on: an input that arrived late, a server it could not reach, or a time window that overlapped another job. I would also confirm the account it ran as still had the permissions it needed, and whether any credential had expired. I would change one thing at a time and watch the next scheduled run. The limit is that the record only shows what the job logged. If the job never wrote a useful message, I may need to add logging before I can find the cause, and I should say so rather than guess.
rubricPoints: Start with the run history and step outputs, not a rerun.
Check dependencies and timing such as inputs arriving late or overlapping jobs.
Check the identity, its permissions and any expired credentials.
Name a limit: the troubleshooting is only as good as the logs the job writes.

suggested.rationale: Reading a failing service's logs in order to find the real cause is the same evidence-first habit this objective needs, even though the mission is about an API rather than a database job.

lessons.plain: When a database server fails, two questions decide how you recover. The first is how much recent work you can afford to lose, measured as a length of time. If you can lose five minutes of changes, that is your recovery point target. The second is how long the service can be down before the business is hurt, which is your recovery time target. Choosing a high availability or disaster recovery setup means matching the design to those two numbers, not picking the most impressive option. Cheap designs accept more lost data or longer outages, while expensive ones cost more to run and can slow normal work.
lessons.guessPrompt: A payments database may lose no more than about 30 seconds of committed data, and it must be back within 5 minutes after its primary server dies in one data centre. Before reading on, which would you try first: nightly backups, asynchronous copies to another region, or a synchronous replica in the same region? Say why.
lessons.teach:
Two terms first. The Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is the most data, measured in time, that you are willing to lose: an RPO of 5 minutes means that after recovery, the newest surviving change may be up to 5 minutes older than the failure. The Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is the longest acceptable time for the service to be unavailable after a failure. The business sets these targets, and the technical design is chosen to meet them.

The main options differ in how they copy data. Synchronous replication waits until a second copy has the change before confirming the write to the application, so RPO is near zero, but every write pays a latency cost and the copy must be close enough to keep that cost low. Asynchronous replication confirms writes immediately and ships changes behind, so a failover can lose changes still in transit: RPO roughly equals the typical replication lag. Log shipping sends transaction log backups on a schedule, so RPO is about the backup interval, and recovery usually needs a manual restore, which pushes RTO up. Backups alone give an RPO equal to the time since the last backup and an RTO equal to the restore duration.

Worked example: RPO 30 seconds, RTO 5 minutes, same-region failure. Step 1: log shipping every 15 minutes fails the RPO, because up to 15 minutes could be lost. Step 2: asynchronous replication to a distant region usually keeps lag within seconds, which meets the RPO, but a manual failover may take longer than 5 minutes. Step 3: a synchronous replica in the same region meets both targets with fast automatic failover, which points to a high availability design. A regional disaster still needs a separate copy elsewhere.

Common mistake: treating a replica as a backup. Replicas copy a bad delete or corruption almost instantly, so they do not replace point-in-time backups.

In a running system, a failover that loses 40 seconds of acknowledged orders means the application must reconcile them, and that is the real cost of a missed RPO.

questions.prompt: A small ticketing company has a Recovery Point Objective (RPO, the most data in time it can afford to lose) of 2 minutes and a Recovery Time Objective (RTO, the longest acceptable outage) of 10 minutes for a failure inside one region. Its current design takes one full backup a week. Step 1: weekly backups are rejected, because up to seven days of bookings could be lost. Step 2: log shipping, which copies transaction log backups on a schedule, runs every 1 minute and keeps the RPO near 1 minute, but recovery is a manual restore that may take longer than 10 minutes under pressure. Step 3 is missing. Which conclusion completes the analysis?
choices: Move to an asynchronous replica in a distant region, because distant copies always give the fastest failover.
Keep log shipping and shorten the full backup to once a day, since the restore step will then be faster.
Add longer backup retention, because keeping more backups lowers the RPO.
Use a synchronous replica in the same region with automatic failover, because it meets both targets for a same-region failure.
questions.why: A synchronous replica in the same region confirms each write only after a second copy has it, giving near-zero RPO, and automatic failover keeps RTO within 10 minutes for a same-region failure.

questions.prompt: A reporting team says their RTO is 4 hours. Which statement describes this correctly?
choices: The average time between scheduled backups.
The delay between a primary write and its arrival on a secondary.
The most data, measured in time, that may be lost after a failure.
The longest acceptable time the service may be unavailable after a failure.
questions.why: RTO is the longest acceptable outage after a failure, while the data-loss limit is the RPO and the other two options describe backup or replication timing.

questions.prompt: An asynchronous replica typically runs 800 milliseconds behind the primary. A failover happens at a moment when 3 seconds of committed orders have not yet reached the replica. Which statement best describes the impact?
choices: Nothing is lost, since the replica replays missing changes when it restarts.
Only about 800 milliseconds is lost, because the typical lag is the upper bound.
The 3 seconds of orders not yet shipped can be lost and must be reconciled.
Nothing is lost, since asynchronous replication confirms writes only after the copy has them.
questions.why: Asynchronous replication confirms writes before the copy receives them, so changes still in transit at failover can be lost, and the lag at that moment sets the loss rather than the typical figure.

questions.prompt: A team uses a continuously synced secondary as their only backup. A developer runs a DELETE on the wrong table at 10:00, and the secondary applies it within seconds. What is the problem?
choices: The secondary copied the bad delete almost at once, so the rows cannot be recovered without a point-in-time backup.
Replicas never apply deletes, so the lost rows are still on the secondary.
The secondary is too far behind to apply the delete, so the data is still safe.
The only problem is RTO, because the restore from the secondary takes too long.
questions.why: Replicas copy changes, including harmful ones, almost immediately, so only a point-in-time backup from before 10:00 can restore the deleted rows.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should use geo-replication for everything because it gives us a disaster copy. Explain to them how you would choose between high availability and disaster recovery options for a given RPO and RTO, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the two numbers, not the product. RPO tells me how much recent data we can lose, and RTO tells me how long we can be down. Then I ask what failure we are protecting against. A server or zone failure needs high availability: a synchronous replica close by gives near-zero data loss and fast automatic failover, but it does not help if the whole region goes down. A regional disaster needs a copy in another region, which is usually asynchronous, so there is lag and a failover can lose changes not yet shipped; the RPO is about that lag. Geo-replication is reasonable for DR if the lag fits the RPO, but a manual failover may exceed a short RTO, so I would check whether an automatic failover arrangement is needed. The tradeoff I would name is that synchronous copies slow every write, and cross-region copies can lose data at failover.
rubricPoints: RPO is the maximum tolerable data loss in time and RTO is the maximum tolerable downtime
Synchronous replication gives near-zero RPO but adds write latency and limits distance
Asynchronous or log-based copies lose data equal to their lag or backup interval
High availability covers local failures, while disaster recovery needs a separate region or copy
Replicas are not backups and do not protect against logical errors

suggested.rationale: The dr-planner engine would let the learner enter RPO and RTO targets and test which HA/DR option fits, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: A hybrid deployment means part of your system runs in your own data centre and part runs in the cloud. Evaluating high availability and disaster recovery (HA/DR) for it means asking whether the database can keep working when a server, a whole site, or the link between them fails, and how much data and time you could lose doing so. The hard part is that the two halves depend on each other. A copy of the data that crosses a slow or unreliable network, a failover that needs the office network to answer, or a decision-maker placed on the wrong side can each break the plan. You judge any option by where each copy lives, how it reaches the other side, and what still works when one side goes dark.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your database's only live copy is on a server in your office, and the web tier runs in the cloud. The office internet link fails for two hours. What can the cloud web tier still do, and what single change would most reduce the risk of that outage?
lessons.teach: Hybrid means some of the system runs on your own hardware and some runs in Azure, joined by a network link. High availability (HA) keeps a database running through a local failure, such as one server crashing, usually automatically and quickly. Disaster recovery (DR) gets service back after a larger loss, such as a whole site going dark, and usually accepts more downtime. Two numbers frame every choice. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data, measured in time, you can afford to lose. The recovery time objective (RTO) is the longest you can afford to be down. A replica is a second copy of the database kept up to date. Synchronous replication waits for the copy to confirm each write before reporting success, so little or nothing is lost, but every write pays the network delay. Asynchronous replication reports success first and sends changes afterward, so it is fast but the copy can lag behind. A failover switches service to the copy. A quorum is the majority vote that decides which side may act as primary, and a witness is an extra voter that breaks ties. Worked example: the primary is on-premises, an asynchronous replica sits in Azure, and at 10:00:00 the office link drops while the replica is 8 seconds behind. Step one: those 8 seconds of committed changes never reached Azure. Step two: if you fail over to Azure, they are lost, so the real RPO for this event is 8 seconds. Step three: 8 seconds was measured on a quiet afternoon, so the true worst case under peak load is larger, and you must test at peak. Common mistake: judging RPO from average lag, and forgetting that the witness or quorum voter sits on the side that fails. Consequence: if the office goes dark and the Azure side cannot form a majority, the healthy copy stays fenced off, and your RTO grows from minutes to however long a person takes to intervene.

questions.prompt: A ticketing firm runs its primary SQL database in its own data centre and keeps an asynchronous replica in Azure, reached over one internet VPN. Step 1: at 14:00 the data centre loses power. The replica was 3 seconds behind at 02:00 but 22 seconds behind at 14:00 under peak sales load. Step 2: the 22 seconds of committed orders that never reached Azure would be lost by a failover, so the RPO for this event is 22 seconds. Step 3 is missing. Before the team signs off its RPO target, it should do which of these?
choices: Quote the 3-second overnight figure as the RPO, because it is the lowest measured lag.
Test the failover at peak load and set the RPO against the worst observed peak lag, not the quiet-hours figure.
Average the 3-second and 22-second readings to 12.5 seconds, since average lag is the fairest measure.
Move the witness into Azure so that it cannot be cut off along with the data centre.
questions.why: The true RPO must be judged from the worst peak lag, because quiet-hours or averaged lag understates the data that could be lost when the link fails under load.

questions.prompt: A regional bank keeps its primary database on premises and an asynchronous replica in Azure. Which measure tells you the most committed data you could lose on a failover?
choices: The lag at the moment of failure, measured under peak load
The number of votes the Azure side holds in the quorum
The recovery time objective, meaning how long the bank can be down
The replica's average lag over the past month
questions.why: RPO is the most data you can lose, and for an asynchronous replica that is the lag present at the moment of failure, judged at peak rather than on average.

questions.prompt: A county government stores its primary database on premises and places the witness voter in the same building. The building loses its network link to Azure. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The Azure replica is promoted at once with no delay and no data loss.
The RPO automatically drops to the average lag of the previous day.
The Azure side may be unable to form a majority, so the healthy copy stays fenced off and recovery waits for a person to intervene.
Writes switch to synchronous replication so the RPO becomes zero.
questions.why: The witness sits on the failing side, so the surviving Azure side may lack the majority it needs to act, which stretches RTO from minutes to however long manual intervention takes.

questions.prompt: A retailer needs almost no data loss between its on-premises database and its Azure copy and accepts the network delay on every write. Which replication style fits?
choices: Asynchronous, because it reports success first and is therefore faster
Daily log backups copied to Azure, which avoid any per-write delay
Synchronous, because the copy confirms each write before success is reported
Asynchronous with a witness, because the witness stores the changes
questions.why: Synchronous replication waits for the copy to confirm each write, so little or nothing is lost, and the cost is paid as network delay on every write, which matches the stated trade-off.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would evaluate an HA/DR setup for a database that runs partly on-premises and partly in Azure. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would lean toward.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the two numbers. I would ask how much data we can lose and how long we can be down, then check each option against them. For a hybrid setup I would look at three things: where each copy lives, whether the replication is synchronous or asynchronous, and where the quorum or witness sits. If I lean toward an asynchronous replica in Azure, the tradeoff is that the copy lags, so the data we could lose at failure is the lag at that moment, not the average. Under peak load that lag can be much larger, so I would measure it under peak load before I trust the RPO. I would also confirm that the Azure side can form a majority on its own, because otherwise a healthy copy stays unusable when the office goes dark.
rubricPoints: Ties the choice to both RPO and RTO rather than general resilience
Explains that asynchronous replication means possible data loss equal to the lag at failure
Notes that quorum or witness placement can block failover when one site is lost
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff of the chosen option, such as latency or lag under peak load

suggested.rationale: A planned disaster-recovery planner engine would let the learner set RPO and RTO for a hybrid topology and see which replication and quorum placements meet them, which no current mission covers.

lessons.plain: High availability (HA) means a system keeps working when one part fails, usually by switching quickly to a spare. Disaster recovery (DR) means getting back to work after something larger goes wrong, such as a whole data center or region going dark. Cloud vendors offer ready-made options for both, but they differ in how much recent data you can lose and how long service takes to return. Evaluating these options means matching each one to those two limits, not picking the most impressive name.
lessons.guessPrompt: A payments database must lose no more than a few seconds of data if its primary region fails. Would you expect a copy in another region to meet that by default, and why or why not?
lessons.teach: Start with two numbers. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data, measured in time, that the business accepts losing: an RPO of 5 minutes means up to the last five minutes of writes may be lost. The recovery time objective (RTO) is how long the service may be down before it must work again. Every Azure HA/DR option is a trade between cost, how fast it recovers, and how little data it can lose.  Azure options fall into a few families. Zone redundancy keeps copies in separate availability zones (physically separate data centers) inside one region. The copy is synchronous, meaning a commit is confirmed only after the copy has it, so data loss is near zero, but it only protects against a zone failure. Active geo-replication keeps a readable secondary database in another region using asynchronous replication: the primary confirms a write before the secondary has it. RPO is therefore usually seconds but not zero, and failover is a manual action you start per database. Failover groups build on geo-replication for a set of databases, add automatic failover after a grace period, and provide stable listener endpoints so applications do not need connection strings changed. Backups kept in geo-redundant storage protect against regional loss, but a restore takes the longest, so RTO is measured in hours and RPO depends on backup frequency.  Worked example: a ticketing database needs RPO of 1 minute and RTO of 5 minutes across a regional outage. Step 1: restoring from backup misses the RTO because a restore takes far longer. Step 2: a single geo-replica with manual failover can meet the RPO but relies on an operator acting within minutes. Step 3: a failover group with automatic failover fits both, provided the grace period is set so brief blips do not trigger a regional switch.  Common mistake: treating a readable secondary as a backup, or assuming geo-replication means zero data loss. Replication lag means the newest commits can disappear in a failover. Consequence: after an unplanned failover, transactions committed on the primary but not yet shipped are gone unless the business has a reconciliation step to recover them.

questions.prompt: A clinic's scheduling database must lose no committed bookings at all and must keep running through a full regional outage. Step 1: zone redundancy keeps a synchronous copy, so loss is near zero, but it only protects against one availability zone failing, so it does not cover a regional outage. Step 2: active geo-replication covers the whole region, but it is asynchronous, so its RPO is seconds rather than zero. Step 3: [missing]. Which choice completes the reasoning?
choices: Choose zone redundancy after all, because near-zero loss is the same as zero loss for this clinic.
Choose geo-redundant backups, since their RPO can be set to zero by increasing backup frequency.
Conclude that no option described here gives zero loss across a region, so the requirement must be relaxed or a reconciliation step added for any lost commits.
Choose a failover group, because failover groups use synchronous replication across regions.
questions.why: The options described give either synchronous protection within a region or asynchronous protection across regions, so no listed option delivers zero loss across a region, and the requirement has to change or be supported by a reconciliation process.

questions.prompt: A retail company's order database has an RPO of 3 minutes. What does that number mean?
choices: The secondary database must always lag the primary by exactly 3 minutes.
Up to the last 3 minutes of committed writes may be lost in a disaster.
The service must be back online within 3 minutes of an outage.
Backups must be taken every 3 minutes and kept for 3 days.
questions.why: RPO is the maximum amount of recent data, measured in time, that the business accepts losing, so 3 minutes means up to the last 3 minutes of writes may be lost.

questions.prompt: A payments firm runs active geo-replication from a primary in one region to a readable secondary in another. During an unplanned regional outage they fail over and find 40 seconds of confirmed orders missing from the new primary. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Zone redundancy was enabled, which forces writes to be lost across regions.
Asynchronous replication had not yet shipped those commits to the secondary when the primary was lost.
The secondary was configured as a backup, so it discarded writes during failover.
The failover group's grace period was too short, so the orders were deleted.
questions.why: Geo-replication is asynchronous, so the primary confirms writes before the secondary has them, and commits still in transit at the moment of an unplanned failover can be lost unless reconciled.

questions.prompt: A small internal app's database can tolerate losing up to 1 hour of data and must be running again within 4 hours after a regional outage. Which option is the least costly that meets both numbers?
choices: Geo-redundant backups restored in another region.
Zone redundancy inside the primary region.
A failover group with automatic failover and a 30-second grace period.
Active geo-replication with a manual failover for each database.
questions.why: A restore from geo-redundant backups protects against regional loss at the lowest cost, and its multi-hour recovery time fits a 4-hour RTO, while zone redundancy does not cover a regional outage and the replication options cost more than the numbers require.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we can simply turn on geo-replication and call the database highly available. Explain to them what geo-replication does and does not guarantee, naming one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: Geo-replication keeps a second copy of the database in another region, so if the primary region fails we can fail over and keep serving reads and writes. It does not make the database safe from every failure. Replication is asynchronous, so the primary confirms a write before the secondary has it. If the primary dies, the most recent commits that had not yet reached the secondary are lost, which means the RPO is seconds rather than zero. Failover is also not automatic in a plain geo-replica setup, so someone has to decide and trigger it, which adds to the RTO. It also does not replace backups, because a mistaken delete replicates to the secondary too. So before calling it highly available, we should check it against our stated RPO and RTO and decide whether automatic failover, a failover group, or a backup strategy is also needed.
rubricPoints: Explains that geo-replication copies data to another region using asynchronous replication
States that the most recent unreplicated commits can be lost, so RPO is not zero
Notes that failover in a plain setup is manual or delayed, which affects RTO
Points out that replication does not protect against logical errors such as accidental deletes
Connects the choice back to the stated RPO and RTO rather than a general label

suggested.rationale: The dr-planner engine would let the learner test which HA/DR option meets a given RPO and RTO, which is the core judgment this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Testing a disaster-recovery setup means deliberately causing a failure in a safe, planned way and checking that the backup copy takes over as promised, within the time and data-loss limits the business agreed to. Think of a fire drill: nobody trusts that the exits work until people actually walk out through them. A test plan writes down what will be broken, what should happen, how long it should take, who does what, how you will know it worked, and how you will undo the test if it goes wrong. Recovery plans that were never tested often fail in the first real emergency because one step, password, or setting was never checked.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team has a database with a standby copy in another region, and the plan says failover takes ten minutes. Name two things you would want to measure during a test before you trust that ten-minute number, without touching the live system.
lessons.teach:
A disaster-recovery (DR) test is a planned, controlled exercise that proves a standby copy of a system can take over. Failover means switching the work from the primary copy to the standby. Two targets from the business drive the test. The Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is the most recent data you can afford to lose, measured as a time window. The Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is the longest the service may be down. A test plan states, before anything is broken, its acceptance criteria: measured failover time must be at or under the RTO, and the data missing from the new primary must fit inside the RPO.

Why this works: a plan is a prediction, and only a test measures the real numbers, such as how far the standby lags behind and how long applications take to reconnect. A good plan names the scope (usually a non-production copy first), the trigger, the exact start and stop points for the timer, the people and their roles, the evidence to collect, a rollback step, and a stop condition that aborts the test if customers would be harmed.

Worked example. The requirement is an RTO of 15 minutes and an RPO of 5 minutes. First, before the test, the team records the standby's replication lag: 2 minutes. Second, at the agreed time, they trigger failover and start a timer. Third, the service answers again at minute 11, so the RTO check passes. Fourth, they compare the last committed transaction on the old primary with the last one on the new primary and find a 3-minute gap, inside the 5-minute RPO. Fifth, they confirm applications reconnect through their stable endpoint name without a configuration change. Sixth, they fail back and write down every result.

Common mistake: testing with a nearly empty database and an idle system, so the timings look far better than production would be. In a running system, that means during a real regional outage the failover takes longer than the RTO, and the business learns the plan was wrong at the worst possible moment. Untested failover is a guess, not a recovery capability.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union runs a loan-servicing database with an RTO of 20 minutes and an RPO of 2 minutes. Before the test, the team records the standby's replication lag as 45 seconds. Step 1: at 14:00 they trigger a planned failover and start the timer. Step 2: the service answers again at 14:12, so the RTO check passes. Step 3: they confirm applications reconnect through their stable endpoint name with no configuration change. Step 4 is missing. Step 5: they fail back and record every result. Which action belongs in step 4?
choices: Raise the RTO to 30 minutes so the test is easier to pass.
Shut down the old primary before measuring anything so no new writes arrive.
Restart the timer from zero and repeat the failover with a larger database.
Measure the data gap between the old and new primary and check it fits inside the 2-minute RPO.
questions.why: The acceptance criteria require both the time check and the data-loss check, and the data side is measured by comparing the two copies' last committed transactions against the RPO.

questions.prompt: In a DR test plan, what does the Recovery Point Objective (RPO) describe?
choices: The speed at which the standby copy replicates new writes.
The longest time the service may be down after a failure.
The most recent data the business can afford to lose, measured as a time window.
The number of people needed to run the failover.
questions.why: The RPO is the maximum acceptable window of lost data, while the RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime.

questions.prompt: A team's plan sets an RTO of 10 minutes and an RPO of 3 minutes. In the test, the service returns after 12 minutes, and the data gap between the old and new primary is 1 minute. What is the correct test outcome?
choices: Pass, because the data gap is smaller than the RPO.
Pass, because the test finished and every result was recorded.
Pass, because the RTO and RPO are both roughly the same size.
Fail, because the measured downtime exceeds the RTO even though the data gap fits the RPO.
questions.why: Acceptance requires both criteria to hold, so a failover that takes longer than the RTO fails the test regardless of a good data gap.

questions.prompt: A company tests failover only on a small development copy with almost no traffic, then reports that production failover will take 4 minutes. Production is much larger and busier. What is the main problem with this test?
choices: Four minutes is too short a time to be a useful estimate.
The test was not run with a rollback step, which is the only real flaw.
The test ran on an unrealistic copy, so its timings are likely far better than production would achieve.
The development copy should have been named differently from production.
questions.why: A test on an idle, small copy produces optimistic timings, so the predicted failover time cannot be trusted for a busy production system.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never run a DR drill how you would plan a test of a failover setup, and name one limit or tradeoff of the test you would run.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by writing the acceptance criteria before anything is touched: the failover must finish within the RTO, and the data missing afterwards must be within the RPO. Then I would write the test plan: which copy to test on, the exact trigger, when the timer starts and stops, who does what, what evidence we record, how we fail back, and when we stop the test early. I would run it first on a non-production copy with realistic data volume. The main limit is that a test copy will not match production load, so timings and replication lag measured there are optimistic. I would say that explicitly in the report, and I would plan a later, carefully scheduled production drill with a stop condition, because the only proof that matters is the one measured under real conditions.
rubricPoints: Acceptance criteria are defined before the test, tied to RTO and RPO.
The plan covers scope, trigger, timing points, roles, evidence, rollback, and a stop condition.
Test on a non-production copy first, with realistic data volume.
Names a limit such as test load not matching production, and says how that changes the conclusions.

suggested.rationale: The planned disaster-recovery planner engine would let the learner draft a test plan against RTO and RPO targets and check the results, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: A backup is a saved copy of a database that you can go back to if data is lost or damaged. A restore is the act of putting that copy back. Choosing a backup strategy means deciding how often copies are taken, what kinds of copies to take, how long to keep them, and how quickly the data could be rebuilt. Think of a notebook you keep safe: you might copy the whole book once a week and add new pages to a second copy every day, so if something goes wrong you lose at most a day of notes and the rebuild takes a known amount of time. The job is to match those choices to how much work the business can afford to lose and how long it can wait.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a database has only one full backup each night at midnight and fails at 11:55 p.m., roughly how much recent data could be lost, and what single change would reduce that loss?
lessons.teach:
Start with two numbers. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data, measured as a span of time, that the business accepts losing. The recovery time objective (RTO) is the longest the business accepts being down while it recovers. A backup strategy mostly serves the RPO, and the restore process decides whether the RTO is met.

A full backup copies the whole database. A differential backup copies only what has changed since the last full backup. A transaction log backup copies the transaction log, which is the ordered record of every change, and covers only the changes since the previous log backup. Log backups are what shrink the RPO: if you take one every 10 minutes, a failure loses at most about 10 minutes of changes.

Worked example. A database has a full backup on Sunday at midnight, a differential every night at 1 a.m., and a log backup every 10 minutes. The system fails on Thursday at 14:05. To restore, you start from Sunday's full backup, apply Wednesday night's differential, then replay the log backups in order up to the last one, taken at 14:00. The loss is about 5 minutes, so the RPO is met. The restore time depends on how much log must be replayed, so the RTO is a measured quantity, not something you can read off the schedule.

A common mistake is assuming that because backups exist, recovery is planned. Teams often never test a restore, and then discover a gap in the log chain or a restore that takes four hours when the RTO is one hour.

On Azure SQL Database, the service runs full, differential and log backups for you and offers point-in-time restore within a retention window, which creates a new database rather than overwriting the old one. Retention is how many days backups are kept; longer retention costs more storage.

A backup strategy is only as good as its tested restore time measured against its stated RPO and RTO.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic's database has a full backup every Saturday at 22:00, a differential every night at 02:00, and a log backup every 15 minutes. The system fails on Wednesday at 09:40, and the last log backup finished at 09:30. The restore steps are: (1) restore Saturday's full backup; (2) [missing step]; (3) replay the log backups in order up to the one finished at 09:30. Which choice fills step 2?
choices: Apply the Wednesday 02:00 differential, since it is the most recent differential taken before the failure.
Restore the Saturday full backup a second time as a new base, so that the differential can be applied to a clean copy.
Apply the Tuesday 02:00 differential, since it is the most recent differential taken before the Wednesday failure, and then continue.
Apply the Wednesday 09:30 log backup first, then return to the differential so the order of changes is preserved.
questions.why: A differential holds all changes since the last full backup, so the newest differential before the failure (Wednesday 02:00) is the one applied in step 2, before the log replay.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team takes a log backup every 30 minutes. Their system fails at 16:50, and the most recent log backup finished at 16:30. Based on the recovery point objective idea, how much recent change is lost?
choices: About 30 minutes, because that is the full interval between log backups.
About 2 hours, because the restore has to replay the whole day's logs.
About 20 minutes, the span between the last log backup and the failure.
Zero, because the log backup schedule guarantees every change is saved.
questions.why: The loss is the time between the last saved log backup and the failure, which here is 16:30 to 16:50, or about 20 minutes.

questions.prompt: A logistics company states its recovery time objective is 45 minutes. A test restore of its backups took 3 hours and 10 minutes. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: The RTO is met as long as the RPO is under 45 minutes, since the two numbers offset each other.
Nothing needs to change, because the RTO only measures how long the backups take to create.
The backup strategy fails the RTO, so the restore process or the backup design must change.
The RTO is met because the restore finished within the same working day.
questions.why: The RTO is the longest acceptable downtime, and a measured restore of 3 hours 10 minutes exceeds 45 minutes, so the strategy does not meet it.

questions.prompt: A small startup uses Azure SQL Database with 14-day retention. A developer accidentally deletes rows from a table yesterday and wants to recover them using point-in-time restore. What does the service produce?
choices: It copies only the deleted rows back into the original database automatically, with no new database created.
It creates a new database containing the state from the chosen time, leaving the original database in place.
It overwrites the live database with the state from the chosen time, discarding all changes since then.
It creates a new full backup of the current database and stores it, without restoring any earlier state.
questions.why: Point-in-time restore on Azure SQL Database creates a new database from an earlier moment within the retention window, and the original database is not overwritten.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose a database backup strategy from an RPO and an RTO, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the two numbers. The RPO tells me how often log backups must run: if the business accepts losing 15 minutes, log backups need to happen at least about every 15 minutes, because anything since the last log backup is gone after a failure. The RTO tells me whether the restore path is fast enough. A restore starts from a full backup, applies a differential, and then replays logs, and the replay time grows with the amount of log. So I would pick a weekly full backup, daily differentials, and log backups frequent enough to meet the RPO, then measure a real restore against the RTO. The tradeoff is cost and complexity: more frequent logs and longer retention use more storage and more to monitor, and a restore that looks fine on paper can still miss the RTO until it has been tested.
rubricPoints: RPO sets how often log backups must run, because changes since the last log backup are lost on failure.
RTO depends on restore time: the full backup, then the differential, then log replay.
A strategy has to be checked with a real restore, not assumed to work.
Names a tradeoff such as storage cost, retention length, or operational complexity.

suggested.rationale: A planned disaster-recovery planner engine would let the learner set backup frequency against RPO and RTO targets and see whether the restore time fits.

lessons.plain: A database backup is a saved copy of the data, taken at a moment you choose or on a schedule, so you can rebuild the database if it is lost or damaged. Native tools are the backup features built into the database product itself, rather than third-party software. This lesson covers SQL Server, which you can run on a virtual machine you manage or use through Azure's managed database services. The core skill is choosing the right kind of backup and confirming that it can actually be restored. Think of it like keeping photocopies of a filing cabinet: a copy only helps if you can read it back.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a full backup ran on Sunday night and a table was accidentally deleted on Wednesday afternoon. Can Sunday's backup alone bring back everything up to Wednesday afternoon, and what else would you want to have?
lessons.teach:
A full backup copies the whole database. A differential backup copies only what changed since the last full backup. A transaction log backup copies the record of changes made since the previous log backup. The transaction log is the database's ordered journal of every change, and it is what makes recovery to a chosen moment possible. Native tools include SQL Server Management Studio's backup wizard, Azure Data Studio, the sqlcmd command line, and backup statements run directly against the server.

Why it works: the database writes each change to its log before applying it. A full backup plus a chain of later log backups lets you replay history up to any point covered by the chain. A restore therefore needs the full backup, then the newest differential if you have one, then every log backup after that in order.

Worked example: a full backup runs Sunday at 22:00, a differential runs nightly at 22:00, and log backups run every 15 minutes. At Wednesday 14:10 a table is dropped. Step 1: restore Sunday's full backup and leave the database in a state that accepts more restores. Step 2: restore Tuesday's differential, taken at 22:00. Step 3: restore each log backup after that point in sequence, stopping just before 14:10. Step 4: bring the database online.

Common mistake: assuming a backup is good because its job reported success. Backups that are never restored in a test may be incomplete or unusable, and a test restore is the only real proof.

Consequence: without regular log backups, the log keeps growing and recovery can only reach the last full or differential backup, so the potential data loss equals all the time since then. On Azure SQL Database, backups are taken automatically and you configure retention rather than running a manual database backup, while SQL Server on a virtual machine is where you run native backups yourself.

questions.prompt: A parts distributor runs SQL Server on an Azure virtual machine, which means it runs its own native backups. Its full backup runs Friday at 03:00, a differential backup (a copy of only what changed since the last full backup) runs every night at 03:00, and a transaction log backup (a copy of the changes recorded since the previous log backup) runs every 10 minutes. On Tuesday at 09:40 a staff member runs an UPDATE with no WHERE clause, changing every row in the orders table. The team wants the database back as it was at 09:39. Step 1: restore Friday's full backup and leave the database in a state that still accepts more restores. Step 2: restore Monday's differential, taken at 03:00. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: bring the database online.
choices: Restore Sunday's differential, since an older differential covers more of the changes
Restore each log backup taken after Monday at 03:00 in order, stopping just before 09:40
Take a fresh full backup of the damaged database before restoring anything else
Restore only the most recent log backup, since it already holds everything since Friday
questions.why: After the newest differential, every log backup made after that differential must be replayed in order, stopping before the damaging change, so the database returns to 09:39.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes what a transaction log backup copies?
choices: Every change made since the last full backup, regardless of any log backups taken in between
The table definitions and user permissions, but none of the stored rows
Only the changes recorded since the previous log backup
The entire database file, including empty space that has never been used
questions.why: A transaction log backup holds the ordered record of changes since the previous log backup, which is why a chain of them can be replayed to a chosen moment.

questions.prompt: A database has a full backup every Sunday at 22:00. No transaction log backups have ever been scheduled. The server fails on Thursday at 16:00 and the only recoverable copy is the Sunday full backup. Using the principle that recovery can only reach the last full or differential backup without a log chain, what is the most data that could be lost?
choices: About 90 hours, all changes made since Sunday at 22:00
Only the changes made during the most recent full backup run
About 15 minutes, because the default schedule is every 15 minutes
Nothing, because the full backup job reported success every Sunday
questions.why: With no log backups, everything written after the Sunday full backup, which is about 90 hours of changes from Sunday 22:00 to Thursday 16:00, is at risk.

questions.prompt: A database has a full backup on Monday at 00:00, a differential backup on Wednesday at 00:00, and transaction log backups every 15 minutes from Wednesday 00:15 onward. At Thursday 08:00 a bad data load occurs, and the team wants the database restored to 07:50 Thursday. Which restore sequence is correct?
choices: Monday full, then the log backups from Tuesday onward, skipping the differential entirely
Wednesday differential first, then Monday full, then all log backups from Wednesday 00:15 onward
Monday full, then only the latest log backup before 07:50, since it contains all earlier changes
Monday full, then Wednesday differential, then the log backups in order from Wednesday 00:15 up to 07:50
questions.why: A restore starts with the full backup, applies the newest differential, and then replays every later log backup in order, stopping at the chosen time.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a full backup on its own is usually not enough to recover a production database, and name one limit or tradeoff of the backup schedule you would choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: A full backup captures the database as it was at one moment, so anything written after it is lost if you only restore that file. To recover to a point closer to the failure, you need the differential backups and the transaction log backups taken after the full one, restored in order. The main tradeoff is frequency against cost and load. Frequent log backups shrink the window of possible data loss, but they create many more files to store and restore, and each one is another link that must be intact. Less frequent log backups are cheaper to run but leave a bigger gap. The schedule also has to fit the recovery time target, because a long chain takes longer to restore. I would choose the interval from the amount of data we can afford to lose, then test a restore to confirm the chain works.
rubricPoints: A full backup alone can only restore to the moment it was taken.
Differential and transaction log backups must be restored in order after the full backup.
Backup frequency trades data-loss window against storage cost and restore complexity.
A backup is only trustworthy after a test restore.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly backup types, the restore chain and console or product steps, which are best learned by reading the course material rather than a listed mission.

lessons.plain: A database restore is the act of rebuilding a database from a copy you made earlier, called a backup. Think of a backup as a saved game: if the live database is corrupted, deleted, or damaged by a bad change, you load the saved copy to get back to a known good state. Native tools means the database product's own built-in commands and interfaces, rather than a third-party product. Restoring is only useful if you can do it under pressure, in the right order, and with the right options, because a backup you cannot restore is not really a backup.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you have a full copy of a database from last night and a separate set of files recording every change made since then. Before reading any rules, what would you expect to go wrong if you restored only the full copy and skipped the change files, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
Terms first. A full backup is a complete copy of the database as it was at one moment. A differential backup holds only the changes made since the last full backup. A transaction log backup holds the record of changes made since the previous log backup. Together these files form a chain, and a restore is the process of rebuilding the database by replaying that chain in order.

Why it works: the restore engine first recreates the data files from the full backup, then applies the differential or log backups in the order they were taken. Each file must connect to the one before it, so a gap breaks the chain. The option NORECOVERY tells the engine that more files are coming, so the database stays in a restoring state and cannot be used yet. The final file is restored with RECOVERY, which finishes any unfinished transactions and opens the database for use. The option MOVE relocates each logical file to a new physical path, which you need when the target server has different folders from the original.

Worked example: a full backup on Sunday at 00:00, a differential at 12:00, and log backups every 15 minutes after that. To rebuild on a new server, step 1 restores the full backup with NORECOVERY and MOVE for the data and log files. Step 2 restores the differential with NORECOVERY. Step 3 restores each log backup after 12:00 in sequence, all with NORECOVERY. Step 4 restores the last log file with RECOVERY, and the database opens.

Common mistake: using RECOVERY on an earlier file. That closes the chain, so the later files cannot be applied and the changes they hold are lost.

In a running system, the database is unavailable for the entire restore, so the time this takes is your real recovery time, and every application that depends on it fails until it is back. The rule to hold onto is that the chain must stay unbroken, and only the final file gets RECOVERY.

questions.prompt: A clinic booking system called ClinicDB has a full backup taken Monday at 01:00 and transaction log backups every 10 minutes after that. The new server uses different folder paths, so the engineer restores the full backup with NORECOVERY and MOVE for both files. Next, the engineer restores the log backups from 01:10 through 09:40 in order, each with NORECOVERY. The 09:50 log backup is the last file in the chain. Which step completes the rebuild?
choices: Restore the full backup again with RECOVERY so the restoring state is cleared.
Restore the 09:50 log backup with RECOVERY so the engine finishes unfinished transactions and opens the database.
Restore a differential backup taken after 09:40 with RECOVERY, because a differential closes the chain.
Restore the 09:50 log backup with NORECOVERY, then run a separate command to bring the database online.
questions.why: Only the final file in the chain gets RECOVERY, which finishes unfinished transactions and opens the database for use.

questions.prompt: What does the NORECOVERY option do during a native restore?
choices: It opens the database in read-only mode straight away so users can check the data before more files arrive.
It moves the data and log files to new folder paths on the target server.
It keeps the database in a restoring state, signalling that more backup files will follow in the chain.
It deletes the earlier backup files once they have been applied to the database.
questions.why: NORECOVERY tells the restore engine that more files are coming, so the database stays in a restoring state and cannot yet be used.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has a full backup from Friday 18:00, a differential from Sunday 03:00, and log backups every 5 minutes after the differential. Which restore sequence keeps the chain intact?
choices: Restore the Sunday differential first with RECOVERY, then the full backup with NORECOVERY, then the log backups in order.
Restore the full backup with RECOVERY so the database comes online quickly, then apply the differential and every later log file with NORECOVERY so they still attach to the chain.
Full backup with NORECOVERY, differential with NORECOVERY, each later log with NORECOVERY, final log with RECOVERY.
Restore the full backup with NORECOVERY, skip the differential, then restore the logs from Sunday 03:05 onward with RECOVERY on the last one.
questions.why: The chain must be applied in the order taken, with NORECOVERY on every file except the last, which gets RECOVERY.

questions.prompt: An engineer restored the 10:15 log backup of a hospital pharmacy database with RECOVERY, then tries to restore the 10:30 log backup. What is the result?
choices: The 10:30 log applies normally because RECOVERY only pauses the restore for a moment.
The 10:30 log applies, but the database stays read-only until a full backup is restored again.
The 10:30 log cannot be applied because the database is already online and the chain is closed, so changes after 10:15 are lost unless restored another way.

The restore engine reverts the database to the restoring state and then applies the 10:30 log automatically, as long as the file is in the same folder as the earlier backups and the server has enough free disk space for the operation to complete.
questions.why: Once a file is restored with RECOVERY the chain is closed, so later log files cannot be attached and their changes are lost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a restore from a full backup plus log backups must be applied in order, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach compared with copying back a single file.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each backup in the chain records changes that only make sense on top of the one before it. The full backup gives the starting state, the differential or log files add later changes, and each file assumes the previous one has already been applied. If you apply them out of order or skip one, the data can end up inconsistent or missing changes that cannot be recovered. The restore is also done in steps: every file except the last is restored with NORECOVERY so more can follow, and only the last one uses RECOVERY to open the database. The tradeoff is time and complexity. Replaying many log files takes longer than copying back one file, so the restore takes longer and depends on every file in the chain being present and readable. A single missing log file can stop the whole recovery at that point, which is why teams check that the chain is complete before they need it.
rubricPoints: Explains that the backups form a chain applied in order
Explains that NORECOVERY keeps the database restoring until the last file
Names a tradeoff such as longer restore time or dependence on every file in the chain
Notes that a missing or damaged file can block the recovery

suggested.rationale: The planned SQL lab would let a learner practise restore sequencing and recovery options, which a read-only lesson cannot do, though no listed mission covers this objective today.

lessons.plain: Point-in-time restore means rebuilding a database as it looked at a moment you choose, such as just before someone ran a bad delete. The platform or your tools keep regular copies of the data plus a running record of every change, called a transaction log. To go back to a moment, the system starts from an older full copy, replays the recorded changes up to that moment, and stops. The result is a separate new copy of the database, so the live one is left alone while you check what came back. This is what you reach for when the damage is logical, meaning the data is wrong, rather than the server being broken.
lessons.guessPrompt: A script deleted rows at 10:14. It is now 10:40, and you need the data as it was at 10:13. Would you restore over the live database or into a separate new database, and why?
lessons.teach: A point-in-time restore recreates a database as it was at a specific timestamp inside its retention window, which is the span of days during which backups are kept. A full backup is a complete copy of the database. A differential backup holds only the changes made since the last full backup. A transaction log backup holds the ordered record of every committed change, and it is taken every few minutes.
