questions.why: A stale secondary that is promoted loses the changes it never received, so a 4-minute gap means roughly 4 minutes of data is lost, exceeding a 1-minute recovery point objective.

questions.prompt: During an incident, an engineer immediately reseeds a lagging secondary from a fresh copy without first measuring where the lag occurs. What problem does this approach create?
choices: Reseeding can take hours on a large database and can hide the original cause of the lag, so the fault may return.
Reseeding permanently lengthens the recovery point objective by a fixed 24 hours each time it is run.
Reseeding automatically points applications at the wrong region, so writes are sent to the lagging copy.
Reseeding deletes the primary's transaction log, so the primary stops accepting writes until the copy finishes.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that reseeding a large database can take hours and hides the original cause, so measuring first is the safer order.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would troubleshoot a standby copy that has fallen behind the primary, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would separate three questions: is the copy getting the changes, is it applying them fast enough, and can clients reach the right place. For a standby that is a minute behind, I would measure lag on both the primary and the secondary, then check the link carrying the change records. If records arrive but apply slowly, I would look for a long-running query or a busy disk on the secondary. I would not fail over or reseed first, because reseeding a large copy takes a long time and hides the cause. The limit is that lag is a measurement, not a guarantee. A copy with five seconds of lag can still lose those five seconds if it is promoted during an outage, so I would check RPO against the lag I actually see.
rubricPoints: Separates the stages: changes sent, changes received, changes applied.
Measures lag on both primary and secondary before changing anything.
Checks the link and apply-side load, such as long queries or slow storage.
Recognises that observed lag sets real data-loss exposure at failover time.

suggested.rationale: That mission has dispatchers reading a minute-old replica, which practises tracing lag to its cause the same way this objective requires.

scenarios.title: Choosing a managed home and a migration cutover for a shipment-tracking database
scenarios.scenario: Harrowgate Freight Co. is a fictional logistics company. Its shipment-tracking system runs on one SQL Server 2016 instance in the company's own data centre. The main database, called ShipTrack, is 1.6 TB. The team wants to move it to Azure. Some terms first: SQL Server Agent is a built-in scheduler that runs nightly jobs inside the server. A cross-database query joins tables in two databases on the same server in a single statement. Downtime is the time the application cannot write to the database. Requirements: the application depends on SQL Server Agent jobs and on cross-database queries that join ShipTrack to a second database called Billing. The business cannot accept more than about 15 minutes of downtime at cutover, which is the moment users are switched from the old server to the new one. The team also wants Microsoft to handle operating system patching and backups, so they prefer a managed service over a virtual server they patch themselves. The team is comparing three options: Azure SQL Database, which is a fully managed single database or elastic pool; Azure SQL Managed Instance, which is a managed server that keeps most SQL Server engine features and sits inside a private virtual network; and SQL Server on an Azure virtual machine, which is a virtual server you patch yourself. Separately, a table called Scans holds 900 million scan events, most from the last 18 months, and storage costs are high. Your manager has asked you to write the plan. Answer these three sub-tasks: 1. Recommend one of the three offerings and name the requirement that rules out Azure SQL Database and the requirement that rules out SQL Server on an Azure virtual machine. 2. Choose an offline or an online migration strategy for the cutover and explain how the 15-minute downtime limit drives your choice. 3. Recommend a way to reduce storage for the Scans table, name the approach (table partitioning, data compression, or both), and explain why it fits the data.
subParts: Recommend an offering and name the two rule-out requirements
Choose offline or online migration and link it to the 15-minute limit
Reduce Scans table storage with partitioning or compression
modelAnswer: Recommend Azure SQL Managed Instance. Azure SQL Database is ruled out by the need for SQL Server Agent jobs and cross-database queries, because a single Azure SQL Database does not run that kind of server-level scheduler or join across separate databases in the same way. SQL Server on an Azure virtual machine is ruled out by the requirement that Microsoft handle patching and backups, since a virtual server leaves that work with the team. Managed Instance keeps the SQL Server engine features the application needs while still being a managed service.

Choose an online migration. An offline migration stops writes to the source, copies the full 1.6 TB, then starts the target, so downtime equals the full copy and cutover time, which for this size will far exceed 15 minutes. An online migration copies the data first while the source stays in use, then continuously sends changes made during the copy to the target. At cutover only the last small set of changes must be applied and the application is switched, so downtime can stay within the 15-minute limit. The team should still rehearse the cutover and confirm the remaining change backlog is small before the switch.

Use table partitioning and data compression together, with partitions split by month on the scan date. Partitioning divides the table into separate pieces by a key, so each month is stored as its own piece. Compression stores the data in a more compact form. Recent months, which are queried often, can stay in a lightly compressed or uncompressed form, while older monthly partitions get stronger page compression. This reduces storage for the bulk of the 900 million rows without moving recent data. The trade-off is extra CPU work when compressed data is read or written, so the team should measure query speed on the older partitions after the change.

scenarios.title: Clinic Booking Database: Who Sees What
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lane Clinics is a fictional chain of three outpatient clinics. It runs its appointment booking system on Azure SQL Database, a managed cloud database service in which Microsoft handles the server hardware and patching while the customer controls the data and who can access it. The appointments table holds a patient name, a clinic identifier, a phone number, and a card token, which is a stand-in value for a payment card. A compliance review set three requirements. First, staff must sign in with their own company work accounts from Microsoft Entra ID (the cloud identity service that holds company user accounts and groups, formerly called Azure Active Directory) rather than with a shared SQL password. Second, front-desk staff at each clinic may see only their own clinic's rows, and call-centre agents must see phone numbers partly hidden unless their role allows more. Third, the card token must stay unreadable even to database administrators who can query the table during support work. Answer the following. 1. Name the authentication method you would configure, and describe how you would create a database user for a Microsoft Entra group so that members sign in without a separate database password. 2. For the two visibility rules, name the specific control for each (one restricts which rows a user sees, one hides parts of column values), explain which one is a true access boundary and which is only a convenience for honest users, and state the design choice that makes the clinic rule hold. 3. Name the encryption control that keeps the card token unreadable to administrators who have query rights, explain why transparent data encryption alone does not meet this requirement, and state where the key that unlocks the column should be kept.
subParts: Authentication method and creating a user from a Microsoft Entra group
Row-level security versus dynamic data masking, and which is a real boundary
Always Encrypted versus transparent data encryption, and where the key lives
modelAnswer: Configure Microsoft Entra ID authentication on the logical server by setting a Microsoft Entra admin, and choose whether sign-in is Entra-only or mixed, based on policy. Then, connected as that Entra admin, run a CREATE USER statement FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER for the group name. This creates a database user that is linked to the Entra group rather than storing a SQL password in the database. Grant that user only the roles it needs, such as read access on the booking schema, so access follows group membership. Staff are then added or removed by changing the Entra group, not by editing database logins. A common mistake is granting broad roles such as db_owner to the group, which breaks least privilege, the principle of giving each identity only the rights its job needs.

Row-level security (RLS) is a security policy that attaches a filter function to a table so that each query returns only the rows the signed-in user is allowed to see. The database engine enforces it on every query, so it is a true access boundary. Dynamic data masking (DDM) changes how a column value appears in query results, for example showing only the last four digits of a phone number. It does not stop a user with broader rights, or one who can infer values through other queries, from reading the underlying data, so it is a convenience for honest users rather than a security boundary. The clinic rule should use RLS, with a predicate function that compares each row's clinic identifier to the clinic mapped to the signed-in user, for example through a lookup table keyed by user name. The design choice that makes it hold is that the filter function and the security policy are owned by an administrator account, not by the users being restricted, and that no role grants direct table access that would bypass the policy.

Always Encrypted encrypts the card token column on the client side using a column encryption key, which is itself protected by a column master key kept outside the database, typically in Azure Key Vault (a cloud service for storing keys and secrets). The database engine only stores and handles ciphertext, so an administrator with query rights sees scrambled bytes rather than the card token. Transparent data encryption (TDE) encrypts the database files and backups at rest and decrypts pages automatically for anyone who runs a query. It protects against theft of disks or backup files, but not against an administrator who can read the table, so it does not meet this requirement on its own. The column master key should be kept in Azure Key Vault, with access granted only to the application identity that needs to decrypt values, and never stored in the database itself or held by the same administrator account that queries the table.

scenarios.title: Slow order lookups after a Tuesday release at Brightwater Logistics
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Logistics Ltd is a fictional parcel company whose order-tracking data lives in an Azure SQL Database, which is a managed database service where the vendor runs the server hardware and patching for you. After Tuesday's release, the customer portal's order lookup slowed from about 200 milliseconds to several seconds. The overnight import job also sometimes waits for hours. Query Store, a built-in feature that records how long each query ran and which execution plan it used over time, is already turned on for this database. An execution plan is the step-by-step method the database engine chooses to fetch the data. A dynamic management view (DMV) is a built-in system view that shows the live state of the server, such as current sessions and waits. Blocking happens when one session holds a lock, a reservation on rows that stops other sessions from changing them.

You are the database administrator on call. Complete the following.

1. Before anyone changes a setting, name the metric source that lets you compare query duration before and after Tuesday's release, and explain how you would set up the operational baseline it provides.

2. Users report that the import job is stuck. Name the DMV you would query to find which session is blocking which, and state the two or three columns you would read first.

3. Query Store shows that the lookup query switched to a new execution plan on Tuesday. Choose between forcing the older plan through Query Store and waiting for automatic tuning to correct it, justify your choice, and name the database setting you would check to confirm automatic tuning is active.
subParts: Metric source and baseline for the release comparison
Finding the blocking session with a DMV
Plan regression: forcing a plan versus automatic tuning
modelAnswer: Query Store is the right source because it keeps a history of query runtime statistics and the plan each query used, grouped by time interval, so you can compare durations before and after the release without relying on memory. To set up an operational baseline, capture a representative window before Tuesday, such as two weeks of normal daily load, record average duration, CPU use and execution count for the lookup query, and store that snapshot so later readings can be compared against it. A live DMV only shows the present, so it cannot prove what changed.

Query the sys.dm_exec_requests DMV, which lists currently running requests, and read the blocking_session_id column, which names the session that is holding the lock this request is waiting for. Read the session_id, the status, and the wait_type columns next. A non-zero blocking_session_id points to the blocker, and you then look up that blocker in sys.dm_exec_sessions or the request view to see what it is running. Common mistake: looking only at the waiting import job and killing it; the waiting session is usually a victim, and the real fix is to find and address the blocker, such as a long open transaction that was never committed.

Forcing the older plan through Query Store is a targeted, reversible action: you select the good plan ID for the lookup query and the engine uses that plan until you unforce it. Waiting for automatic tuning is less predictable because it depends on the service's own analysis and can take time. For a clear regression after a known release, forcing the last good plan is the more controllable choice, while you then investigate the root cause such as a changed index or statistics. Check that automatic tuning is set to active for the FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN option, since that control is what lets the service revert regressions on its own. Consequence on a live system: forced plans can become stale as data grows, so review them after the next data-load cycle.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Logistics: choosing and checking database automation
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Logistics is a fictional freight company. Its order system runs on one SQL Server instance installed on an Azure virtual machine, which is a rented virtual computer in Microsoft's cloud. The company also has forty small Azure SQL databases, one per customer, that are managed as a group. Priya, a new engineer, has been asked to review the automation. There are three requirements. First, every night at 1 AM the index maintenance on the main order database must run, and the on-call person must receive an email if it fails. Index maintenance means rebuilding or reorganising the lookup structures that make queries fast. Second, every Sunday a cleanup script that deletes old temporary rows must run against all forty customer databases. Third, the staging environment must be rebuilt from a written definition every time, so that a rebuild in another region matches production. A written definition here means a file that describes the Azure resources, which the cloud platform reads and creates for you. Answer the following.
1. Name the tool that fits the nightly maintenance on the virtual machine. Explain how you would set its schedule and its failure email, and where you would look first if the job stopped running.
2. Name the tool that fits the Sunday cleanup across forty databases. Explain why a separate schedule inside each database would be a poor choice.
3. Name the tool that fits the repeatable environment rebuild. Explain how you would check a deployment that failed halfway through.
subParts: Nightly maintenance on the virtual machine: tool, schedule, failure email, and first troubleshooting step
Sunday cleanup across forty databases: tool and why per-database schedules are a poor fit
Repeatable environment rebuild: tool and how to check a failed deployment
modelAnswer: The tool is SQL Server Agent, the scheduler built into SQL Server that runs jobs made of ordered steps. A job here has one step holding the maintenance T-SQL, which is the query language SQL Server uses, and one schedule that runs it daily at 01:00. To send failure emails, create an operator, which is a named contact with an email address, and set the job's notification to email that operator when the job fails. Notification depends on Database Mail, the built-in email feature, so its profile must work first. The most common mistake is configuring the notification but never testing Database Mail, so failures happen silently. The consequence is that broken index maintenance can go unnoticed for many nights and queries slowly degrade. If the job stops running, first check the job history for the step's error message, then confirm the SQL Server Agent service is running and the schedule is enabled.

The right tool is elastic jobs, a managed Azure service that runs T-SQL against a group of Azure SQL databases from one central place. It uses a target group, which is a list of the databases to include, and a job agent database that stores the schedule, the run history, and the results. SQL Server Agent is a poor fit because it runs inside one SQL Server instance and cannot act as a central scheduler for many separate Azure SQL databases. Creating a separate schedule in each of the forty databases is a poor choice because it is hard to keep the forty copies identical. Over time one copy is edited and the others drift apart. The consequence is that one customer database is cleaned differently from the rest, or silently skipped, and nobody notices until a report is wrong.

The tool is an Azure Resource Manager template, which is a declarative file describing the resources to create, written in JSON. Bicep is a shorter, more readable language that compiles to the same Resource Manager format. You deploy either one with Azure CLI, the command-line tool for Azure, or Azure PowerShell, the scripting tool for Azure. To check a failed deployment, open the resource group's deployment history, find the failed deployment, and read the error message for the specific resource that failed. Fix the definition and run it again, because the template describes the end state, so re-running it brings the environment in line. A common mistake is fixing the failed resource by hand in the portal instead of changing the file. This causes configuration drift, meaning the rebuilt environment no longer matches the written definition, and the next rebuild in another region reproduces the wrong setup.

scenarios.title: Harbourline Freight order database: choosing and testing a disaster recovery setup
scenarios.scenario:
Harbourline Freight is a fictional logistics company that runs its order-tracking system on Azure SQL Database, a managed database service in which Microsoft operates the servers, patching and backups, so the team only manages the database itself. The system uses two databases, Orders and Shipments, which must always be failed over together because the application joins them in one transaction flow. The business has set two targets. The Recovery Point Objective (RPO), which is the maximum amount of recent data the company accepts losing in a disaster, is 5 minutes. The Recovery Time Objective (RTO), which is the maximum time the system may be down while recovering, is 30 minutes. The company also needs a read-only copy for its reporting team, so reports do not slow down live orders. A regional outage is the disaster being planned for. Auditors additionally require that full database backups be kept for seven years. You are the new database administrator, and the engineering lead has asked you to handle the following. Answer each numbered sub-task in your own words.

1. Recommend a high availability and disaster recovery configuration for the two databases that meets the 5-minute RPO and 30-minute RTO, and name the specific Azure feature you would use. Explain why it fits better than a plain backup-and-restore approach.

2. Explain how you would keep the application connecting correctly after a failover, and how the reporting team's read-only access should be handled.

3. Describe a testing procedure that proves the recovery design works before a real regional outage, including what you would measure to confirm the RPO and RTO are met.

4. Recommend a backup retention plan that covers the seven-year audit requirement while keeping point-in-time restore available for recent recovery.
subParts: Recommend the HA/DR configuration and feature for the 5-minute RPO and 30-minute RTO
Explain connection handling after failover and read-only reporting access
Describe a testing procedure and what to measure against RPO and RTO
Recommend a backup retention plan for the seven-year audit requirement
modelAnswer: Use an Azure SQL failover group, which is a named group that links the Orders and Shipments databases to a secondary logical server in another Azure region and fails them over together. It relies on active geo-replication underneath, which means each database has a continuously updated copy in the secondary region. Replication is asynchronous, so the secondary is usually only a few seconds behind the primary, which fits a 5-minute RPO. Asynchronous means the primary commits a change without waiting for the secondary to confirm it, so in a sudden outage the most recent few seconds may be lost; this is why the answer should say the RPO is typically met rather than guaranteed. The 30-minute RTO fits because failover is a switch to an already-running copy, not a rebuild from backup. A plain restore from backup would take far longer for a database of meaningful size and could lose up to the time since the last backup, so it does not meet these targets. Automatic failover with a grace period can be configured, but the team should state whether it accepts automatic failover or wants a manual decision.

Use the failover group's listener endpoints rather than the individual server names. A listener is a fixed DNS address that always points at whichever region is currently primary, so the application connection string does not change after failover. There is a read-write listener for the live application and a read-only listener for reads. For reporting, the reporting application connects through the read-only listener, which routes its queries to a readable secondary, so reports do not compete with order traffic on the primary. The common mistake is to hard-code the primary server name in the application, which makes every failover a manual application change and can keep the application pointed at a server that no longer accepts writes. After failover, the old primary becomes the secondary and the listener follows the new primary automatically, so the application needs no edits.

Test in a non-production failover group or with a planned failover during a scheduled maintenance window, with the business informed in advance. Before the test, record the timestamp of the last committed order and the current replication lag, which is visible in the database's replication monitoring views. Trigger a planned failover, then measure the time from the start of failover until the application successfully writes a new order through the read-write listener; this measured duration is the actual recovery time to compare against 30 minutes. Compare the last order present on the new primary with the last order committed before the failover to estimate data loss, and compare that with 5 minutes. Run the reporting queries through the read-only listener and confirm they return data. Then fail back, record results in a runbook, and repeat on a schedule because the replication lag and the application behaviour can change over time. A test that only checks the configuration screen does not prove the RTO or RPO.

Keep two separate retention mechanisms. Point-in-time restore uses the automatic backups that Azure SQL Database takes, and its retention period can be set between 1 and 35 days; choose a value such as 35 days so that recent mistakes like accidental deletes can be undone quickly. This short window is not enough for seven years. For the audit requirement, configure long-term retention, which copies selected full backups to longer-lived storage under a retention policy, for example keeping weekly full backups for seven years and keeping the policy for both databases. Long-term retention is a separate policy and does not extend the point-in-time window. The common mistake is to assume that setting point-in-time restore to its maximum satisfies the seven-year rule; once the automatic backups expire, they are gone, so the long-term policy must be configured explicitly and its restore process tested, because a retained backup that cannot be restored does not satisfy the audit.
